{"mom":"### Introductions, agenda, and project brief
{{p:2}} introduced herself as Sarah, the Project Manager, and said this was the group’s first meeting. The agenda was to get to know one another, complete tool training, discuss the project plan, and share ideas; they had 25 minutes for the meeting. The team was developing a remote control intended to be original and not already available in shops, trendy and appealing to a wide market, but not made as a block of metal. It should be user-friendly for everyone from children to older people, and perhaps even dogs. {{p:2}} outlined three design stages: functional design, to identify the product’s needs, effects, and how it would achieve them; conceptual design, to develop the idea; and detailed design, to work out how to put it into practice.

### Animal-drawing exercise
{{p:2}} invited the group to draw favorite animals on the whiteboard and describe their characteristics, beginning with a tiger. {{p:2}} described the tiger as majestic, independent, and proud. {{p:1}} drew a seated dog and identified its qualities as supportive, a best friend that does not discriminate, loyal, and intuitive—able to distinguish a thief from another person. {{p:3}} then drew an animal that changed in interpretation as the drawing developed: it began as an attempted T. Rex, became a pelican, and could be a crocodile. {{p:3}} described it as scary and strong. {{p:4}} drew an eagle, initially struggled to make the picture resemble the intended animal, and described eagles as independent, free-spirited, flying around doing their own thing, birds of prey, and intrepid. The group joked about whether eagles were good at golf; {{p:3}} clarified that the animal was an eagle.

### Price, costs, profit, and target market
{{p:2}} said the proposed selling price was 25 euros and asked for its approximate value in pounds. Participants estimated about £17, with {{p:1}} suggesting roughly 1.4 euros to a pound; {{p:2}} remarked that £17 seemed expensive. {{p:3}} noted that remote controls already on the market cost about £20, so the team would need to buy one. {{p:4}} raised the question of whether to undercut the price or risk making the product look like a cheap option. {{p:2}} said production cost was 12.50 and that about half the selling price would be taken up by building the product. The stated profit aim was 50 million euros; when {{p:4}} asked whether that was for the first year, {{p:2}} said she presumed so. The intended market was international, including Australia and America, and the product should be accessible and usable by all age groups rather than focused on business users. {{p:2}} said different languages did not need to be a key design point.

### Remote-control experience and usability
{{p:2}} described a universal remote used with three video devices, a television, and an amplifier. It had to be programmed for each device, but repeatedly lost its signals and needed reprogramming; {{p:2}} thought it might have been a cheap model. Its advantage was replacing the need to keep six separate remotes in front of the user. {{p:4}} said their experience was mostly using the remote supplied with a device for basic functions such as power, volume, and channels, and that the product should remain usable for someone with limited experience of programming remotes. {{p:2}} agreed these were the main functions and said a remote covered in many small buttons and tiny labels could be confusing, especially when searching for a specific control such as teletext.

{{p:1}} and {{p:4}} discussed simplifying the controls with a small LCD display and menus, similar to a mobile phone, so users could browse and navigate more easily without an excessive number of buttons. {{p:2}} suggested keeping the main controls on the front and placing less-used functions—such as sound, options, and recording—in a menu or section that opens up, so the remote would be straightforward to understand at first glance. {{p:4}} asked whether this approach would work for older people. {{p:2}} gave the example of a grandfather who could answer his mobile phone but would not know how to text; {{p:4}} asked whether he could program a remote or would need basic operation only. The group acknowledged that older users might find technology difficult regardless of design. {{p:3}} said the interface should be self-intuitive, with pictures and symbols that make functions clear, as on newer phones. {{p:2}} cautioned that some newer phones with Windows-based operating systems were confusing and described getting lost while trying to use a friend’s phone.

{{p:3}} questioned what quality of screen could be afforded at a selling price of 25 euros and production cost of 12.50 euros, suggesting the display would likely need to be a black-and-white LCD. {{p:4}} proposed an extra button to enlarge the text for older users, like large-print books, and noted that displaying less on the screen would be acceptable if the text remained readable. {{p:2}} suggested a dual-function design: basic buttons for play, volume, and programme functions, plus a menu with clear pictures and symbols for recording and other controls. {{p:4}} also proposed a flip-top remote, with a larger screen visible when the top was flipped open. {{p:2}} raised cost as a concern, while {{p:1}} noted that a flip-top might save space and make the product look less bulky, though it could have cost implications.

### Materials, style, and next steps
{{p:4}} said the remote did not need to be as fashionable or stylish as a mobile phone and could instead use lightweight plastic that was easy to mould and produce. Near the end, {{p:3}} referred to the company website’s emphasis on putting fashion into electronics and suggested the design could still look good in plastic. {{p:4}} clarified that the main point was that metal was not necessary and said plastic would presumably be cheaper. {{p:2}} cited Sky remotes, which are moulded and look different, and Telewest remotes made of silver plastic, which look smarter; the group agreed that style and material were considerations.

{{p:2}} said the team had half an hour before the next meeting and would work individually, then return to coordinate. She said she would prepare another PowerPoint presentation. The meeting was paused, with the group due to meet again in half an hour; {{p:4}} asked whether they should return to their room, and {{p:2}} agreed."}

Notes could be retrieved or put in a shared folder.","mom":"### Introductions, agenda, and project brief
{{p:2}} introduced herself as Sarah, the Project Manager, and said this was the group’s first meeting. The agenda was to get to know one another and feel more comfortable together, complete tool training, discuss the project plan, and share ideas; they had 25 minutes. The team was developing a remote control intended to be original and not already available in shops, trendy and appealing to a wide market, but not made as a block of metal. It should be user-friendly for everyone from children to older people, and perhaps even dogs. {{p:2}} outlined three design stages: functional design, to identify the product’s needs, effects, and how it would achieve them; conceptual design, to develop the idea; and detailed design, to work out how to put it into practice.

### Animal-drawing exercise
{{p:2}} invited the group to draw favorite animals on the whiteboard and describe their characteristics, beginning with a tiger, and said she would leave space for everyone else. {{p:2}} described the tiger as majestic, independent, and proud. {{p:1}} drew a seated dog and identified its qualities as supportive, a best friend that does not discriminate, loyal, and intuitive—able to distinguish a thief from another person. {{p:3}} then drew an animal that changed in interpretation as the drawing developed: it began as an attempted T. Rex, became a pelican, and could be a crocodile. {{p:3}} described it as scary and strong. {{p:4}} drew an eagle, initially struggled to make the picture resemble the intended animal, and described eagles as independent, free-spirited, flying around doing their own thing, birds of prey, and intrepid. The group joked about whether eagles were good at golf; {{p:3}} clarified that the animal was an eagle.

### Price, costs, profit, and target market
{{p:2}} said the proposed selling price was 25 euros and asked for its approximate value in pounds. Participants estimated about £17, with {{p:1}} suggesting roughly 1.4 euros to a pound; {{p:2}} remarked that £17 seemed expensive. {{p:3}} noted that remote controls already on the market cost about £20, so the team would need to buy one. {{p:4}} raised the question of whether to undercut the price or risk making the product look like a cheap option. {{p:2}} said production cost was 12.50 and that about half the selling price would be taken up by building the product. The stated profit aim was 50 million euros; when {{p:4}} asked whether that was for the first year, {{p:2}} said she presumed so. The intended market was international, including Australia and America, and the product should be accessible and usable by all age groups rather than focused on business users. {{p:2}} said different languages did not need to be a key design point.

### Remote-control experience and usability
{{p:2}} described a universal remote used with three video devices, a television, and an amplifier. It had to be programmed for each device, but repeatedly lost its signals and needed reprogramming; {{p:2}} thought it might have been a cheap model. Its advantage was replacing the need to keep six separate remotes in front of the user. {{p:4}} said their experience was mostly using the remote supplied with a device for basic functions such as power, volume, and channels, and that the product should remain usable for someone with limited experience programming remotes. {{p:2}} agreed these were the main functions and said a remote covered in many small buttons and tiny labels could be confusing, especially when searching for a specific control such as teletext.

{{p:1}} and {{p:4}} discussed simplifying the controls with a small LCD display and menus, similar to a mobile phone, so users could browse and navigate more easily without an excessive number of buttons. {{p:2}} suggested keeping the main controls on the front and placing less-used functions—such as sound, options, and recording—in a menu or section that opens up, so the remote would be straightforward to understand at first glance. {{p:4}} asked whether this approach would work for older people. {{p:2}} gave the example of a grandfather who could answer his mobile phone but would not know how to text; {{p:4}} asked whether he could program a remote or would need basic operation only. The group acknowledged that older users might find technology difficult regardless of design. {{p:3}} said the interface should be self-intuitive, with pictures and symbols that make functions clear, as on newer phones. {{p:2}} cautioned that some newer phones with Windows-based operating systems were confusing and described getting lost while trying to use a friend’s phone.

{{p:3}} questioned what quality of screen could be afforded at a selling price of 25 euros and production cost of 12.50 euros, suggesting the display would likely need to be a black-and-white LCD. {{p:4}} proposed an extra button to enlarge the text for older users, like large-print books, and noted that displaying less on the screen would be acceptable if the text remained readable. {{p:2}} suggested a dual-function design: basic buttons for play, volume, and programme functions, plus a menu with clear pictures and symbols for recording and other controls. {{p:4}} also proposed a flip-top remote, with a larger screen visible when the top was flipped open. {{p:2}} raised cost as a concern, while {{p:1}} noted that a flip-top might save space and make the product look less bulky, though it could have cost implications.

### Materials, style, and next steps
{{p:4}} said the remote did not need to be as fashionable or stylish as a mobile phone and could instead use lightweight plastic that was easy to mould and produce. {{p:3}} referred to the company website’s emphasis on putting fashion into electronics and suggested the design could still look good in plastic. {{p:4}} clarified that the main point was that metal was not necessary and said plastic would presumably be cheaper. {{p:2}} cited Sky remotes, which are moulded and look different, and Telewest remotes made of silver plastic, which look smarter; the group agreed that style and material were considerations.

{{p:2}} said the team had half an hour before the next meeting and that everyone would work individually, then return to coordinate. She said she would prepare another PowerPoint presentation. The meeting was paused, with the group due to meet again in half an hour; {{p:4}} asked whether they should return to their room, and {{p:2}} agreed. {"title":"ES2004b Remote-Control Design and Requirements","summary":"{{p:2}} opened the second meeting by reviewing prior decisions: a universal handset for TV and video equipment, accessible across a wide age range, reflecting the company’s fashionable electronics image while remaining uncluttered and affordable, with a flip-open design and an electronic panel for additional functions. {{p:3}} proposed a compact, low-cost infrared remote with a range of about five metres, noting that AAA batteries make existing controls bulky and that battery choice and power consumption still needed consideration; the basic circuit was preliminary, and the team discussed ways to prevent the handset from getting lost. {{p:1}} and {{p:2}} developed a simple, user-friendly flip-top concept with frequently used controls readily available and less-used functions inside; research indicated that users often leave 30–40% of buttons unused, and {{p:1}} referred to potential production at 50 million units for economies of scale. {{p:4}} presented usability-lab research involving 100 people—male and female participants aged 15 and over: 75% found most remotes ugly, 80% would pay more for a fancier-looking one, 75% channel-hopped, 50% used only 10% of the buttons, 50% were frustrated by losing the remote, and 34% said learning to use one took too long; slightly more than a quarter reported repetitive-strain concerns, while most respondents under 35 wanted an LCD and speech recognition, preferences that diminished in older groups. The updated requirements excluded teletext and specified a TV control, with video use discussed as an implication; the group also considered Videoplus as a way to simplify recording, a lost-remote alert, rechargeable batteries with a docking station, varied exterior designs for different markets, and a distinctive corporate identity, while agreeing the internal engineering design should remain the same. Repetitive-strain mitigation remained unresolved, speech recognition was considered expensive, and the group discussed targeting a mid-range business-class market and offering accessible instructions and customer support; {{p:4}} was asked to research instruction manuals before the next meeting, and the meeting ended around lunchtime with further questions to be emailed to {{p:2}}."}

{"mom":"### Review of previous meeting and agenda
{{p:2}} said this was the second meeting and that they might be somewhat disorganized. They reviewed the previous decisions: a universal control, one handset for all television and video equipment; accessibility to a wide range of consumers and ages; reflecting the company’s image by combining fashion with electronics; keeping the product uncluttered and unthreatening while balancing the budget with the desired appearance; and considering a flip-open design, a smaller control, and an electronic panel for additional features such as programming. {{p:2}} invited {{p:4}} to present first, but {{p:4}} asked to postpone until later to obtain more information. {{p:3}} then presented the working design, followed by {{p:1}} and then {{p:4}}.

### Industrial design concept and technical requirements
{{p:3}} described the product as a device that sends signals to change the state of a television or another appliance, including power, channel, and volume. They had reviewed other products for inspiration, while noting that the design should stand out. Most controls use infrared, which {{p:3}} said was presumably due to cost and the small amount of information transmitted. They noted that most controls use batteries, often AAA batteries, which contribute to bulky designs; smaller batteries could reduce size, subject to power-consumption and data-transmission needs. The control should be small and easy to carry, but not so easy to lose; {{p:3}} suggested considering a way to prevent it slipping down the side of a sofa, a concern {{p:4}} said had also appeared in market research. The proposed components included a power source, a chip to decode user input and convert it to an infrared signal, and a user interface. The sketch was not a verified circuit, and {{p:3}} was unsure whether it would work or whether the wiring was correct. They said the system would need to conform to the communication format used by televisions, which use infrared. The wireless range was estimated at about five metres, considered adequate for most television viewers. Components should be low-cost to support a wide audience, and the product should differ enough from alternatives to attract customers.

### User interface and form
{{p:1}} said the purpose was to simplify interaction with the television and make the product user-friendly rather than burden it with many complex buttons. They proposed a flip-top design: frequently used functions on top, with more complex functions, such as programming favourite channels, inside the middle section. This could serve a broad audience while allowing additional features such as a shock-proof body. {{p:1}} reported that many users prefer simple controls and may leave 30–40 percent of buttons unused even after a year of use. They also mentioned the team’s discussion of production at 50 million units, which could achieve economies of scale, lower costs, and make additional features more affordable. {{p:1}} suggested a trendy flip-top design and examining whether the buttons should be soft or firm, since buttons can become hard with continued use. The overall aim was a simple, user-friendly design.

{{p:1}} described a Nokia design from about six or seven years earlier: a flat, box-like control could strain the thumb because it sits raised, while a curved, banana- or boat-like shape would reduce how much the thumb bends. They suggested a smooth, hand-moulded form. {{p:2}} proposed incorporating the company logo and associated imagery into the product’s shape, giving as an example a vague “C” shape that opens like a shell. {{p:1}} preferred placing a logo at a corner rather than shaping the whole product like a shell. {{p:4}} considered the shell-opening flip-top idea attractive, suggesting lightweight plastic that fits in the palm and might reduce repetitive strain by requiring the user to insert a finger between the covers; they also suggested conch- or scallop-shell exterior designs. {{p:2}} proposed interchangeable fascias or casings, like mobile phones, including psychedelic designs for younger people and sleek alternatives. {{p:4}} added that a distinctive, attractive control might be less likely to disappear down a sofa and could be displayed on a mantelpiece. {{p:1}} suggested developing five or six designs and selecting the most appealing as the common design.

### Market research findings
{{p:4}} reported that the company’s usability lab observed 100 members of the general public, male and female, across all age groups from 15 upwards, using remote controls. The overall finding was that users dislike the look and feel of current controls. Seventy-five percent found most controls ugly, and 80 percent said they would spend more for a better-looking control. Seventy-five percent of users channel-hop frequently, which {{p:4}} said had power implications. Fifty percent use only 10 percent of the buttons, suggesting both a design opportunity and a possible way to reduce cost by limiting functions. Half were especially frustrated by controls getting lost, often down the back of a sofa. Thirty-four percent said controls take too long to learn, which {{p:4}} linked to users not bothering with unused functions. Slightly more than a quarter said controls were bad for repetitive strain injury, with small movements potentially causing shoulder and elbow problems.

{{p:4}} said the vast majority of respondents aged 35 and under wanted an LCD and speech recognition, partly to help locate a lost control. They suggested, as an idea not tested in the research, that a lost control might emit a beep periodically or flash. Interest in those features decreased among people aged 35–45 and reversed in older groups. {{p:4}} offered to email additional research details if needed.

### Requirements and product scope
{{p:2}} stated that teletext would not be included because consumers consider it outdated now that the internet is available. The control was specified for television only, rather than as a universal combined control, which {{p:2}} said would reduce cost and make it easier for consumers to understand. The group discussed whether the control could also operate video equipment: {{p:4}} asked whether video programming was possible, and {{p:2}} said the requirement specified television only, although some Sky functions might be incorporated. {{p:3}} noted that a Sky box can record directly from the television to its hard drive. {{p:2}} understood that play, stop, and programming functions would still be needed.

{{p:4}} asked whether market research had examined demand for a combined control. {{p:4}} said it had not, but recalled the finding that most people use only 10 percent of buttons; those are generally basic channel-hopping and video on/off or fast-forward functions. They added that programming video recorders is widely considered a nightmare. {{p:3}} said speech recognition would probably be expensive to incorporate and was not very good. {{p:4}} clarified that the research table combined responses to two questions: whether respondents preferred a multifunction remote with an LCD and whether they would pay more for speech recognition. Responses varied across age groups, with many older respondents saying they did not know, which {{p:4}} attributed to general fear of new technology.

### Lost-control solutions and budget
{{p:3}} suggested a whistle-activated key fob that makes a loud noise to help locate a lost control. {{p:2}} emphasized that the budget was externally constrained and proposed a cheaper alternative: a unit on the television with a button that makes the remote beep. {{p:2}} considered this cheaper than adding speech recognition and said the finding function should address the problem of losing the control. {{p:4}} endorsed the television-button idea. Later, {{p:3}} suggested combining a beeper with a rechargeable battery arrangement.

### Target markets, design variations, and ergonomics
{{p:2}} said the corporate image should be incorporated into the handset through a logo and a fashionable, trendy appearance, reflecting research that people would pay more for a good-looking product. {{p:4}} said further research would be needed to establish what is attractive to different ages and international markets, contrasting a 15-year-old with someone aged 60, a trendy New Yorker with a retired South African, and noting that preferences vary around the world. The engineering design could stay the same while the interface and fashionable appearance change for different markets. {{p:1}} asked whether the team meant one model or five or six designs. {{p:3}} said the internal design could remain identical while the exterior differed; {{p:1}} agreed that features could stay the same while the body looked slightly different.

{{p:3}} raised ergonomics, citing the Xbox controller, for which two sizes were made because the original was too large for users in Japan; they said Japanese people generally have smaller hands and proposed varying button or controller sizes by country. {{p:1}} suggested a slightly larger model for the United States and a smaller one for Japan. {{p:2}} argued for designing one product first and letting the company adapt its size or features, while keeping the internal engineering design the same, rather than letting the team become bogged down in many possibilities. {{p:4}} cautioned that a small touch screen might not sufficiently address repetitive strain injury, since RSI is caused by repetitive small movements; they said this remained an open question that might need to be postponed to a future meeting. {{p:2}} and {{p:3}} discussed speech recognition as a possible way to avoid repetitive movement, but {{p:2}} said it was extremely expensive.

{{p:4}} asked whether the team should initially focus on a younger age group and broaden the market later, rather than target everyone immediately. {{p:1}} suggested focusing on the biggest market, mentioning people aged 20–35. {{p:2}} said the company wanted a fashionable, trendy product, but that older generations, including baby boomers, represent a larger population than younger people; they favored a mid-range business-class target. {{p:4}} stressed budget considerations and avoiding wasted spending, suggesting that marketing should first focus where purchasing power for this product is greatest.

### Functions, programming, and batteries
{{p:2}} discussed television and video functions and proposed using VideoPlus, the code printed with programme details, as an alternative to entering recording dates and times. They explained that users can enter the five- or six-digit number listed in a newspaper or television guide; the recording information then identifies the programme, such as a Tuesday at 10 o’clock on the 17th, avoiding manual entry of dates and times. {{p:3}} said the function had been available for a long time but was not well advertised. {{p:2}} said better awareness could help, while {{p:3}} noted that Sky users can select a programme to record it, and press again to record the whole series. {{p:3}} nevertheless supported including the function. {{p:2}} explained that VideoPlus could replace separate buttons for date, channel, and related programming inputs, simplifying the control; it could also be promoted through advertising and explained in the instruction manual.

The group considered rechargeable batteries. {{p:3}} said mobile-phone batteries are purpose-made and come with a charger, which could be bundled with the control. {{p:2}} noted that rechargeable batteries last a long time and suggested a charging cradle, like that used for a cordless phone, to reduce the product’s size. {{p:1}} confirmed the idea of a rechargeable control with a docking station. {{p:3}} said this would also avoid repeatedly buying batteries, and {{p:2}} agreed it would be cheaper over the long run.

### Customer support and instruction materials
{{p:4}} proposed offering help through retail outlets, like mobile-phone shops, so older users who were unsure which button to press could receive assistance. {{p:3}} noted that mobile-phone providers have an obligation to assist customers who have contracts, and questioned the cost of providing similar help for a remote control. {{p:2}} suggested a customer-service phone number so users could explain that a button was not working without paying a call-out charge or walking to a high-street shop. {{p:1}} thought a shop visit might be too much effort for a remote, since users could consult a manual; {{p:4}} noted that the product’s functions should be simple. {{p:2}} said the manual should be as user-friendly as possible because manuals often have tiny print and many pages, which puts people off; users often leave manuals in a drawer until something goes wrong. {{p:4}} asked what marketing should investigate before the next meeting. {{p:2}} suggested looking at instruction manuals and how to make them useful, since people commonly have a pile of manuals but do not use them. {{p:2}} said the team could email questions; the meeting ended around lunchtime."}

The meeting participants noted that the schedule was at lunchtime and that they needed to get back.","mom":"### Review of previous meeting and agenda
{{p:2}} said this was the second meeting and that they might be somewhat disorganized. They reviewed the previous decisions: a universal control, one handset for all television and video equipment; accessibility to a wide range of consumers and ages; reflecting the company’s image by combining fashion with electronics; keeping the product uncluttered and unthreatening while balancing the budget with the desired appearance; and considering a flip-open design, a smaller control, and an electronic panel for additional features such as programming. {{p:2}} invited {{p:4}} to present first, but {{p:4}} asked to postpone until later to obtain more information. {{p:3}} then presented the working design, followed by {{p:1}} and then {{p:4}}. {{p:2}} said they would review the decisions from the previous meeting.

### Industrial design concept and technical requirements
{{p:3}} described the product as a device that sends signals to change the state of a television or another appliance, including power, channel, and volume. They had reviewed other products for inspiration, while noting that the design should stand out. Most controls use infrared, which {{p:3}} said was presumably due to cost and the small amount of information transmitted. They noted that most controls use batteries, often AAA batteries, which contribute to bulky designs; smaller batteries could reduce size, subject to power-consumption and data-transmission needs. The control should be small and easy to carry, but not so easy to lose; {{p:3}} suggested considering a way to prevent it slipping down the side of a sofa, a concern {{p:4}} said had also appeared in market research. The proposed components included a power source, a chip to decode user input and convert it to an infrared signal, and a user interface. The sketch was not a verified circuit, and {{p:3}} was unsure whether it would work or whether the wiring was correct. They said the system would need to conform to the communication format used by televisions, which use infrared. The wireless range was estimated at about five metres, considered adequate for most television viewers. Components should be low-cost to support a wide audience, and the product should differ enough from alternatives to attract customers. {{p:3}} also said battery choice would need further discussion and raised power consumption and how much data would need to be transmitted.

### User interface and form
{{p:1}} said the purpose was to simplify interaction with the television and make the product user-friendly rather than burden it with many complex buttons. They proposed a flip-top design: frequently used functions on top, with more complex functions, such as programming favourite channels, inside the middle section. This could serve a broad audience while allowing additional features such as a shock-proof body. {{p:1}} reported that many users prefer simple controls and may leave 30–40 percent of buttons unused even after a year of use. They also mentioned the team’s discussion of production at 50 million units, which could achieve economies of scale, lower costs, and make additional features more affordable. {{p:1}} suggested a trendy flip-top design and examining whether the buttons should be soft or firm, since buttons can become hard with continued use. The overall aim was a simple, user-friendly design.

{{p:1}} described a Nokia design from about six or seven years earlier: a flat, box-like control could strain the thumb because it sits raised, while a curved, banana- or boat-like shape would reduce how much the thumb bends. They suggested a smooth, hand-moulded form. {{p:2}} proposed incorporating the company logo and associated imagery into the product’s shape, giving as an example a vague “C” shape that opens like a shell. {{p:1}} preferred placing a logo at a corner rather than shaping the whole product like a shell. {{p:4}} considered the shell-opening flip-top idea attractive, suggesting lightweight plastic that fits in the palm and might reduce repetitive strain by requiring the user to insert a finger between the covers; they also suggested conch- or scallop-shell exterior designs. {{p:2}} proposed interchangeable fascias or casings, like mobile phones, including psychedelic designs for younger people and sleek alternatives. {{p:4}} added that a distinctive, attractive control might be less likely to disappear down a sofa and could be displayed on a mantelpiece. {{p:1}} suggested developing five or six designs and selecting the most appealing as the common design. The group also discussed a touch-screen panel: {{p:2}} thought it might appeal to younger, trendy users if clearly labelled and not daunting to older generations, while {{p:4}} cautioned that a small touch screen might not address repetitive-strain concerns.

### Market research findings
{{p:4}} reported that the company’s usability lab observed 100 members of the general public, male and female, across all age groups from 15 upwards, using remote controls. The overall finding was that users dislike the look and feel of current controls. Seventy-five percent found most controls ugly, and 80 percent said they would spend more for a better-looking control. Seventy-five percent of users channel-hop frequently, which {{p:4}} said had power implications. Fifty percent use only 10 percent of the buttons, suggesting both a design opportunity and a possible way to reduce cost by limiting functions. Half were especially frustrated by controls getting lost, often down the back of a sofa. Thirty-four percent said controls take too long to learn, which {{p:4}} linked to users not bothering with unused functions. Slightly more than a quarter said controls were bad for repetitive strain injury, with small movements potentially causing shoulder and elbow problems.

{{p:4}} said the vast majority of respondents aged 35 and under wanted an LCD and speech recognition, partly to help locate a lost control. They suggested, as an idea not tested in the research, that a lost control might emit a beep periodically or flash. Interest in those features decreased among people aged 35–45 and reversed in older groups. {{p:4}} offered to email additional research details if needed.

### Requirements and product scope
{{p:2}} stated that teletext would not be included because consumers consider it outdated now that the internet is available. The control was specified for television only, rather than as a universal combined control, which {{p:2}} said would reduce cost and make it easier for consumers to understand. The group discussed whether the control could also operate video equipment: {{p:4}} asked whether video programming was possible, and {{p:2}} said the requirement specified television only, although some Sky functions might be incorporated. {{p:3}} noted that a Sky box can record directly from the television to its hard drive. {{p:2}} understood that play, stop, and programming functions would still be needed.

{{p:4}} asked whether market research had examined demand for a combined control. {{p:4}} said it had not, but recalled the finding that most people use only 10 percent of buttons; those are generally basic channel-hopping and video on/off or fast-forward functions. They added that programming video recorders is widely considered a nightmare. {{p:3}} said speech recognition would probably be expensive to incorporate and was not very good. {{p:4}} clarified that the research table combined responses to two questions: whether respondents preferred a multifunction remote with an LCD and whether they would pay more for speech recognition. Responses varied across age groups, with many older respondents saying they did not know, which {{p:4}} attributed to general fear of new technology.

### Lost-control solutions and budget
{{p:3}} suggested a whistle-activated key fob that makes a loud noise to help locate a lost control. {{p:2}} emphasized that the budget was externally constrained and proposed a cheaper alternative: a unit on the television with a button that makes the remote beep. {{p:2}} considered this cheaper than adding speech recognition and said the finding function should address the problem of losing the control. {{p:4}} endorsed the television-button idea. Later, {{p:3}} suggested combining a beeper with a rechargeable battery arrangement.

### Target markets, design variations, and ergonomics
{{p:2}} said the corporate image should be incorporated into the handset through a logo and a fashionable, trendy appearance, reflecting research that people would pay more for a good-looking product. {{p:4}} said further research would be needed to establish what is attractive to different ages and international markets, contrasting a 15-year-old with someone aged 60, a trendy New Yorker with a retired South African, and noting that preferences vary around the world. The engineering design could stay the same while the interface and fashionable appearance change for different markets. {{p:1}} asked whether the team meant one model or five or six designs. {{p:3}} said the internal design could remain identical while the exterior differed; {{p:1}} agreed that features could stay the same while the body looked slightly different.

{{p:3}} raised ergonomics, citing the Xbox controller, for which two sizes were made because the original was too large for users in Japan; they said Japanese people generally have smaller hands and proposed varying button or controller sizes by country. {{p:1}} suggested a slightly larger model for the United States and a smaller one for Japan. {{p:2}} argued for designing one product first and letting the company adapt its size or features, while keeping the internal engineering design the same, rather than letting the team become bogged down in many possibilities. {{p:4}} cautioned that a small touch screen might not sufficiently address repetitive strain injury, since RSI is caused by repetitive small movements; they said this remained an open question that might need to be postponed to a future meeting. {{p:2}} and {{p:3}} discussed speech recognition as a possible way to avoid repetitive movement, but {{p:2}} said it was extremely expensive.

{{p:4}} asked whether the team should initially focus on a younger age group and broaden the market later, rather than target everyone immediately. {{p:1}} suggested focusing on the biggest market, mentioning people aged 20–35. {{p:2}} said the company wanted a fashionable, trendy product, but that older generations, including baby boomers, represent a larger population than younger people; they favored a mid-range business-class target. {{p:4}} stressed budget considerations and avoiding wasted spending, suggesting that marketing should first focus where purchasing power for this product is greatest.

### Functions, programming, and batteries
{{p:2}} discussed television and video functions and proposed using VideoPlus, the code printed with programme details, as an alternative to entering recording dates and times. They explained that users can enter the five- or six-digit number listed in a newspaper or television guide; the recording information then identifies the programme, such as a Tuesday at 10 o’clock on the 17th, avoiding manual entry of dates and times. {{p:3}} said the function had been available for a long time but was not well advertised. {{p:2}} said better awareness could help, while {{p:3}} noted that Sky users can select a programme to record it, and press again to record the whole series. {{p:3}} nevertheless supported including the function. {{p:2}} explained that VideoPlus could replace separate buttons for date, channel, and related programming inputs, simplifying the control; it could also be promoted through advertising and explained in the instruction manual.

The group considered rechargeable batteries. {{p:3}} said mobile-phone batteries are purpose-made and come with a charger, which could be bundled with the control. {{p:2}} noted that rechargeable batteries last a long time and suggested a charging cradle, like that used for a cordless phone, to reduce the product’s size. {{p:1}} confirmed the idea of a rechargeable control with a docking station. {{p:3}} said this would also avoid repeatedly buying batteries, and {{p:2}} agreed it would be cheaper over the long run.

### Customer support and instruction materials
{{p:4}} proposed offering help through retail outlets, like mobile-phone shops, so older users who were unsure which button to press could receive assistance. {{p:3}} noted that mobile-phone providers have an obligation to assist customers who have contracts, and questioned the cost of providing similar help for a remote control. {{p:2}} suggested a customer-service phone number so users could explain that a button was not working without paying a call-out charge or walking to a high-street shop. {{p:1}} thought a shop visit might be too much effort for a remote, since users could consult a manual; {{p:4}} noted that the product’s functions should be simple. {{p:2}} said the manual should be as user-friendly as possible because manuals often have tiny print and many pages, which puts people off; users often leave manuals in a drawer until something goes wrong. {{p:4}} asked what marketing should investigate before the next meeting. {{p:2}} suggested looking at instruction manuals and how to make them useful, since people commonly have a pile of manuals but do not use them. {{p:4}} was asked to research instruction manuals before the next meeting. {{p:2}} said the team could email questions; The team discussed a clip-on attachment to reduce the chance of losing the remote, but {{p:4}} said this had not emerged in focus groups or market research, so it remained an idea to consider rather than a decision. For the controls, the concept developed into a flip-top with an LCD display and touch interface on the top section and rubberized, anti-RSI buttons on the bottom; the circuit boards could be separated and connected with wiring. The body was to be plastic, with a removable rubberized cover for grip and a spongy feel, available in fruit- and vegetable-inspired colors rather than a literal fruit or vegetable shape; replaceable covers would allow later design updates. The interface discussion emphasized reducing clutter and inconsistency, retaining familiar volume and channel controls, and considering a black-and-white LCD first with a possible upgrade later; a GUI and voice recognition for locating a lost remote were also considered, subject to financial feasibility, with a whistle as a fallback if voice recognition proved too costly. The team agreed to investigate the cost of the locating feature and to incorporate the company logo into the design; the meeting closed with the team indicating it had a clear direction."}

{"mom":"### Meeting purpose and review of previous decisions
{{p:2}} opened the conceptual design meeting, saying the team was slightly ahead of where they had left things at the previous meeting. The agenda covered properties, materials, user interface, and trend-watching. Reviewing prior decisions, {{p:2}} said teletext could not be used as the control for everything, the company image needed to be incorporated, voice recognition had previously been left out, and the design was to be a flip form with an unusual shape, possibly shell-like. The team had also planned to investigate rechargeable batteries and consider a port and an alarm to help locate a lost remote. The intended market was a young business-oriented range.

### Marketing research and trends
{{p:4}} reported that the marketing department had conducted its usual market research with 100 subjects to identify the most important requirements for a remote control, and had consulted fashion and design consultants in Paris and Milan. The research ranked a fancy look and feel as the leading priority, twice as important as technological innovation; innovation was in turn twice as important as ease of use. Ease of use remained important, but ranked third for the subject group. The fashion consultants had attended design and fashion fairs and reported that fruit and vegetables were expected to influence clothing, shoes, and furniture. They also identified a trend toward spongy-feeling materials, in contrast to the previous year. {{p:4}} asked whether the team should draw on the fruit-and-vegetable theme in the remote’s design.

### Components and battery options
{{p:3}} presented findings on component design and factory stock availability. The standard chip identified as TA 1835 was used in most remote controls, sending standard signals based on user input, and was used for TV remotes. No rechargeable option was available among the components investigated. Standard AA and AAA batteries were considered bulky; dynamo charging would require a winding handle and take up more space. {{p:3}} described solar charging as an option, while the group discussed whether it would work under artificial light and whether relying on sunlight could limit international customers or people in basement flats. {{p:2}} noted that charging during the day could leave the remote charged for evening use. {{p:3}} proposed kinetic charging, as used in wristwatches: ordinary movement could charge a small cell about the size of a watch battery, and the user would not need to shake the remote deliberately. {{p:3}} could not confirm how long the cell would last, but said they had never seen one run out. {{p:2}} questioned whether a remote left on a table would move enough compared with a watch worn all day; {{p:3}} argued that a remote sends a signal for only a very short time and that kinetic watches continue running overnight when left aside.

{{p:1}} asked which option would be lightest and highlighted the need to consider size. {{p:3}} said a dynamo would take more space because it needs a physical winding handle. The group also considered whether solar charging could be paired with standard batteries. {{p:3}} said a dual-power arrangement might be possible, but solar cells would have to be placed on the case, would affect the exterior design, and could be relatively expensive and vulnerable to drops. Calculators were cited as a comparison, but remotes are handled and thrown around more. {{p:1}} asked which battery option would last longest and said customers should not have to recharge the remote every day like a mobile phone. The team ultimately agreed to kinetic charging with a watch-type battery; no AA-versus-AAA decision was made for that option, since {{p:3}} explained that the kinetic mechanism uses a much smaller watch-style cell.

### Possible attachment for locating the remote
{{p:2}} suggested considering an attachment or closing feature that could let the user clip the remote to a pocket, reducing the chance of losing it. {{p:4}} said this had not emerged from focus groups or market research, and recommended keeping it as an idea to consider rather than adding it immediately; market research should be done before committing to it. {{p:2}} noted that a clip could make sense for a small, portable, unusually shaped kinetic remote, while acknowledging that it might not help in the ongoing household contest over control of the remote.

### Circuit boards, buttons, and standby lighting
{{p:3}} explained that current remotes commonly use a silicone-button printed circuit board, with close contacts connected to chip legs; pressing a rubber button completes the circuit, the chip translates the input into a code, and an LED sends it as a sequence of on-and-off bursts. The board can be made large or small, with room for nine buttons, and thin tracks allow small switches to be placed close together. {{p:3}} also suggested a black-and-white LCD touch display as an alternative: it would be thin and compact and could show an arranged set of touch controls, but its flat form would limit curved designs. A bare printed circuit board might also be touched directly, potentially in different colours.

To conserve battery life, {{p:3}} proposed standby mode when the remote was not being used. If the buttons were illuminated from behind, the lights could turn off after five or ten seconds of inactivity. {{p:1}} asked whether the flip-top design could use separate circuits for different button types. {{p:3}} said this would be straightforward using two circuit boards connected by wires or cabling through the flip section.

### Materials, casing, and changeable covers
{{p:3}} said plastic was the practical choice for the main case and could accommodate curved shapes, while wood might be impractical. Titanium would be expensive to process and, according to {{p:3}}, would be restricted to a standard box shape; although light and strong, it was better suited to aircraft design than a remote. {{p:4}} noted that a titanium mobile phone could be marked when dropped. Rubber was considered for the spongy feel identified by marketing, especially for the buttons, which the factory described as using material from stress-ball manufacturing and as anti-RSI; {{p:3}} said they were unsure how effective that claim would be given the short finger movements involved.

{{p:1}} asked whether customers could change the cover or colour, like a mobile-phone skin, and whether this would work with titanium or only plastic. {{p:3}} said replaceable titanium cases would be very expensive. {{p:4}} proposed a plastic mould with a removable rubber cover, providing the spongy feel while allowing different facias; {{p:3}} agreed that the covers could peel off. {{p:2}} compared the idea to the removable grips on pens. {{p:4}} said replacement covers would be a cheap way for customers to change the appearance, and {{p:2}} observed that interchangeable phone covers had been popular.

The team settled on a plastic case with a removable rubberized cover. They would use fruit- and vegetable-inspired colours, rather than shaping the product to look like a fruit, vegetable, or shell. {{p:2}} cautioned against a tacky result and said the emphasis should be on the material’s feel; because the material was inexpensive, a range of colours could be offered. {{p:4}} asked whether a palm-sized plastic device with a spongy rubber cover would satisfy the market research’s leading requirement for a fancy look and feel. {{p:2}} replied that the design would be different from existing products, and discussed either matching the beige-and-black appearance of many homes or creating a contrasting, distinctive object that could become a talking point. {{p:4}} agreed that existing remotes looked anonymous and similar, and said the proposed design would stand out; the replaceable, inexpensive covers could also be updated if design-fair feedback showed that trends had changed, for example in a year’s time.

### Touch interface and stylus suggestion
{{p:3}} revisited the proposed touch-screen interface and described a black-and-white LCD with touch buttons as one option, alongside rubber buttons made of the anti-RSI material. {{p:2}} said that if the whole device were rubber, opening it should reveal an attractive contrasting interior, and asked how users would know where to press on a bare surface. {{p:4}} suggested that users might operate the controls with a finger or use a small stylus kept inside. {{p:3}} warned that a removable stylus could easily be lost, while {{p:2}} suggested that it would need to be attached. {{p:1}} added that frequent channel-changing or repeated use of a particular function could make a touch pad irritating and wear it quickly, especially if users pressed it with a pointer. {{p:4}} said users could also use an ordinary pencil or pen, rather than needing a supplied pointer. The team left the pointer idea for later discussion.

### Competitor review and proposed interface layout
{{p:1}} presented a competitor review based on the previous meeting’s input from marketing and industrial design, assessing customer needs and feasibility. The competitor models showed little variety: most were rectangular and monotonous, and users were bored with black-and-white designs. The channel and volume controls were the only common features; other buttons were disorganized and inconsistent across models. {{p:1}} proposed a graphic user interface in the middle of the flip-top, with icons or touch controls, and physical buttons for frequently repeated operations such as volume and channel changes.

{{p:2}} suggested placing the frequently used controls on the lower part so that users holding the open device could operate them with their thumbs, like a mobile phone. After discussion of how the open shell would sit in the hand, {{p:2}} described a layout with the LCD at the top and volume and program controls on the lower side. {{p:1}} agreed. The team’s decisions were to use an LCD display on the top side of the flip-top and rubberized buttons on the bottom side.

### Voice recognition and locating a lost remote
{{p:1}} reported that a company division had developed a new speech-recognition feature, and proposed checking its financial feasibility for the remote. Customers had expressed interest in a way to find a lost remote: the user could ask where it was, and it could answer or emit a beep or other sound. {{p:1}} said this could make the product more fashionable and technologically innovative. {{p:2}} and {{p:3}} supported investigating the feature, with {{p:2}} noting that the main risk was cost and that the team might need to cut other features if it proved expensive. {{p:3}} added that the required parts were already in stock, which could make remanufacturing them inexpensive. The team agreed to find out more about the cost before deciding.

{{p:1}} also recalled a suggestion from William in the previous meeting: a whistle device on a key chain. If voice recognition proved financially infeasible, the team could consider a whistle as an alternative way to locate the remote. The meeting did not settle on either option as final.

### Company identity and remaining design decisions
{{p:1}} said the company logo would be incorporated into the design. {{p:4}} emphasized that the company identity should be obvious rather than hidden in a small mark. {{p:2}} agreed that the product would have a logo, but said it should stand out through its distinctive design and that advertising could associate the company name with the product.

In the closing recap, {{p:4}} listed the decisions reached: kinetic charging using a watch-type battery, an LCD display on the top side of the flip-top, rubberized buttons on the bottom side, a plastic case, and fruit- and vegetable-inspired colours for the rubber cover. The team also agreed on the basic component arrangement and planned to investigate the cost of voice recognition. The meeting ended with {{p:2}} saying the design discussion had established a clear direction."}

{"summary":"{{p:2}} opened the conceptual design meeting, noting the team was slightly ahead of the previous meeting, and reviewed the plan: omit teletext as a universal control and voice recognition as initially discussed, incorporate the company image, use a flip design and a non-standard shape, and target a young-business market. {{p:4}} reported market research with 100 subjects and fashion consultations in Paris and Milan: customers ranked a fancy look and feel first, twice as important as technological innovation, which was in turn twice as important as ease of use; consultants also noted fruit and vegetable themes and spongy-feel materials as trends. {{p:3}} described the standard remote-control chip (TA1835), component and material availability, and charging possibilities: standard AA or AAA batteries were considered bulky, dynamo charging would need extra space, and solar panels could affect the case design and durability; kinetic charging like that used in watches was favored, though battery life still needed consideration. The team discussed a clip-on attachment to reduce the chance of losing the remote, but {{p:4}} said this had not emerged in focus groups or market research, so it remained an idea to consider rather than a decision. For the controls, the concept developed into a flip-top with an LCD display and touch interface on the top section and rubberized, anti-RSI buttons on the bottom; the circuit boards could be separated and connected with wiring. The body was to be plastic, with a removable rubberized cover for grip and a spongy feel, available in fruit- and vegetable-inspired colors rather than a literal fruit or vegetable shape; replaceable covers would allow later design updates. The interface discussion emphasized reducing clutter and inconsistency, retaining familiar volume and channel controls, and considering a black-and-white LCD first with a possible upgrade later; a GUI and voice recognition for locating a lost remote were also considered, subject to financial feasibility, with a whistle as a fallback if voice recognition proved too costly. The team agreed to investigate the cost of the locating feature and to incorporate the company logo into the design; the meeting closed with the team indicating it had a clear direction.","mom":"### Meeting purpose and review of previous decisions
{{p:2}} opened the conceptual design meeting, saying the team was slightly ahead of where they had left things at the previous meeting. The agenda covered properties, materials, user interface, and trend-watching. Reviewing prior decisions, {{p:2}} said teletext could not be used as the control for everything, the company image needed to be incorporated, voice recognition had previously been left out, and the design was to be a flip form with an unusual shape, possibly shell-like. The team had also planned to investigate rechargeable batteries and consider a port and an alarm to help locate a lost remote. The intended market was a young business-oriented range. {{p:2}} said the group would review the points already touched on, then proposed starting with the inside of the design and working outward.

### Marketing research and trends
{{p:4}} reported that the marketing department had conducted its usual market research with 100 subjects to identify the most important requirements for a remote control, and had consulted fashion and design consultants in Paris and Milan. The research ranked a fancy look and feel as the leading priority, twice as important as technological innovation; innovation was in turn twice as important as ease of use. Ease of use remained important, but ranked third for the subject group. The fashion consultants had attended design and fashion fairs and reported that fruit and vegetables were expected to influence clothing, shoes, and furniture. They also identified a trend toward spongy-feeling materials, in contrast to the previous year. {{p:4}} asked whether the team should draw on the fruit-and-vegetable theme in the remote’s design.

### Components and battery options
{{p:3}} presented findings on component design and factory stock availability. The standard chip identified as TA1835 was used in most remote controls, sending standard signals based on user input, and was used for TV remotes. No rechargeable option was available among the components investigated. Standard AA and AAA batteries were considered bulky; dynamo charging would require a winding handle and take up more space. {{p:3}} described solar charging as an option, while the group discussed whether it would work under artificial light and whether relying on sunlight could limit international customers or people in basement flats. {{p:2}} noted that charging during the day could leave the remote charged for evening use. {{p:3}} proposed kinetic charging, as used in wristwatches: ordinary movement could charge a small cell about the size of a watch battery, and the user would not need to shake the remote deliberately. {{p:3}} could not confirm how long the cell would last, but said they had never seen one run out. {{p:2}} questioned whether a remote left on a table would move enough compared with a watch worn all day; {{p:3}} argued that a remote sends a signal for only a very short time and that kinetic watches continue running overnight when left aside.

{{p:1}} asked which option would be lightest and highlighted the need to consider size. {{p:3}} said a dynamo would take more space because it needs a physical winding handle. The group also considered whether solar charging could be paired with standard batteries. {{p:3}} said a dual-power arrangement might be possible, but solar cells would have to be placed on the case, would affect the exterior design, and could be relatively expensive and vulnerable to drops. Calculators were cited as a comparison, but remotes are handled and thrown around more. {{p:1}} asked which battery option would last longest and said customers should not have to recharge the remote every day like a mobile phone; {{p:1}} also stressed that battery life needed to be considered. The team ultimately agreed to kinetic charging with a watch-type battery; no AA-versus-AAA decision was made for that option, since {{p:3}} explained that the kinetic mechanism uses a much smaller watch-style cell.

### Possible attachment for locating the remote
{{p:2}} suggested considering an attachment or closing feature that could let the user clip the remote to a pocket, reducing the chance of losing it. {{p:4}} said this had not emerged from focus groups or market research, and recommended keeping it as an idea to consider rather than adding it immediately; market research should be done before committing to it. {{p:2}} noted that a clip could make sense for a small, portable, unusually shaped kinetic remote, while acknowledging that it might not help in the ongoing household contest over control of the remote.

### Circuit boards, buttons, and standby lighting
{{p:3}} explained that current remotes commonly use a silicone-button printed circuit board, with close contacts connected to chip legs; pressing a rubber button completes the circuit, the chip translates the input into a code, and an LED sends it as a sequence of on-and-off bursts. The board can be made large or small, with room for nine buttons, and thin tracks allow small switches to be placed close together. {{p:3}} also suggested a black-and-white LCD touch display as an alternative: it would be thin and compact and could show an arranged set of touch controls, but its flat form would limit curved designs. A bare printed circuit board might also be touched directly, potentially in different colours.

To conserve battery life, {{p:3}} proposed standby mode when the remote was not being used. If the buttons were illuminated from behind, the lights could turn off after five or ten seconds of inactivity. {{p:1}} asked whether the flip-top design could use separate circuits for different button types. {{p:3}} said this would be straightforward using two circuit boards connected by wires or cabling through the flip section.

### Materials, casing, and changeable covers
{{p:3}} said plastic was the practical choice for the main case and could accommodate curved shapes, while wood might be impractical. Titanium would be expensive to process and, according to {{p:3}}, would be restricted to a standard box shape; although light and strong, it was better suited to aircraft design than a remote. {{p:4}} noted that a titanium mobile phone could be marked when dropped. Rubber was considered for the spongy feel identified by marketing, especially for the buttons, which the factory described as using material from stress-ball manufacturing and as anti-RSI; {{p:3}} said they were unsure how effective that claim would be given the short finger movements involved.

{{p:1}} asked whether customers could change the cover or colour, like a mobile-phone skin, and whether this would work with titanium or only plastic. {{p:3}} said replaceable titanium cases would be very expensive. {{p:4}} proposed a plastic mould with a removable rubber cover, providing the spongy feel while allowing different facias; {{p:3}} agreed that the covers could peel off. {{p:2}} compared the idea to the removable grips on pens. {{p:4}} said replacement covers would be a cheap way for customers to change the appearance, and {{p:2}} observed that interchangeable phone covers had been popular.

The team settled on a plastic case with a removable rubberized cover. ### Touch interface and stylus suggestion
{{p:3}} revisited the proposed touch-screen interface and described a black-and-white LCD with touch buttons as one option, alongside rubber buttons made of the anti-RSI material. {{p:2}} said that if the whole device were rubber, opening it should reveal an attractive contrasting interior, and asked how users would know where to press on a bare surface. {{p:4}} suggested that users might operate the controls with a finger or use a small stylus kept inside. {{p:3}} warned that a removable stylus could easily be lost, while {{p:2}} suggested that it would need to be attached. {{p:1}} added that frequent channel-changing or repeated use of a particular function could make a touch pad irritating and wear it quickly, especially if users pressed it with a pointer. {{p:4}} said users could also use an ordinary pencil or pen, rather than needing a supplied pointer. The team left the pointer idea for later discussion.

### Competitor review and proposed interface layout
{{p:1}} presented a competitor review based on the previous meeting’s input from marketing and industrial design, assessing customer needs and feasibility. The competitor models showed little variety: most were rectangular and monotonous, and users were bored with black-and-white designs. The channel and volume controls were the only common features; other buttons were disorganized and inconsistent across models. {{p:1}} proposed a graphic user interface in the middle of the flip-top, with icons or touch controls, and physical buttons for frequently repeated operations such as volume and channel changes.

{{p:2}} suggested placing the frequently used controls on the lower part so that users holding the open device could operate them with their thumbs, like a mobile phone. After discussion of how the open shell would sit in the hand, {{p:2}} described a layout with the LCD at the top and volume and program controls on the lower side. {{p:1}} agreed. The team’s decisions were to use an LCD display on the top side of the flip-top and rubberized buttons on the bottom side.

### Voice recognition and locating a lost remote
{{p:1}} reported that a company division had developed a new speech-recognition feature, and proposed checking its financial feasibility for the remote. {{p:2}} recapped the agreed remote-control specification: a kinetic charger, a standard chip available in various sizes, and a standby function. The case would use soft, rubbery, changeable material, with buttons combining LCD and rubber according to the design. The appearance would use bright, funky, fruit-inspired designs to maintain a hip feel. The team wanted to incorporate voice-recognition software once its cost was clearer, and rubber buttons intended to reduce repetitive strain injury (RSI).

### Prototype presentation and design
{{p:1}} said they and William had worked on a prototype and that William would present it; {{p:3}} then presented the final look-and-feel design. The exterior concept used a plastic body in a neutral standard colour such as white or light blue, covered by an attachable rubberised outer casing available in a wide choice of colours and patterns for customisation. The remote would have a clamshell form, an inset black-and-white touchscreen on the top, and buttons at the bottom so it could close flat. {{p:3}} described kinetic batteries inside and suggested they could potentially gain charge from opening and closing the device; {{p:2}} suggested putting them in the top section rather than the bottom.

{{p:3}} said voice recognition seemed readily available and presumed it would be inexpensive. The example was a user asking where the remote was and the remote answering that it was there. {{p:2}} cautioned that a more elaborate locating response could be too complicated, and the team treated a remote that could indicate its precise location as a possible future feature. For TV operation, the design would use standard infrared transmission and a standard chip. Because the remote was split across two layers, it would need two separate PCBs joined by cabling at the hinge. The infrared sender would be at the front of the lower layer, positioned to face the TV when the remote was open. The upper screen would contain the available remote functions; the lower screen would have standard controls such as volume up and down, channel up and down, and power. A company logo could be placed on the inside as a bezel, inset, or engraving, provided it did not interfere with the product’s exterior appearance.

### Evaluation approach and findings
{{p:4}} explained that the evaluation was the first check of whether the product specification and prototype met the criteria drawn from user requirements and trends in the company’s marketing reports and strategy. The criteria were fancy look and feel, technological innovation, ease of use, current fashion trends—including spongy texture and strong fruit-and-vegetable colours—minimising RSI, and ease of locating the remote. Voice recognition was the favoured locating approach, though the team had also considered a beeper and remained somewhat uncertain. {{p:4}} proposed a seven-point scale, with 1 meaning true and 7 meaning false. The team agreed to rate each criterion individually and average the results, recording the ratings separately by speaker.

For criterion A, fancy look and feel, {{p:4}} rated the prototype 2; {{p:3}} settled on 3 after considering 2 or 3; {{p:2}} rated it 2; and {{p:1}} rated it 4. The recorded average was 2.75, calculated from a total of 11 divided by 4. For criterion B, technological innovation, {{p:4}} rated it 3, {{p:3}} rated it 1, and {{p:2}} rated it 2. {{p:1}} corrected their initial rating to 2; {{p:2}} stated that their own rating was 2.5, and {{p:4}} said the average would be recalculated at the end. The discussion then recorded a total of 8 and an average of 2. For ease of use, {{p:4}} initially rated the design 1; {{p:3}}, {{p:2}}, and {{p:1}} each gave it 2. {{p:4}} described the result as almost 2 rather than using an awkward decimal.

For current fashion trends, {{p:4}} clarified that the prototype’s base plastic would be white or light blue, while the changeable outer faces could provide customised colours, including strong fruit-and-vegetable colours; the rubber casing would supply the spongy feel. {{p:4}} and {{p:3}} each rated the spongy-texture aspect 1, as did {{p:2}} and {{p:1}}. On minimising RSI, {{p:4}} observed that the team had not identified a feasible way to reduce RSI substantially: pointers had been discussed, but the small size of a remote and users’ frequent channel-zapping made the issue difficult. {{p:2}} argued that the planned lower-half buttons were made from material intended to minimise RSI, and that having fewer, larger, more clearly spaced buttons would reduce the need to move around and aim accurately between them. {{p:4}} rated the criterion 4, {{p:3}} rated it 5, and {{p:2}} and {{p:1}} each rated it 4; the average was 4.25.

For ease of locating the remote, the team confirmed voice recognition as the chosen feature and discussed whether its cost was feasible. {{p:3}} said it was feasible, and {{p:4}} noted that the response volume could be adjusted, as with a TV. They considered that a loud response could help someone in another room or when TVs were in different rooms: if the user could not hear it where they were standing, they would realise the remote was elsewhere and go to another room. {{p:4}}, {{p:3}}, and {{p:2}} each rated this criterion 1. In the overall review, {{p:4}} said the highest ratings—indicating the specification was met—were achieved for two of the six criteria: incorporating current fashion trends and being easy to locate. The weakest result was RSI reduction, which was close to neutral. The team agreed it could proceed with the prototype and marketing; {{p:2}} and {{p:3}} expressed agreement. {{p:4}} added that current technology and the team’s capabilities were unlikely to enable much further RSI reduction.

### Costing and specification decisions
While reviewing the finance figures, {{p:2}} confirmed that the team still intended to use kinetic charging, and {{p:3}} and {{p:4}} agreed. {{p:2}} remarked that having the figures earlier might have influenced the choice. The electronics were described as one regular chip on a printed circuit board, one sample sensor, and one sample speaker. The kinetic-cell quantity had mistakenly been entered as 3; {{p:3}} corrected it to 1. The team clarified the component and curve entries, distinguishing one double-curved component from another with curved sides and a slightly flattened bottom so it could sit without rolling over.

{{p:1}} proposed switching from kinetic charging to a standard battery. During the cost review, the team discussed the casing-material entry: {{p:1}} suggested entering 0.5 for rubber because it was used only as a casing and in a much lower quantity than plastic. {{p:2}} pointed out that the form asked for case material, and {{p:3}} said the casing was an extra not included in the cost of the remote as sold. {{p:4}} replied that it would still be part of the total cost and there was nowhere else to record the rubber. {{p:2}} proposed entering half, then suggested entering 1 because plastic was 0; {{p:3}} agreed. They also considered a special colour, which {{p:4}} said might be needed for more exotic colours such as aubergine. In the interface entries, the team identified one push-button and one LCD display.

The group examined the price figures and whether they were in euros or dollars. {{p:3}} suggested the figure might be in dollars, which would translate to about 12 at the exchange rate, but {{p:2}} and {{p:1}} said they had been working in euros. {{p:2}} identified electronics as the highest cost. They then compared keeping kinetic charging with using standard batteries. {{p:3}} said changing to standard batteries would make a difference; {{p:1}} observed that customers had not mentioned the battery, which was internal, and stressed that shape and colours were more visible. The team calculated that removing voice recognition would bring the figure to 12.35; replacing kinetic charging, which was costed at 3, with a battery would subtract 3 and add 2. {{p:2}} suggested offering voice recognition as an optional business-class upgrade, allowing customers to choose it or not. {{p:3}} argued customers had indicated willingness to pay more for a better product, rather than assuming it had to sell for 25 euros. {{p:4}} said the team still needed to meet head-office specifications, but could state recommendations based on its findings and meeting consensus. {{p:2}} suggested adjusting the price to fit the budget if voice recognition were retained. The group also discussed the calculation as 12.25 and compared it with a 25-euro figure; {{p:1}} concluded that they were under budget. The team decided the electronics were covered and no replacement component was needed if the optional bought-on extra was removed.

### Product and teamwork review
{{p:2}} said the team had completed the product evaluation and asked about room for creativity, leadership, and teamwork. The participants agreed they had worked as a team, despite separate tasks. {{p:4}} described substantial interaction, mutual exchange of ideas, and feeling heard; the team had adjusted its remit where necessary. {{p:1}} said the feedback was constructive rather than adversarial and described the work as cohesive teamwork that produced a creative design. {{p:1}} also thanked {{p:2}} for coordinating the work well. {{p:3}} said the project went well, everyone was listened to, and points raised were addressed, while noting that voice recognition had not quite made it into the specification. {{p:3}} thought it might have been included in the final product if marketing information had been available before the initial specification was issued.

{{p:2}} valued being able to suggest ideas and have them challenged without anyone feeling dismissed. The team discussed the prototype model and the communication methods used. {{p:3}} said they might have used the external email system more if they had had more time and had been separated more; {{p:2}} noted that discussing matters directly would have been easier than emailing, though having the shared materials available was useful. {{p:1}} liked moving around the room and having time to work individually. The discussion also noted that the flip-top remote was an unusual design, drawing ideas from other areas and applying them differently. {{p:2}} proposed customisable plastic shells, with customers’ designs made in Photoshop and printed on the plastic for an additional charge, so buyers could choose a distinctive product. The team observed that electronics manufacturers often focus on the main device, such as a DVD player or TV, rather than its remote, even though a distinctive design could make the remote a more considered product.

### Budget and closing
{{p:2}} questioned whether the budget covered overheads such as staff pay and building heating. {{p:4}} and {{p:3}} said the figure appeared to cover only the physical production cost of the product. {{p:2}} noted that the costing suggested a 50% profit while overheads still had to be paid from it, and said increasing the budget might require increasing the sale price. {{p:4}} said the team had met its specific market-research remit and that overheads and raising additional funding would require another project or project team. {{p:4}} felt the team had done well to stay within budget while designing an innovative product people might want. {{p:2}} said the project had been evaluated and mentioned the meeting survey and questionnaire. {{p:2}} said there were about 50 minutes to catch up on outstanding work and that they would delegate in their Project Supervisor role. The team also mentioned a £25 celebration budget, or dancing on the desks as an alternative."}
