{"summary":"The team reviewed the flip-top remote-control prototype and confirmed a kinetic charger with a standard chip, standby function, soft rubberized and customizable casing, LCD touch interface, and anti-RSI rubber buttons; voice recognition remained under consideration pending cost information. The design presentation described a plastic body in neutral white or light blue beneath interchangeable colorful rubber covers, a flush-closing clamshell with an inset black-and-white touchscreen, standard physical controls, infrared transmission, and a possible logo on the interior; opening and closing the lid might also help generate kinetic power. The team evaluated the product against six market-research criteria on a seven-point scale, where 1 meant true and 7 false, using individual ratings and averages: fancy look and feel averaged 2.75, technological innovation averaged 2, ease of use was approximately 2, minimizing repetitive strain injury averaged 4.25, and incorporating fashion trends and being easy to locate received the strongest ratings. The team judged the design sufficiently aligned with the requirements to proceed, while noting that voice recognition could be offered as an upgraded business-class option or omitted to keep the price within budget; without it, the estimate was about 12.25–12.35, and the budget was described as approximately 25, with the currency and calculation discussed. The electronics estimate was corrected to one kinetic cell, one regular chip, one sensor, and one speaker; the team also clarified the curved body, flattened base, and plastic-and-rubber construction, and considered how to account for the rubber casing and special-color costs. In closing, participants said the team worked collaboratively, listened to one another, and gave constructive feedback; they noted that more time or earlier access to marketing research might have affected the specification, and that overheads were not included in the production-cost estimate. The meeting wrapped up with the project evaluation and questionnaires; the Project Manager said there were about 50 minutes to catch up on outstanding work, and mentioned a £25 celebration.","mom":"### Product specification
{{p:2}} recapped the agreed remote-control specification: a kinetic charger, a standard chip available in various sizes, and a standby function. The case would use soft, rubbery, changeable material, with buttons combining LCD and rubber according to the design. The appearance would use bright, funky, fruit-inspired designs to maintain a hip feel. The team wanted to incorporate voice-recognition software once its cost was clearer, and rubber buttons intended to reduce repetitive strain injury (RSI).

### Prototype presentation and design
{{p:1}} said they and William had worked on a prototype and that William would present it; {{p:3}} then presented the final look-and-feel design. The exterior concept used a plastic body in a neutral standard colour such as white or light blue, covered by an attachable rubberised outer casing available in a wide choice of colours and patterns for customisation. The remote would have a clamshell form, an inset black-and-white touchscreen on the top, and buttons at the bottom so it could close flat. {{p:3}} described kinetic batteries inside and suggested they could potentially gain charge from opening and closing the device; {{p:2}} suggested putting them in the top section rather than the bottom.

{{p:3}} said voice recognition seemed readily available and presumed it would be inexpensive. The example was a user asking where the remote was and the remote answering that it was there. {{p:2}} cautioned that a more elaborate locating response could be too complicated, and the team treated a remote that could indicate its precise location as a possible future feature. For TV operation, the design would use standard infrared transmission and a standard chip. Because the remote was split across two layers, it would need two separate PCBs joined by cabling at the hinge. The infrared sender would be at the front of the lower layer, positioned to face the TV when the remote was open. The upper screen would contain the available remote functions; the lower screen would have standard controls such as volume up and down, channel up and down, and power. A company logo could be placed on the inside as a bezel, inset, or engraving, provided it did not interfere with the product’s exterior appearance.

### Evaluation approach and findings
{{p:4}} explained that the evaluation was the first check of whether the product specification and prototype met the criteria drawn from user requirements and trends in the company’s marketing reports and strategy. The criteria were fancy look and feel, technological innovation, ease of use, current fashion trends—including spongy texture and strong fruit-and-vegetable colours—minimising RSI, and ease of locating the remote. Voice recognition was the favoured locating approach, though the team had also considered a beeper and remained somewhat uncertain. {{p:4}} proposed a seven-point scale, with 1 meaning true and 7 meaning false. The team agreed to rate each criterion individually and average the results, recording the ratings separately by speaker.

For criterion A, fancy look and feel, {{p:4}} rated the prototype 2; {{p:3}} settled on 3 after considering 2 or 3; {{p:2}} rated it 2; and {{p:1}} rated it 4. The recorded average was 2.75, calculated from a total of 11 divided by 4. For criterion B, technological innovation, {{p:4}} rated it 3, {{p:3}} rated it 1, and {{p:2}} rated it 2. {{p:1}} corrected their initial rating to 2; {{p:2}} stated that their own rating was 2.5, and {{p:4}} said the average would be recalculated at the end. The discussion then recorded a total of 8 and an average of 2. For ease of use, {{p:4}} initially rated the design 1; {{p:3}}, {{p:2}}, and {{p:1}} each gave it 2. {{p:4}} described the result as almost 2 rather than using an awkward decimal.

For current fashion trends, {{p:4}} clarified that the prototype’s base plastic would be white or light blue, while the changeable outer faces could provide customised colours, including strong fruit-and-vegetable colours; the rubber casing would supply the spongy feel. {{p:4}} and {{p:3}} each rated the spongy-texture aspect 1, as did {{p:2}} and {{p:1}}. On minimising RSI, {{p:4}} observed that the team had not identified a feasible way to reduce RSI substantially: pointers had been discussed, but the small size of a remote and users’ frequent channel-zapping made the issue difficult. {{p:2}} argued that the planned lower-half buttons were made from material intended to minimise RSI, and that having fewer, larger, more clearly spaced buttons would reduce the need to move around and aim accurately between them. {{p:4}} rated the criterion 4, {{p:3}} rated it 5, and {{p:2}} and {{p:1}} each rated it 4; the average was 4.25.

For ease of locating the remote, the team confirmed voice recognition as the chosen feature and discussed whether its cost was feasible. {{p:3}} said it was feasible, and {{p:4}} noted that the response volume could be adjusted, as with a TV. They considered that a loud response could help someone in another room or when TVs were in different rooms: if the user could not hear it where they were standing, they would realise the remote was elsewhere and go to another room. {{p:4}}, {{p:3}}, and {{p:2}} each rated this criterion 1. In the overall review, {{p:4}} said the highest ratings—indicating the specification was met—were achieved for two of the six criteria: incorporating current fashion trends and being easy to locate. The weakest result was RSI reduction, which was close to neutral. ### Prototype presentation and design
{{p:1}} said they and William had worked on a prototype and that William would present it; {{p:3}} then presented the final look-and-feel design. The exterior concept used a plastic body in a neutral standard colour such as white or light blue, covered by an attachable rubberised outer casing available in a wide choice of colours and patterns for customisation. The remote would have a clamshell form, an inset black-and-white touchscreen on the top, and buttons at the bottom so it could close flat. {{p:3}} described kinetic batteries inside and suggested they could potentially gain charge from opening and closing the device; {{p:2}} suggested putting them in the top section rather than the bottom.

{{p:3}} said voice recognition seemed readily available and presumed it would be inexpensive. The example was a user asking where the remote was and the remote answering that it was there. {{p:2}} cautioned that a more elaborate locating response could be too complicated, and the team treated a remote that could indicate its precise location as a possible future feature. For TV operation, the design would use standard infrared transmission and a standard chip. Because the remote was split across two layers, it would need two separate PCBs joined by cabling at the hinge. The infrared sender would be at the front of the lower layer, positioned to face the TV when the remote was open. The upper screen would contain the available remote functions; the lower screen would have standard controls such as volume up and down, channel up and down, and power. A company logo could be placed on the inside as a bezel, inset, or engraving, provided it did not interfere with the product’s exterior appearance.

{{p:4}} explained that the evaluation was the first check of whether the product specification and prototype met the criteria drawn from user requirements and trends in the company’s marketing reports and strategy. The criteria were fancy look and feel, technological innovation, ease of use, current fashion trends—including spongy texture and strong fruit-and-vegetable colours—minimising RSI, and ease of locating the remote. {"mom":"### Introductions and agenda
{{p:1}} opened the first meeting and said it would last 25 minutes, with time to get acquainted. {{p:4}} introduced herself as Robin, the Marketing Manager; {{p:3}} introduced herself as Louisa, the User Interface Designer; {{p:2}} introduced himself as Nick, the Industrial Designer; and {{p:1}} introduced himself as Alastair, the project leader. The agenda included tool training, a project plan and trying out the whiteboard. When asked about required tool training, {{p:3}} said she was unsure what that meant, and {{p:1}} agreed that he was unsure too.

### Project goals and process
{{p:1}} said the team was to develop a new remote-control device, starting from the existing product. The new device should be more user-friendly and trendier, with the aim of reaching a bigger audience and gaining more market share. The work would be divided into functional design, conceptual design and detailed design, with the designers taking part in each phase and meeting during the day to develop a better solution. The team would make various designs during the day toward that goal.

### Whiteboard exercise
As a tool-training exercise, {{p:1}} asked everyone to draw their favourite animal on the whiteboard to check that it worked. There were some microphone and camera issues while participants moved to the board. {{p:3}} drew a cat, describing cats as independent, intelligent, affectionate and able to look after themselves. {{p:2}} drew a bear, saying he liked bears partly because many cartoon characters were based on bears, including characters from The Jungle Book. {{p:4}} drew a dog, saying dogs were loyal, cheerful and fun to spend time with, provided exercise, and were cute when tired. {{p:1}} drew fish, which his daughters currently had as pets; he said he was not keen on pets generally but considered fish low-maintenance, explaining that a feeder could feed them during a couple of weeks away, the water needed changing every couple of months, and plants could be added. He noted that the fish kept dying.

### Price, costs and market
{{p:1}} said the expected selling price was 25 euros, based on information from {{p:4}}. The product was intended for international sales, not just Europe, and the target production cost was 12.5 euros per unit. He clarified that this was not the profit margin because overheads and other costs still had to be deducted; the overhead costs would determine how many units the team projected to sell.

### Initial remote-control requirements and concepts
{{p:2}} said remote-control buttons could be too small and difficult to press, and suggested making them easy to press because that was the device’s main function. {{p:1}} summarized the desired device as robust, so it would not be damaged easily, and easy to use and see, with accessible buttons.

{{p:3}} asked whether the brief was for a television remote or a combined remote for systems such as TV/video or TV/DVD, noting that having five remotes at home was annoying. {{p:1}} said he would confirm the scope, but agreed that having three or four devices around a room was frustrating and raised the possibility of one device for all remotes. {{p:4}} added that market research found people were often confused by the number of buttons. She also observed that a remote could be left elsewhere in the room, forcing someone to get up to retrieve it, and suggested considering a remote that could move around the room. {{p:3}} joked about it coming when called; {{p:4}} suggested that might be a future possibility when people could talk to their television.

{{p:1}} noted a tension between combining devices and keeping the remote simple, with few buttons, and said the team needed a design that anyone could use. He suggested that users’ growing familiarity with remote controls might allow devices to become more complicated over time. {{p:2}} proposed better instructions and asked whether the work covered the remote itself or its instructions. {{p:4}} described research into cutting-edge handheld devices, many of which resembled mini-laptops, and suggested a miniature computer that could control a television, stereo and future devices added to the system.

### Work for the next session and scope clarification
{{p:1}} said there were five minutes left in the meeting and that the next meeting would be in 30 minutes. He outlined the work: a working design for Industrial Design, a technical-functions design for User Interface Design, and a user-requirements specification for Marketing. Specific instructions would be sent by each person’s personal coach. The group confirmed it understood the objectives for the next 30 minutes.

{{p:3}} said she was still unclear what the remote was for and asked whether it should be multifunctional or whether the team should decide as they worked. {{p:2}} recalled that it had been described as a television remote and suggested sticking to that unless told otherwise. {{p:1}} agreed that later information or meetings might change the direction, but said that for now the team should design a TV remote. The team would break off and work there; {{p:1}} would write up minutes, and they would reconvene in half an hour."}

{{p:1}} opened the first meeting and said it would last 25 minutes, with time to get acquainted. {{p:4}} introduced herself as Robin, the Marketing Manager; {{p:3}} introduced herself as Louisa, the User Interface Designer; {{p:2}} introduced himself as Nick, the Industrial Designer; and {{p:1}} introduced himself as Alastair, the project leader. The agenda included tool training, a project plan and trying out the whiteboard. When asked about required tool training, {{p:3}} said she was unsure what that meant, and {{p:1}} agreed that he was unsure too.

### Project goals and process
{{p:1}} said the team was to develop a new remote-control device, starting from the existing product. The new device should be more user-friendly and trendier, with the aim of reaching a bigger audience and gaining more market share. The work would be divided into functional design, conceptual design and detailed design, with the designers taking part in each phase and meeting during the day to develop a better solution. The team would make various designs during the day toward that goal.

### Whiteboard exercise
As a tool-training exercise, {{p:1}} asked everyone to draw their favourite animal on the whiteboard to check that it worked. There were some microphone and camera issues while participants moved to the board. {{p:3}} drew a cat, describing cats as independent, intelligent, affectionate and able to look after themselves. {{p:2}} drew a bear, saying he liked bears partly because many cartoon characters were based on bears, including characters from The Jungle Book. {{p:4}} drew a dog, saying dogs were loyal, cheerful and fun to spend time with, provided exercise, and were cute when tired. {{p:1}} drew fish, which his daughters currently had as pets; he said he was not keen on pets generally but considered fish low-maintenance, explaining that a feeder could feed them during a couple of weeks away, the water needed changing every couple of months, and plants could be added. He noted that the fish kept dying.

### Price, costs and market
{{p:1}} said the expected selling price was 25 euros, based on information from {{p:4}}. The product was intended for international sales, not just Europe, and the target production cost was 12.5 euros per unit. He clarified that this was not the profit margin because overheads and other costs still had to be deducted; the overhead costs would determine how many units the team projected to sell.

### Initial remote-control requirements and concepts
{{p:2}} said remote-control buttons could be too small and difficult to press, and suggested making them easy to press because that was the device’s main function. {{p:1}} summarized the desired device as robust, so it would not be damaged easily, and easy to use and see, with accessible buttons.

{{p:3}} asked whether the brief was for a television remote or a combined remote for systems such as TV/video or TV/DVD, noting that having five remotes at home was annoying. {{p:1}} said he would confirm the scope, but agreed that having three or four devices around a room was frustrating and raised the possibility of one device for all remotes. {{p:4}} added that market research found people were often confused by the number of buttons. She also observed that a remote could be left elsewhere in the room, forcing someone to get up to retrieve it, and suggested considering a remote that could move around the room. {{p:3}} joked about it coming when called; {{p:4}} suggested that might be a future possibility when people could talk to their television.

{{p:1}} noted a tension between combining devices and keeping the remote simple, with few buttons, and said the team needed a design that anyone could use. He suggested that users’ growing familiarity with remote controls might allow devices to become more complicated over time. {{p:2}} proposed better instructions and asked whether the work covered the remote itself or its instructions. {{p:4}} described research into cutting-edge handheld devices, many of which resembled mini-laptops, and suggested a miniature computer that could control a television, stereo and future devices added to the system.

### Work for the next session and scope clarification
{{p:1}} said there were five minutes left in the meeting and that the next meeting would be in 30 minutes. He outlined the work: a working design for Industrial Design, a technical-functions design for User Interface Design, and a user-requirements specification for Marketing. Specific instructions would be sent by each person’s personal coach. The group confirmed it understood the objectives for the next 30 minutes.

{{p:3}} said she was still unclear what the remote was for and asked whether it should be multifunctional or whether the team should decide as they worked. {{p:2}} recalled that it had been described as a television remote and suggested sticking to that unless told otherwise. {{p:1}} agreed that later information or meetings might change the direction, but said that for now the team should design a TV remote. The new device should be more user-friendly and trendier, with the aim of reaching a bigger audience and gaining more market share. The work would be divided into functional design, conceptual design and detailed design. The designers would contribute through the phases and meet during the day to develop a better solution; they would make various designs through the day toward that goal.

### Whiteboard exercise
As a tool-training exercise, {{p:1}} asked everyone to draw their favourite animal on the whiteboard to check that it worked. There were some microphone and camera issues while participants moved to the board. {{p:3}} drew a cat, describing cats as independent, intelligent, affectionate and able to look after themselves. {{p:2}} drew a bear, saying he liked bears partly because many cartoon characters were based on bears, including characters from The Jungle Book. {{p:4}} drew a dog, saying dogs were loyal, cheerful and fun to spend time with, provided exercise, and were cute when tired. {{p:1}} drew fish, which his daughters currently had as pets; he said he was not keen on pets generally but considered fish low-maintenance, explaining that a feeder could feed them during a couple of weeks away, the water needed changing every couple of months, and plants could be added. He noted that the fish kept dying.

### Price, costs and market
{{p:1}} said the expected selling price was 25 euros, based on information from {{p:4}}. The product was intended for international sales, not just Europe, and the target production cost was 12.5 euros per unit. He clarified that this was not the profit margin because overheads and other costs still had to be deducted; the overhead costs would determine how many units the team projected to sell.

### Initial remote-control requirements and concepts
{{p:2}} said remote-control buttons could be too small and difficult to press, and suggested making them easy to press because that was the device’s main function. {{p:1}} summarized the desired device as robust, so it would not be damaged easily, and easy to use and see, with accessible buttons.

{{p:3}} asked whether the brief was for a television remote or a combined remote for systems such as TV/video or TV/DVD, noting that having five remotes at home was annoying. {{p:1}} said he would confirm the scope, but agreed that having three or four devices around a room was frustrating and raised the possibility of one device for all remotes. {{p:4}} added that market research found people were often confused by the number of buttons. She also observed that a remote could be left elsewhere in the room, forcing someone to get up to retrieve it, and suggested considering a remote that could move around the room. {{p:3}} joked about it coming when called; {{p:4}} suggested that might be a future possibility when people could talk to their television.

{{p:1}} noted a tension between combining devices and keeping the remote simple, with few buttons, and said the team needed a design that anyone could use. He suggested that users’ growing familiarity with remote controls might allow devices to become more complicated over time. {{p:2}} proposed better instructions and asked whether the work covered the remote itself or its instructions. {{p:4}} described research into cutting-edge handheld devices, many of which resembled mini-laptops, and suggested a miniature computer that could control a television, stereo and future devices added to the system.

### Work for the next session and scope clarification
{{p:1}} said there were five minutes left in the meeting and that the next meeting would be in 30 minutes. He outlined the work: a working design for Industrial Design, a technical-functions design for User Interface Design, and a user-requirements specification for Marketing. Specific instructions would be sent by each person's personal coach. The group confirmed it understood the objectives for the next 30 minutes.

{{p:3}} said she was still unclear what the remote was for and asked whether it should be multifunctional or whether the team should decide as they worked. {{p:2}} recalled that it had been described as a television remote and suggested sticking to that unless told otherwise. {{p:1}} agreed that later information or meetings might change the direction, but said that for now the team should design a TV remote. The team would break off and work there; {{p:1}} would write up minutes, and they would reconvene in half an hour.","actionItems":[],"notCommitments":[{"i":34,"reason":"This is a general description of the design handoff across phases, not a specific commitment to perform an action."}]}

{"mom":"### Meeting purpose and project constraints
{{p:1}} opened by noting that there were three presentations and 40 minutes for the meeting to consider the options. The project requirements included limiting the remote to television control, a corporate logo, colour scheme and slogan, and removing teletext because it was becoming dated as internet use grew. The team had not obtained further information about teletext; {{p:1}} said the corporate image information had arrived by email. The television-only scope was intended to prevent the project becoming too complex and putting time to market at risk. {{p:1}} stressed that quick delivery was critical, with about four hours remaining in the project window, and that a simple product addressing major consumer concerns should take priority over optional extras.

### Industrial design presentation: remote components and power
{{p:2}} presented research on the working design of a television remote, based on research into existing models found on the internet. The presentation covered the remote’s components and how they interact with the television: a power supply, likely batteries, user-interface buttons, an internal chip, and an infrared sender; the television contains the receiver. The battery supply could use two or four batteries, depending on the design. {{p:2}} explained that pressing a button sends a message to the chip, which interprets the selected button and sends the appropriate message to the infrared sender. A battery was preferred because a cable would undermine the remote’s portability, and infrared had worked successfully with a reasonably powered battery without requiring the user to point directly at the television. {{p:2}} drew the system on a board after having difficulty presenting it in PowerPoint.

### User-interface presentation and button simplicity
{{p:3}} presented technical functions for a television remote: volume up and down, channel selection by number or channel up and down, and switching the television on or off, possibly using standby. Comparing two example remotes, {{p:3}} preferred the simpler, more user-friendly design, with large, clearly labelled buttons, symbols as well as words, and some colour. {{p:1}} reminded the group that the product must carry the company’s logo, corporate colour and slogan, based on an email requirement; the existing example appeared to show red as its only colour. The group discussed removing video-related controls, including a circular section, because the product was intended for television only.

{{p:3}} initially suggested that numbers one through six plus channel up and down might suffice, questioning how often users needed seven, eight and nine. {{p:1}} noted that viewers had five standard channels at the time, the BBC had introduced a further six, and the number of channels was expanding, including through Sky and other services. {{p:3}} observed that cable and satellite services might use a separate remote for their larger channel ranges. The group considered keeping all ten digits, with a short delay allowing multiple digits to be entered, so users could access any channel number. {{p:2}} noted that a tenth key could act as a digit-combination function; {{p:1}} agreed that the approach would allow numbers such as 50 to be entered. The group discussed keeping the design user-friendly while accommodating future channels.

### Market research and consumer needs
{{p:4}} reported that the team had researched desired remote-control functions using a questionnaire. Three quarters of respondents found remote controls ugly, and an even higher proportion would pay more for a fancier-looking model. Respondents rarely used picture, brightness and audio-setting buttons; they focused on channel, volume and power buttons. The most common frustration was losing the remote somewhere in the room, followed by difficulty learning a new remote’s buttons and functions. Younger respondents were more receptive to speech recognition, while interest declined among people around 35 to 45 and older; many older respondents were unsure whether they wanted the feature.

{{p:4}} recommended a sleek, good-looking, high-tech design with fewer buttons, focused on channels, power and volume. A small LCD menu for less-used functions and speech recognition were raised as possibilities, with younger consumers potentially a target market. {{p:4}} suggested speech recognition might help locate a lost remote, but warned that using speech to change channels could make the television respond to its own audio. {{p:2}} cautioned that speech-recognition technology might be too advanced and exceed the 12.50 budget. The group also considered a lost-remote alert: {{p:2}} proposed a sensor or buzzer that could be activated from a button kept in a fixed place, but {{p:4}} noted this would mean adding a second product and likely increase cost. {{p:3}} suggested a simple whistle- or clap-responsive key-ring device; {{p:1}} preferred avoiding a separate product and discussed triggering the remote with a sharp sound.

### Agreed direction for core and additional functions
The group favoured a simple lost-remote finder as a potential differentiator because losing the remote was the most frequently reported frustration. They discussed speech recognition but considered its development time, cost and risk of the television accidentally triggering the remote. {{p:2}} suggested concentrating on a sound-response feature for now, and {{p:1}} said any additional feature had to be simple and quick to implement. {{p:3}} noted that people of different ages could clap, whereas some might not be able to whistle. The group therefore settled on a clap option rather than a whistle, aiming for an accessible, simple feature that could help address the lost-remote problem.

The group agreed to omit teletext, since management considered it outdated in light of internet use. They also discussed retaining ten number keys and enabling multi-digit channel entry, with a one- or two-second interval for pressing another digit. {{p:2}} estimated that a 14-button remote would be manageable to explain in a user guide, but the later function count was 16. The group considered a menu for infrequently used functions, including brightness, contrast and audio settings, while keeping the frequently used controls visible. {{p:2}} noted that users need to tune a television when setting it up and may need to retune when replacing a television; {{p:1}} said relying on televisions to tune themselves would make the remote inoperable in some circumstances and would not suit an international, lower-cost market. {{p:4}} pointed out that replacement remotes may be used with older televisions, supporting retention of a tuning function.

{{p:3}} proposed a sliding lower panel that would conceal less-used controls while keeping the front uncluttered. {{p:1}} and {{p:2}} supported hiding detailed functions at the back, and {{p:3}} said this could also suit older users who prefer labelled buttons to navigating menus. The group noted that it still needed to decide which controls would go on the front and which on the back. Front controls discussed were the ten number buttons, volume up and down, channel up and down, mute, power and standby. {{p:4}} counted the proposed front controls as 16 buttons. The discussion of back-panel functions included brightness, contrast, audio functions, and television tuning up and down; {{p:4}} suggested an enter/select button to confirm a tuning choice. The group agreed to keep audio functions simple, with volume up and down, and to investigate whether other sound options such as Dolby surround controls needed to be included.

{{p:3}} raised whether the standby function should be discouraged because of electricity use, citing advertisements about wasted energy; the example given was that leaving a television on standby could power Blackpool for a period. The group discussed whether this could deter purchasers who did not already have a standby-equipped television. {{p:1}} asked whether standby should remain on the front, and {{p:3}} suggested making it smaller as a compromise.

### Follow-up, responsibilities and next meeting
{{p:1}} said the team needed decisions on the remote’s functions so each person could identify their task before the next meeting. The team would report progress and identify what had or had not been achieved at that meeting. Any new information relevant to others’ decisions should be shared by email as soon as possible rather than held until the next meeting; information received just before the meeting could be brought along for discussion. {{p:2}} suggested that one person prepare a list of the functions and report it at the start of the next meeting, including the front and back controls. The group also agreed to research the additional audio functions and return with findings. {{p:1}} said they would write the minutes. The next meeting was expected in 40 minutes, though {{p:1}} was unsure of the exact timing."}

{"summary":"{{p:1}} opened the meeting on new project requirements, noting three presentations and 40 minutes for discussion. The team had previously agreed the remote would control television only; teletext was considered outdated, though no one had obtained further information on it. {{p:1}} had received the corporate-image information by email. The project had about four hours remaining, making quick delivery a priority. {{p:2}} presented research on remote components and operation: a power source, likely two or four batteries, buttons, a chip, an infrared sender, and a television receiver. Battery power was preferred to avoid a cable, and infrared was considered reliable without requiring the remote to be pointed directly at the television. {{p:3}} (Louisa) favored a simpler, user-friendly remote with large, clearly labelled buttons, symbols and some colour; {{p:1}} reminded the team the product must use the corporate logo, colour scheme and slogan. The group agreed to remove video-specific controls and teletext, retain all ten number keys to support multi-digit channel entry, and include channel up/down. The design should have a clean, simple front and less-used functions hidden behind a sliding panel. Marketing research presented by {{p:4}} found that three quarters of respondents considered remotes ugly, more respondents would pay extra for a better-looking model, channel, volume and power controls were used most, and losing a remote and learning a replacement were major frustrations. Younger respondents were more receptive to speech recognition, with interest declining among older age groups. The team prioritized a quick, simple, TV-only product because time to market was critical. A clap-activated locator was favored as a potentially inexpensive way to address lost remotes; speech recognition and an LCD menu were not settled, with cost, complexity, development time and accidental activation concerns noted. The proposed front controls totaled 16: ten number buttons, volume up/down, mute, power, standby and channel up/down. Relevant new information should be emailed before then so it could inform decisions.","mom":"### Meeting purpose and project constraints
{{p:1}} opened by noting that there were three presentations and 40 minutes for the meeting to consider the options. The project requirements included limiting the remote to television control, a corporate logo, colour scheme and slogan, and removing teletext because it was becoming dated as internet use grew. The team had not obtained further information about teletext; {{p:1}} said the corporate-image information had arrived by email. The television-only scope was intended to prevent the project becoming too complex and putting time to market at risk. {{p:1}} stressed that quick delivery was critical, with about four hours remaining in the project window, and that a simple product addressing major consumer concerns should take priority over optional extras. The project was intended for an international market and the lower end of the cost scale.

### Industrial design presentation: remote components and power
{{p:2}} presented research on the working design of a television remote, based on research into existing models found on the internet. The presentation covered the remote’s components and how they interact with the television: a power supply, likely batteries, user-interface buttons, an internal chip, and an infrared sender; the television contains the receiver. The battery supply could use two or four batteries, depending on the design. {{p:2}} explained that pressing a button sends a message to the chip, which interprets the selected button and sends the appropriate message to the infrared sender. A battery was preferred because a cable would undermine the remote’s portability, and infrared had worked successfully with a reasonably powered battery without requiring the user to point directly at the television. {{p:2}} drew the system on a board after having difficulty presenting it in PowerPoint.

### User-interface presentation and button simplicity
{{p:3}} presented technical functions for a television remote: volume up and down, channel selection by number or channel up and down, and switching the television on or off, possibly using standby. Comparing two example remotes, {{p:3}} preferred the simpler, more user-friendly design, with large, clearly labelled buttons, symbols as well as words, and some colour. {{p:1}} reminded the group that the product must carry the company’s logo, corporate colour and slogan, based on an email requirement; the example appeared to show red as its only colour. The group discussed removing video-related controls, including a circular section, because the product was intended for television only.

{{p:3}} initially suggested that numbers one through six plus channel up and down might suffice, questioning how often users needed seven, eight and nine. {{p:1}} noted that viewers had five standard channels at the time, the BBC had introduced a further six, and the number of channels was expanding, including through Sky and other services. {{p:3}} observed that cable and satellite services might use a separate remote for their larger channel ranges. The group considered keeping all ten digits, with a short delay allowing multiple digits to be entered, so users could access any channel number. {{p:2}} noted that a tenth key could act as a digit-combination function; {{p:1}} agreed that the approach would allow numbers such as 50 to be entered. The group discussed keeping the design user-friendly while accommodating future channels.

### Market research and consumer needs
{{p:4}} reported that the team had researched desired remote-control functions using a questionnaire. Three quarters of respondents found remote controls ugly, and an even higher proportion would pay more for a fancier-looking model. Respondents rarely used picture, brightness and audio-setting buttons; they focused on channel, volume and power buttons. The most common frustration was losing the remote somewhere in the room, followed by difficulty learning a new remote’s buttons and functions. Younger respondents were more receptive to speech recognition, while interest declined among people around 35 to 45 and older; many older respondents were unsure whether they wanted the feature.

{{p:4}} recommended a sleek, good-looking, high-tech design with fewer buttons, focused on channels, power and volume. A small LCD menu for less-used functions and speech recognition were raised as possibilities, with younger consumers potentially a target market. {{p:4}} suggested speech recognition might help locate a lost remote, but warned that using speech to change channels could make the television respond to its own audio. {{p:2}} cautioned that speech-recognition technology might be too advanced and exceed the 12.50 budget. The group also considered a lost-remote alert: {{p:2}} proposed a sensor or buzzer that could be activated from a button kept in a fixed place, but {{p:4}} noted this would mean adding a second product and likely increase cost. {{p:3}} suggested a simple whistle- or clap-responsive key-ring device; {{p:1}} preferred avoiding a separate product and discussed triggering the remote with a sharp sound.

### Agreed direction for core and additional functions
The group favoured a simple lost-remote finder as a potential differentiator because losing the remote was the most frequently reported frustration. They discussed speech recognition but considered its development time, cost and risk of the television accidentally triggering the remote. {{p:2}} suggested concentrating on a sound-response feature for now, and {{p:1}} said any additional feature had to be simple and quick to implement. {{p:3}} noted that people of different ages could clap, whereas some might not be able to whistle. The group therefore settled on a clap option rather than a whistle, aiming for an accessible, simple feature that could help address the lost-remote problem.

The group agreed to omit teletext, since management considered it outdated in light of internet use. They also discussed retaining ten number keys and enabling multi-digit channel entry, with a one- or two-second interval for pressing another digit. {{p:2}} estimated that a 14-button remote would be manageable to explain in a user guide, but the later function count was 16. The group considered a menu for infrequently used functions, including brightness, contrast and audio settings, while keeping the frequently used controls visible. {{p:2}} noted that users need to tune a television when setting it up and may need to retune when replacing a television; {{p:1}} said relying on televisions to tune themselves would make the remote inoperable in some circumstances and would not suit an international, lower-cost market. {{p:4}} pointed out that replacement remotes may be used with older televisions, supporting retention of a tuning function.

{{p:3}} proposed a sliding lower panel that would conceal less-used controls while keeping the front uncluttered. {{p:1}} and {{p:2}} supported hiding detailed functions at the back, and {{p:3}} said this could also suit older users who prefer labelled buttons to navigating menus. The group noted that it still needed to decide which controls would go on the front and which on the back. Front controls discussed were the ten number buttons, volume up and down, channel up and down, mute, power and standby. {{p:4}} counted the proposed front controls as 16 buttons. The discussion of back-panel functions included brightness, contrast, audio functions, and television tuning up and down; {{p:4}} suggested an enter/select button to confirm a tuning choice. The group agreed to keep audio functions simple, with volume up and down, and to investigate whether other sound options such as Dolby surround controls needed to be included.

{{p:3}} raised whether the standby function should be discouraged because of electricity use, citing advertisements about wasted energy; the example given was that leaving a television on standby could power Blackpool for a period. The group discussed whether this could deter purchasers who did not already have a standby-equipped television. {{p:1}} asked whether standby should remain on the front, and {{p:3}} suggested making it smaller as a compromise.

### Follow-up, responsibilities and next meeting
{{p:1}} said the team needed decisions on the remote’s functions so each person could identify their task before the next meeting. The team would report progress and identify what had or had not been achieved at that meeting. Any new information relevant to others’ decisions should be shared by email as soon as possible rather than held until the next meeting; information received just before the meeting could be brought along for discussion. {{p:2}} suggested that one person prepare a list of the functions and report it at the start of the next meeting, including the front and back controls. The group also agreed to research the additional audio functions and return with findings. {{p:1}} said they would write the minutes. They agreed on a kinetic power supply to avoid replacing batteries, a simple push-button interface rather than a scroll wheel, and a simple circuit board to control cost; speech recognition would be an optional finder function, subject to checking its cost and whether it affects the board. Marketing research highlighted a fancy, distinctive look as the top priority, technological innovation second, and ease of use third; the team discussed fruit-and-vegetable fashion trends but rejected making the whole remote or its buttons trend-shaped, while considering rubber buttons and a rubber case as a more restrained way to convey a soft feel. The team settled on a single-curved case, simple button shapes and clear, self-explanatory labels, with a distinct apple-shaped standby button that could add colour; they also noted that rubber buttons require a rubber case. They discussed—but did not decide on—changeable cases, citing uncertain demand, production and packaging costs, and the need to retain the company logo; future feature variants could address specialist markets, while the basic model should target the international market. {"mom":"### Previous meeting recap and agenda
{{p:1}} said the minutes from the last meeting had not been sent successfully, so they gave a brief recap: the remote would incorporate the company logo in its colour scheme; the device design would stay simple to help finish the project on time; and it would have two pages, with the most wanted customer features on the front and backup features on the second page to meet technical requirements without making customers see them often. {{p:2}} proposed that the team review the presentations and discuss decisions as they went; {{p:1}} agreed to decide on each issue when its presentation was being discussed, while the details were visible, rather than returning to all the presentations later. {{p:3}} agreed this would be better for immediate discussion.

### Components and power supply
{{p:2}} described the remote’s components as the user interface and buttons, a chip, a sender, and a power supply. The power options were a standard battery, a hand-wound dynamo, a kinetic mechanism like those used in watches that recharge through movement, and solar cells. The kinetic option would avoid battery replacement but might cost more. {{p:2}} preferred kinetic power to avoid batteries running out and needing replacement. In response to {{p:1}} asking how it would recharge, {{p:2}} said it used an internal mechanism, possibly ball bearings, that generated power through movement; users would move or shake the remote to power it.

### Buttons, circuit boards, and speech recognition
{{p:2}} said Real Reaction supplied the component options and suggested choosing from its options for speed and convenience. Button options included standard integrated push buttons and a scroll wheel, potentially for volume. Rubber buttons would require a rubber case. {{p:2}} said button choice did not appear to make much difference to button cost itself, but it affected the circuit board. The supplier offered simple, regular, and advanced boards at different prices; a scroll wheel required at least a regular chip, which was in a higher price range, while standard push buttons required a simple chip and kept costs down. {{p:3}} added that a scroll wheel looked bulky and less sleek, offered no clear benefit, and affected materials and price. The team settled on simple push buttons rather than a scroll wheel.

{{p:2}} described a speech-recognition unit available through the supplier. It would add a component and cost, but would not substantially affect the remote’s size. The team was initially unsure whether it required a more advanced circuit board. {{p:3}} interpreted the example as a separate finder function that would repeat a recorded message rather than send a signal to the television or operate remote functions; the examples included calling out to locate the remote. {{p:2}} and {{p:3}} agreed it could be treated as an extra rather than changing the basic circuit board. {{p:1}} summarized the proposed basic configuration as a simple circuit board and simple push buttons, with speech recognition as an optional extra; the group supported finding out its cost before making a final decision. {{p:3}} noted the information did not specify cost, only that the technology was already in coffee machines, and {{p:2}} said they should find out the cost and decide later to avoid having to change everything at the last minute. The possible finder feature was distinguished from competing as a general voice-recognition feature, since existing products offered good voice recognition and the team’s device might not cover their functions. The team considered marketing the feature as a way to find the remote. {{p:2}} also noted that different languages could complicate voice recognition for an international market, and {{p:4}} observed the product was intended to be inexpensive, limiting how much could be invested in it.

### Market positioning and specialist models
{{p:3}} reported that the remotes reviewed were generally not sleek, had many rubber buttons, and varied in size; curved cases were available. One higher-end model had voice recognition integrated with remote-control functions and could control four devices, including TV, cable, satellite, video, DVD, and audio. {{p:3}} suggested not competing directly with such multifunction remotes, but positioning this product differently as a finder for a lost remote. {{p:3}} also mentioned children’s remotes with fewer buttons, bright colours, and programming that restricted access to selected channels, but questioned whether that market fit the project. {{p:1}} said the intended market was international rather than local and suggested a basic model with optional, separately priced features for specialist market segments. The group agreed not to focus the basic product on specialist remotes such as children’s models.

### Appearance, fashion trends, and materials
{{p:4}} summarized the market research: customers wanted a product that looked and felt fancy rather than merely functional; technological innovation was the second priority, and ease of use was third. Fashion research in Paris and Milan indicated interest in fruit-and-vegetable themes and spongy-feeling materials, reportedly different from the previous year’s trend. {{p:4}} suggested highlighting a stylish design, adding an innovation such as locating the remote with a hand clap, keeping the product easy to use with fewer buttons and functions, and possibly incorporating fruit or vegetable shapes, rubber buttons, or even a banana- or courgette-shaped remote.

{{p:3}} cautioned that fruit-shaped buttons might make the remote harder to use. {{p:1}} emphasized that confusing shapes could mislead users and that functionality mattered because customers disliked having to read instructions. The group discussed incorporating a trend more subtly, such as making only the standby button an apple while keeping other controls clear. {{p:2}} and {{p:4}} raised concern that fashion trends change, making a highly themed design risky; {{p:1}} noted that changing the whole product could require changes to production schedules and moulds and leave outdated stock that might need to be discounted. The team favored a more universal design and considered a rubber case as a less trend-dependent way to provide a softer feel. {{p:2}} explained that a rubber case required rubber buttons, and {{p:3}} observed that curved or double-curved surfaces could help create a sleek appearance. The group’s eventual direction was a standard rubber case with standard rubber buttons, rather than elaborate fruit-shaped controls or a highly changeable fashion design.

The team also discussed replaceable outer cases, like those available for some Nokia phones, as a way to change appearance while keeping the buttons and remote functions the same. {{p:2}} questioned whether this would add production complexity and cost; {{p:3}} noted each new case would still need the company logo, and {{p:2}} raised the question of whether the secondary market would be large enough. {{p:4}} was not convinced people would buy changeable covers for a remote, unlike mobile phones that people carry visibly. {{p:1}} pointed out that a logo badge could be attached to casings of different colours, but the group did not decide to pursue interchangeable cases.

### Button labelling and design
{{p:3}} warned that button labels and shapes should not conflict: for example, triangular volume controls might suggest the opposite direction from their actual function. {{p:2}} suggested putting the word volume beside the controls and marking the buttons themselves up and down. {{p:1}} recalled that the design was intended to have a limited number of buttons and noted the count had been reduced to 16. The group agreed to keep button shapes simple and labels straightforward and self-explanatory. For the distinct standby button, {{p:3}} suggested an apple as a recognizable shape, and {{p:1}}, {{p:2}}, and {{p:4}} supported an apple-shaped standby button; {{p:3}} suggested it could be red to add colour, subject to confirming the company colour scheme and logo requirements.

### Case curvature, packaging, and decisions
{{p:3}} identified three case options: flat, single-curved, and double-curved. The group discussed whether curves could make the remote look sleeker, while {{p:1}} noted that a standard case could stack for shop storage and that unusual shapes might require special packaging, whose cost could be significant relative to the product’s total cost. After considering a single curve as a compromise between single and double curvature, the group decided on a single-curved case. The decisions recapped near the end were kinetic power, rubber push buttons and a rubber case, a simple circuit board to keep costs down, and speech recognition as a possible finder extra that would not affect the circuit board. The group did not settle the logo or colour scheme and noted a sticker or badge as a possible way to apply the logo. {{p:1}} asked the team to continue developing the decisions; {{p:2}} and {{p:3}} were assigned to work on the physical model using Plasticine."}

{"summary":"The team reviewed the previous direction: incorporate the company logo and its colour scheme, keep the remote simple, and put customers’ most-wanted features on the front with backup technical features on a second page. They agreed on a kinetic power supply to avoid replacing batteries, a simple push-button interface rather than a scroll wheel, and a simple circuit board to control cost; speech recognition would be an optional finder function, subject to checking its cost and whether it affects the board. Marketing research highlighted a fancy, distinctive look as the top priority, technological innovation second, and ease of use third; the team discussed fruit-and-vegetable fashion trends but rejected making the whole remote or its buttons trend-shaped, while considering rubber buttons and a rubber case as a more restrained way to convey a soft feel. The team settled on a single-curved case, simple button shapes and clear, self-explanatory labels, with a distinct apple-shaped standby button that could add colour; they also noted that rubber buttons require a rubber case. They discussed—but did not decide on—changeable cases, citing uncertain demand, production and packaging costs, and the need to retain the company logo; future feature variants could address specialist markets, while the basic model should target the international market. The industrial designer and user-interface representative were asked to continue developing the design, including through modelling with Plasticine.","mom":"### Previous meeting recap and agenda
{{p:1}} said the minutes from the last meeting had not been sent successfully, so they gave a brief recap: the remote would incorporate the company logo in its colour scheme; the device design would stay simple to help finish the project on time; and it would have two pages, with the most wanted customer features on the front and backup features on the second page to meet technical requirements without making customers see them often. {{p:2}} proposed that the team review the presentations and discuss decisions as they went; {{p:1}} agreed to decide on each issue when its presentation was being discussed, while the details were visible, rather than returning to all the presentations later. {{p:3}} agreed this would be better for immediate discussion.

### Components and power supply
{{p:2}} described the remote’s components as the user interface and buttons, a chip, a sender, and a power supply. The power options were a standard battery, a hand-wound dynamo, a kinetic mechanism like those used in watches that recharge through movement, and solar cells. The kinetic option would avoid battery replacement but might cost more. {{p:2}} preferred kinetic power to avoid batteries running out and needing replacement. In response to {{p:1}} asking how it would recharge, {{p:2}} said it used an internal mechanism, possibly ball bearings, that generated power through movement; users would move or shake the remote to power it.

### Buttons, circuit boards, and speech recognition
{{p:2}} said Real Reaction supplied the component options and suggested choosing from its options for speed and convenience. Button options included standard integrated push buttons and a scroll wheel, potentially for volume. Rubber buttons would require a rubber case. {{p:2}} said button choice did not appear to make much difference to button cost itself, but it affected the circuit board. The supplier offered simple, regular, and advanced boards at different prices; a scroll wheel required at least a regular chip, which was in a higher price range, while standard push buttons required a simple chip and kept costs down. {{p:3}} added that a scroll wheel looked bulky and less sleek, offered no clear benefit, and affected materials and price. The team settled on simple push buttons rather than a scroll wheel.

{{p:2}} described a speech-recognition unit available through the supplier. It would add a component and cost, but would not substantially affect the remote’s size. The team was initially unsure whether it required a more advanced circuit board. {{p:3}} interpreted the example as a separate finder function that would repeat a recorded message rather than send a signal to the television or operate remote functions; the examples included calling out to locate the remote. {{p:2}} and {{p:3}} agreed it could be treated as an extra rather than changing the basic circuit board. {{p:1}} summarized the proposed basic configuration as a simple circuit board and simple push buttons, with speech recognition as an optional extra; the group supported finding out its cost before making a final decision. {{p:3}} noted the information did not specify cost, only that the technology was already in coffee machines, and {{p:2}} said they should find out the cost and decide later to avoid having to change everything at the last minute. The possible finder feature was distinguished from competing as a general voice-recognition feature, since existing products offered good voice recognition and the team’s device might not cover their functions. The team considered marketing the feature as a way to find the remote. {{p:2}} also noted that different languages could complicate voice recognition for an international market, and {{p:4}} observed the product was intended to be inexpensive, limiting how much could be invested in it.

### Market positioning and specialist models
{{p:3}} reported that the remotes reviewed were generally not sleek, had many rubber buttons, and varied in size; curved cases were available. One higher-end model had voice recognition integrated with remote-control functions and could control four devices, including TV, cable, satellite, video, DVD, and audio. {{p:3}} suggested not competing directly with such multifunction remotes, but positioning this product differently as a finder for a lost remote. {{p:3}} also mentioned children’s remotes with fewer buttons, bright colours, and programming that restricted access to selected channels, but questioned whether that market fit the project. {{p:1}} said the intended market was international rather than local and suggested a basic model with optional, separately priced features for specialist market segments. The group agreed not to focus the basic product on specialist remotes such as children’s models.

### Appearance, fashion trends, and materials
{{p:4}} summarized the market research: customers wanted a product that looked and felt fancy rather than merely functional; technological innovation was the second priority, and ease of use was third. Fashion research in Paris and Milan indicated interest in fruit-and-vegetable themes and spongy-feeling materials, reportedly different from the previous year’s trend. {{p:4}} suggested highlighting a stylish design, adding an innovation such as locating the remote with a hand clap, keeping the product easy to use with fewer buttons and functions, and possibly incorporating fruit or vegetable shapes, rubber buttons, or even a banana- or courgette-shaped remote.

{{p:3}} cautioned that fruit-shaped buttons might make the remote harder to use. {{p:1}} emphasized that confusing shapes could mislead users and that functionality mattered because customers disliked having to read instructions. The group discussed incorporating a trend more subtly, such as making only the standby button an apple while keeping other controls clear. {{p:2}} and {{p:4}} raised concern that fashion trends change, making a highly themed design risky; {{p:1}} noted that changing the whole product could require changes to production schedules and moulds and leave outdated stock that might need to be discounted. The team favored a more universal design and considered a rubber case as a less trend-dependent way to provide a softer feel. {{p:2}} explained that a rubber case required rubber buttons, and {{p:3}} observed that curved or double-curved surfaces could help create a sleek appearance. The group’s eventual direction was a standard rubber case with standard rubber buttons, rather than elaborate fruit-shaped controls or a highly changeable fashion design.

The team also discussed replaceable outer cases, like those available for some Nokia phones, as a way to change appearance while keeping the buttons and remote functions the same. {{p:2}} questioned whether this would add production complexity and cost; {{p:3}} noted each new case would still need the company logo, and {{p:2}} raised the question of whether the secondary market would be large enough. {{p:4}} was not convinced people would buy changeable covers for a remote, unlike mobile phones that people carry visibly. {{p:1}} pointed out that a logo badge could be attached to casings of different colours, but the group did not decide to pursue interchangeable cases.

### Button labelling and design
{{p:3}} warned that button labels and shapes should not conflict: for example, triangular volume controls might suggest the opposite direction from their actual function. {{p:2}} suggested putting the word volume beside the controls and marking the buttons themselves up and down. {{p:1}} recalled that the design was intended to have a limited number of buttons and noted the count had been reduced to 16. The group agreed to keep button shapes simple and labels straightforward and self-explanatory. For the distinct standby button, {{p:3}} suggested an apple as a recognizable shape, and {{p:1}}, {{p:2}}, and {{p:4}} supported an apple-shaped standby button; {{p:3}} suggested it could be red to add colour, subject to confirming the company colour scheme and logo requirements.

### Case curvature, packaging, and decisions
{{p:3}} identified three case options: flat, single-curved, and double-curved. The group discussed whether curves could make the remote look sleeker, while {{p:1}} noted that a standard case could stack for shop storage and that unusual shapes might require special packaging, whose cost could be significant relative to the product’s total cost. After considering a single curve as a compromise between single and double curvature, the group decided on a single-curved case. The decisions recapped near the end were kinetic power, rubber push buttons and a rubber case, a simple circuit board to keep costs down, and speech recognition as a possible finder extra that would not affect the circuit board. The group did not settle the logo or colour scheme and noted a sticker or badge as a possible way to apply the logo. {{p:1}} asked the team to continue developing the decisions; {{p:2}} and {{p:3}} were assigned to work on the physical model using Plasticine.

### Follow-up actions
{{p:2}} said they would look into whether the speech-recognition/finder component requires a more advanced circuit board (line 93). The group agreed to find out the feature’s cost before making a final decision (lines 348–350). {{p:3}} said they would check the information about the feature (line 341). {{p:1}} assigned {{p:2}} and {{p:3}} to develop the design/model using Plasticine (lines 1172–1173)."}

ES2014d: {"title":"Remote-control prototype evaluation and budget redesign","summary":"The team presented and reviewed a remote-control prototype with curved sides, a pull-down panel for extra function buttons, a company-logo badge, and an apple/cherry motif; they preferred the cherry to avoid the Apple/Mac association. They assessed the prototype against market-research and finance criteria on a scale where 1 meant true, 7 meant false, and 4 was neutral, discussing appearance, technical innovation, ease of use, fashion appeal, and fit with Real Reaction’s corporate identity. The original design was estimated at 13.7 against a production-cost ceiling of 12.5, so the team explored savings while weighing kinetic power against a battery and voice recognition for finding a misplaced remote; they noted that the sample sensor and speaker were major cost items, and that the simple chip and speaker were separate components. They chose a plastic rather than rubber case to bring the design within budget while retaining the kinetic feature and speech recognition; the revised estimate was 11.7, and after allowing for button supplements the team confirmed a total of 12.3, within budget, with about 0.8 remaining and a reported saving of two euros. They also settled on two special button colours in addition to the standard colour, kept the apple/cherry as a special button form, and discussed adding a second distinctive form, possibly lemon-shaped volume buttons; the hidden panel’s buttons could remain small and blue, and the remaining 0.2 could be reserved for profitability or other costs. The group agreed to evaluate the prototype as it stood before making changes, then reassess its criteria after the budget adjustments; they considered the revised design somewhat weaker on fashion and fanciness but retained its innovation, usability, and recognizable product features. In the project-process review, they said creativity had been adequately supported but meeting divisions and information flow could feel disjointed; teamwork went reasonably well, the whiteboard and digital pens helped, leadership was difficult for the team to assess because {{p:1}} was the project manager, and they identified the kinetic remote control and voice recognition as new ideas. They noted that final questionnaires and a meeting summary still needed completing, followed by a celebration, and {{p:1}} said the cost spreadsheet had not appeared to save at 12.3."}

{"mom":"### Prototype design and presentation
{{p:1}} and {{p:4}} initially worked through file-saving and window-navigation issues; after {{p:1}} said transferring the spreadsheet to My Documents had not worked, {{p:4}} advised closing the save window and locating the file elsewhere. {{p:1}} decided to redo it as the easiest option. The team then reviewed its prototype. {{p:3}} described the curved sides and display, a line indicating the pull-down panel, extra function buttons below it, and a company-logo badge; {{p:2}} added an apple-or-cherry design at the top. The team favored the cherry as more playful and summery, while noting a possible Apple/Mac association. The small button labels were difficult to fit, so {{p:3}} said the buttons used simple shapes, with the important volume controls made larger; {{p:2}} described distinguishing volume buttons in orange from channel buttons in blue. {{p:1}} cautioned that extra button colors could affect cost, since the original costing assumed only the red apple button would be a different color.

### Evaluation plan and production-cost options
{{p:1}} listed the prototype presentation, evaluation criteria, and finance as the remaining work, referring to criteria from the previous meeting. The prototype lacked the second layer, but otherwise included the red apple and buttons; the main change was button coloration. The group would also assess production feasibility. The target production cost was below €12.50. {{p:4}} proposed examining production costs using the prototype, and {{p:2}} asked to display the figures. {{p:1}} described the design as having a simple chip, kinetic-energy power source, single curved case, rubber case material, and push-button interface. The group discussed whether button-material supplements applied to one special button or all 16 buttons. {{p:1}} initially understood the red apple as the sole special-form button and wondered whether rubber counted as a special material; {{p:4}} thought the material supplement applied across the buttons rather than per button. They considered standard buttons with one special red apple button, with the remaining buttons in hard plastic, and noted that every design change had cost implications.

The initial costing was reported as €13.7 with all desired features, above the €12.50 limit. {{p:1}} said the current total needed to be reduced by at least 1.2 points. {{p:2}} identified a sample sensor and sample speaker for voice recognition as a significant added cost, putting the total at about 12.7, and suggested removing a special color to retain voice recognition. The team considered replacing kinetic power with a battery, which would save one point but would reintroduce the concern that batteries could run out and cause users to lose the remote. {{p:3}} preferred voice recognition as more impressive than having no battery; {{p:1}} clarified its intended purpose was to help locate a lost remote. The team also considered replacing the rubber case with plastic. {{p:1}} said plastic rather than rubber could reduce costs by two points, keep kinetic power and the sample sensor, and leave about 0.2 points to adjust by removing a special form or color. The group ultimately favored a plastic case, retaining kinetic power and voice recognition, and concluded this combination was within budget. {{p:2}} later calculated the revised cost as 12.3, with 0.8 points remaining; {{p:4}} said the redesign had saved two euros. The team noted the trade-off: a little less fashionability and fanciness, while retaining the other attributes and technical innovations.

### Prototype evaluation criteria and ratings
{{p:4}} explained that the design team made a prototype and the group evaluated it against criteria shaped by market research and finance. Ratings ran from 1 for true to 7 for false, with 4 neutral; a financial criterion would be added. The listed criteria were whether the product looked and felt fancy, demonstrated technical innovation, was easy to use, incorporated fashion to attract buyers, and was recognizable as a Real Reaction product. For fancy appearance, the group considered the single curve and spongy rubber feel; because the prototype did not have a double curve, they agreed on a rating around 2–3 and entered 2. For technical innovation, they discussed kinetic power and speech recognition and selected 2. They rated ease of use 1. For fashion, they considered the cherry design and sponginess and agreed on 2, while recognizing that the later move to a plastic case would reduce the soft feel. For brand recognition, they cited the logo, the product’s speech feature shared with the coffee machine, and its relationship to the company’s other products, including coffee makers and spacecraft; they settled on 2. {{p:4}} said the average was about 1.8, close to 2. They agreed that the prototype should be evaluated as it stood before making changes, and that the scores would need to be reassessed after adjustments.

### Adjustments to button forms and colors
The group debated how to count special-color and special-form supplements. {{p:1}} had originally counted the red apple as one special color and one special-form button. {{p:2}} and {{p:4}} discussed whether different colored volume buttons meant two or three special colors; {{p:4}} concluded that two color supplements were needed in addition to the original color. The team agreed that the blue volume buttons could be treated as standard and that the extra color count should be two. They also discussed enlarging the volume buttons and whether that would count as another special form. With the second button panel intended to be hidden, {{p:3}} suggested keeping its buttons small, round, and blue; {{p:2}} said the buttons used most often should look good, while the more functional controls could be simpler. {{p:4}} agreed that obvious controls for quickly changing channel or volume mattered most, whereas color differences were less important when users opened the panel and paid closer attention.

To retain some fashionability after changing the case to plastic, {{p:4}} proposed another fruit-shaped button, suggesting lemon shapes for the volume controls. {{p:2}} agreed. The group reasoned that the rubber case had required rubber buttons, but that they could now use plastic casing with the existing rubber buttons. They also discussed keeping the cherry as the special-form button, noting a possible Apple/Mac association with an apple design. {{p:2}} suggested leaving 0.2 points available for profitability or other needs, including possible legal costs. The group confirmed the redesigned product remained within the budget and that the second panel could use standard controls.

### Project-process and course evaluation
After completing the finance, spreadsheet, and redesign work, {{p:1}} moved the discussion to project process and evaluation of the course, including creativity, leadership, teamwork, and resources such as the whiteboard and digital pens. {{p:4}} said the divisions between meetings had sometimes felt arbitrary: related research and design discussions, such as examining remote-control curves and buttons, were split across meetings and did not always follow on naturally. {{p:1}} explained that the process was intended to resemble manufacturing practice: decide actions in a meeting, gather information between meetings, return to discuss findings, make changes, and repeat. {{p:1}} recorded that creativity had seemed adequate but that the flow of information on a given subject was sometimes disjointed. {{p:3}} felt a remote control was not the most creative project; {{p:4}} said the brief to design a television remote was restrictive and that the inexpensive product seemed unlike the company’s high-tech, cutting-edge range. {{p:2}} observed that choosing a familiar product gave the group something concrete to assess and improve within a set timeframe. The group also identified the kinetic-powered remote and voice recognition as new ideas, while noting that voice recognition was a different application of an existing technology.

{{p:2}} said teamwork went reasonably well because members brought separate ideas and discussed them. {{p:4}} felt the budget constrained what the team could do and questioned how well a low-cost remote fit with the company’s high-definition DVD and lightweight, portable seven-inch computer screens. {{p:3}} noted that it was difficult for others to assess leadership fairly because {{p:1}} was the project manager and leader. {{p:1}} said the computer had not worked as well as desired; {{p:4}} and {{p:3}} said the equipment had worked, though computers could be difficult at times. {{p:3}} questioned the value of the digital pens, asking how recordings of writing could be retrieved; {{p:4}} suggested a small chip might be plugged into something, and {{p:3}} thought the output might be a video.

### Closing tasks
{{p:1}} checked the closing requirements: confirm whether costs were within budget and the project had been evaluated, complete the final questionnaire and meeting summary, and then celebrate. {{p:4}} recalled two questionnaires and a report on the last meeting. {{p:1}} said the previous attempt to save the spreadsheet at 12.3 had not appeared to save anywhere, although the earlier figure had been different."}
