{"summary":"The team presented and reviewed a remote-control prototype with curved sides, a pull-down panel for extra function buttons, a company-logo badge, and an apple/cherry motif; they preferred the cherry to avoid the Apple/Mac association. They assessed the prototype against market-research and finance criteria on a scale where 1 meant true, 7 meant false, and 4 was neutral, discussing appearance, technical innovation, ease of use, fashion appeal, and fit with Real Reaction’s corporate identity. The original design was estimated at 13.7 against a production-cost ceiling of 12.5, so the team explored savings while weighing kinetic power against a battery and voice recognition for finding a misplaced remote; they noted that the sample sensor and speaker were major cost items, and that the simple chip and speaker were separate components. They chose a plastic rather than rubber case to bring the design within budget while retaining the kinetic feature and speech recognition; the revised estimate was 11.7, and after allowing for button supplements the team confirmed a total of 12.3, within budget, with about 0.8 remaining and a reported saving of two euros. They also settled on two special button colours in addition to the standard colour, kept the apple/cherry as a special button form, and discussed adding a second distinctive form, possibly lemon-shaped volume buttons; the hidden panel’s buttons could remain small and blue, and the remaining 0.2 could be reserved for profitability or other costs. The group agreed to evaluate the prototype as it stood before making changes, then reassess its criteria after the budget adjustments; they considered the revised design somewhat weaker on fashion and fanciness but retained its innovation, usability, and recognizable product features. In the project-process review, they said creativity had been adequately supported but meeting divisions and information flow could feel disjointed; teamwork went reasonably well, the whiteboard and digital pens helped, leadership was difficult for the team to assess because {{p:1}} was the project manager, and they identified the kinetic remote control and voice recognition as new ideas. They noted that final questionnaires and a meeting summary still needed completing, followed by a celebration, and {{p:1}} said the cost spreadsheet had not appeared to save at 12.3.","mom":"### Prototype design and presentation
{{p:1}} and {{p:4}} initially worked through file-saving and window-navigation issues; after {{p:1}} said transferring the spreadsheet to My Documents had not worked, {{p:4}} advised closing the save window and locating the file elsewhere. {{p:1}} decided to redo it as the easiest option. The team then reviewed its prototype. {{p:3}} described the curved sides and display, a line indicating the pull-down panel, extra function buttons below it, and a company-logo badge; {{p:2}} added an apple-or-cherry design at the top. The team favored the cherry as more playful and summery, while noting a possible Apple/Mac association. The small button labels were difficult to fit, so {{p:3}} said the buttons used simple shapes, with the important volume controls made larger; {{p:2}} described distinguishing volume buttons in orange from channel buttons in blue. {{p:1}} cautioned that extra button colors could affect cost, since the original costing assumed only the red apple button would be a different color. {{p:3}} said the mute button would probably need a label, but the prototype had no buttons small enough to fit the wording. The group also described the mute button as potentially smaller than the volume buttons.

### Evaluation plan and production-cost options
{{p:1}} listed the prototype presentation, evaluation criteria, and finance as the remaining work, referring to criteria from the previous meeting. The prototype lacked the second layer, but otherwise included the red apple and buttons; the main change was button coloration. The group would also assess production feasibility. The target production cost was below €12.50. {{p:4}} proposed examining production costs using the prototype, and {{p:2}} asked to display the figures. {{p:1}} described the design as having a simple chip, kinetic-energy power source, single curved case, rubber case material, and push-button interface. The group discussed whether button-material supplements applied to one special button or all 16 buttons. {{p:1}} initially understood the red apple as the sole special-form button and wondered whether rubber counted as a special material; {{p:4}} thought the material supplement applied across the buttons rather than per button. They considered standard buttons with one special red apple button, with the remaining buttons in hard plastic, and noted that every design change had cost implications.

The initial costing was reported as €13.7 with all desired features, above the €12.50 limit. {{p:1}} said the current total needed to be reduced by at least 1.2 points. {{p:2}} identified a sample sensor and sample speaker for voice recognition as a significant added cost, putting the total at about 12.7, and suggested removing a special color to retain voice recognition. The team considered replacing kinetic power with a battery, which would save one point but would reintroduce the concern that batteries could run out and cause users to lose the remote. {{p:3}} preferred voice recognition as more impressive than having no battery; {{p:1}} clarified its intended purpose was to help locate a lost remote. The team also considered replacing the rubber case with plastic. {{p:1}} said plastic rather than rubber could reduce costs by two points, keep kinetic power and the sample sensor, and leave about 0.2 points to adjust by removing a special form or color. The group ultimately favored a plastic case, retaining kinetic power and voice recognition, and concluded this combination was within budget. {{p:2}} first estimated the adjusted total at 11.7; after allowing for button supplements, {{p:2}} calculated the revised cost as 12.3, with 0.8 points remaining; {{p:4}} said the redesign had saved two euros. The team noted the trade-off: a little less fashionability and fanciness, while retaining the other attributes and technical innovations.

### Prototype evaluation criteria and ratings
{{p:4}} explained that the design team made a prototype and the group evaluated it against criteria shaped by market research and finance. Ratings ran from 1 for true to 7 for false, with 4 neutral; a financial criterion would be added. The listed criteria were whether the product looked and felt fancy, demonstrated technical innovation, was easy to use, incorporated fashion to attract buyers, and was recognizable as a Real Reaction product. For fancy appearance, the group considered the single curve and spongy rubber feel; because the prototype did not have a double curve, they agreed on a rating around 2–3 and entered 2. For technical innovation, they discussed kinetic power and speech recognition and selected 2. They rated ease of use 1. For fashion, they considered the cherry design and sponginess and agreed on 2, while recognizing that the later move to a plastic case would reduce the soft feel. For brand recognition, they cited the logo, the product’s speech feature shared with the coffee machine, and its relationship to the company’s other products, including coffee makers and spacecraft; they settled on 2. {{p:4}} said the average was about 1.8, close to 2. They agreed that the prototype should be evaluated as it stood before making changes, and that the scores would need to be reassessed after adjustments.

### Adjustments to button forms and colors
The group debated how to count special-color and special-form supplements. {{p:1}} had originally counted the red apple as one special color and one special-form button. {{p:2}} and {{p:4}} discussed whether different colored volume buttons meant two or three special colors; {{p:4}} concluded that two color supplements were needed in addition to the original color. The team agreed that the blue volume buttons could be treated as standard and that the extra color count should be two. They also discussed enlarging the volume buttons and whether that would count as another special form. With the second button panel intended to be hidden, {{p:3}} suggested keeping its buttons small, round, and blue; {{p:2}} said the buttons used most often should look good, while the more functional controls could be simpler. {{p:4}} agreed that obvious controls for quickly changing channel or volume mattered most, whereas color differences were less important when users opened the panel and paid closer attention.

To retain some fashionability after changing the case to plastic, {{p:4}} proposed another fruit-shaped button, suggesting lemon shapes for the volume controls. {{p:2}} agreed. The group reasoned that the rubber case had required rubber buttons, but that they could now use plastic casing with the existing rubber buttons. They also discussed keeping the cherry as the special-form button, noting a possible Apple/Mac association with an apple design. {{p:2}} suggested leaving 0.2 points available for profitability or other needs, including possible legal costs. The group confirmed the redesigned product remained within the budget and that the second panel could use standard controls.

### Project-process and course evaluation
After completing the finance, spreadsheet, and redesign work, {{p:1}} moved the discussion to project process and evaluation of the course, including creativity, leadership, teamwork, and resources such as the whiteboard and digital pens. {{p:4}} said the divisions between meetings had sometimes felt arbitrary: related research and design discussions, such as examining remote-control curves and buttons, were split across meetings and did not always follow on naturally. {{p:1}} explained that the process was intended to resemble manufacturing practice: decide actions in a meeting, gather information between meetings, return to discuss findings, make changes, and repeat. {{p:1}} recorded that creativity had seemed adequate but that the flow of information on a given subject was sometimes disjointed. {{p:3}} felt a remote control was not the most creative project; {{p:4}} said the brief to design a television remote was restrictive and that the inexpensive product seemed unlike the company’s high-tech, cutting-edge range. {{p:2}} observed that choosing a familiar product gave the group something concrete to assess and improve within a set timeframe. The group also identified the kinetic-powered remote and voice recognition as new ideas, while noting that voice recognition was a different application of an existing technology.

{{p:2}} said teamwork went reasonably well because members brought separate ideas and discussed them. {{p:4}} felt the budget constrained what the team could do and questioned how well a low-cost remote fit with the company’s high-definition DVD and lightweight, portable seven-inch computer screens. {{p:3}} noted that it was difficult for others to assess leadership fairly because {{p:1}} was the project manager and leader. {{p:1}} said the computer had not worked as well as desired; {{p:4}} and {{p:3}} said the equipment had worked, though computers could be difficult at times. {{p:3}} questioned the value of the digital pens, asking how recordings of writing could be retrieved; {{p:4}} suggested a small chip might be plugged into something, and {{p:3}} thought the output might be a video.

### Closing tasks

IS1009a: {"title":"Remote-Control Design Project Kickoff","summary":"{{p:1}} (Betty), the project manager, opened the meeting by asking the team to introduce their roles: {{p:2}} (Francina) is responsible for user-interface design of the remote control, {{p:4}} (Eileen) handles marketing and how to sell it, and {{p:3}} (Jeanne-Oui) is the industrial designer responsible for technical-functional design and specifications. The team reviewed the work process: functional, conceptual, and detailed design would each involve individual work followed by discussion; they also tried the whiteboard so they could use it in a future presentation. The new remote should be original, trendy, and user-friendly; the financial constraints are a selling price of €25, a company profit aim of €50 million, an international market, and a production cost below €12.50, with materials and cost considered during design. Initial design ideas included a compact, multipurpose remote that could control a TV and other household equipment such as audio players, air conditioning, and heating, as well as distinctive colors, materials, shapes, and a comfortable grip. The group also discussed helping users find a misplaced remote, including a light or beep triggered by a sensor when it is hidden or in darkness; a clap- or voice-activated signal was raised, but {{p:1}} felt those triggers were not specific enough, and the feature was left for later discussion. Before adjourning, {{p:1}} said the next meeting would be in 30 minutes and assigned {{p:3}} the working/technical-functional design, while {{p:4}} would develop user-requirement specifications, including friendliness and a justification for the set price through sufficient features; everyone would receive specific instructions."}

{"mom":"### Introductions and meeting plan
{{p:1}} opened by asking everyone to introduce themselves and describe their functions. {{p:2}} introduced herself as Francina, responsible for user interface work and designing a television remote control. {{p:4}} introduced herself as Eileen, working in marketing and focused on how to sell the product. {{p:3}} introduced herself as Jeanne-Oui, an industrial designer responsible for the technical-functional designs and specifications of the user interface and for working on its design. {{p:1}} introduced herself as Betty, the project manager for the meeting. She proposed reviewing the presentation to clarify the assignment. She said the opening and acquaintance were underway, that the computer appeared to be the tool, and that each person would receive instructions. The project plan fell under the same heading, and she did not expect a major discussion at that point.

### Remote-control design brief and work stages
{{p:1}} said the team would design a new remote control that should be original, trendy, and user-friendly, and asked everyone to note those requirements. She explained that functional, conceptual, and detailed design would each involve individual work followed by discussion at a meeting. {{p:4}} summarized these as three types of design: functional, conceptual, and detailed. During the discussion, {{p:1}} remarked that the writing implement was difficult to write with, and {{p:4}} joked that they could redesign it after finishing the remote control.

### Whiteboard tool practice
{{p:1}} proposed trying the whiteboard as tool training, with participants drawing a favorite animal so they would know how to use it if they needed to present something on it at the next meeting. She invited {{p:4}} to try it; {{p:4}} agreed to see what she could do and drew a cat, noting that she had a very fat cat that liked to sit in that position. {{p:1}} reminded her to press the control so the drawing would record. {{p:1}} then invited {{p:2}} to try the board, and {{p:2}} agreed and asked what to draw. {{p:3}} suggested a snake, which {{p:2}} drew. {{p:4}} hoped the cat would be hungry because she did not like snakes. {{p:1}} said they could discuss erasing the drawing later.

### Financial and market constraints
{{p:1}} presented the project finance figures: the selling price was to be 25 euros; the company’s profit aim was 50 million euros; the market range was unlimited, meaning international; and production cost should hopefully be less than 12.50 euros and must not exceed that amount. {{p:4}} observed that the targets would keep everyone challenged. {{p:1}} said the team should keep the budget in mind when choosing materials and designing the product.

### Initial ideas for the remote control
{{p:1}} asked whether anyone had experience using remote controls and invited ideas about what users disliked or would want changed, including size and button quantity or legibility. {{p:2}} said remotes should be compact, noting that current ones were very long, and suggested a multipurpose device that could control televisions, audio players, household temperature, air conditioners, and heating systems. {{p:1}} restated the concept as a multifunctional gadget for household appliances, and the others agreed. {{p:4}} said that, to market successfully, the product should do more things; {{p:1}} added that it should offer something new and different from existing remotes. The group also considered making it trendy and distinctive through different colors, materials, and shapes. {{p:1}} suggested a kidney-shaped form that might feel better in the hand, and {{p:4}} agreed that a friendly shape would help.

### Finding a misplaced remote
{{p:4}} suggested that the remote could beep when someone claps, because people often lose it and cannot find it. {{p:1}} agreed that remotes can be covered by a newspaper or hidden behind a plant, especially when someone wants to turn off the television and cannot locate it. {{p:1}}, {{p:3}}, and {{p:4}} discussed a sound or signal, such as a beep or blinking light, to help locate it. {{p:3}} said a light could make its location recognizable. In response to {{p:4}} asking what should trigger the signal, {{p:1}} proposed a light sensor that would activate when the remote was hidden in a dark spot, such as beneath a newspaper or sweater or behind a plant, and then emit a light signal or beep. {{p:4}} confirmed the idea as a light sensor activating the signal. {{p:1}} considered voice or clapping insufficiently specific, noting that clap-operated lamps only work to a certain degree. {{p:4}} pointed out that a remote might be in an obvious place and still go unnoticed, for example on top of a bookcase when it is usually kept on a coffee table. {{p:1}} said they had good initial points but needed to move along.

### Assignments and next meeting
{{p:1}} said the next meeting would be in 30 minutes and checked whether everyone had received the computer notices; {{p:2}} and {{p:3}} confirmed receipt. The team clarified the design responsibilities: {{p:3}} would work on the technical-functional or working design, while {{p:2}} would produce the functional design. {{p:1}} assigned {{p:4}} the user-requirements specification, including friendliness and the general ideas discussed, as well as consideration of price. {{p:4}} said the team would need to justify the given price by providing sufficient features to make the product sell at that price, and {{p:1}} agreed. {{p:1}} said they would receive specific instructions, asked for questions or suggestions, and {{p:4}} said she had enough to think about until the next meeting. {{p:1}} closed by saying they would meet in about 30 minutes and see what they could develop."}

The project plan fell under the same heading, and she did not expect a major discussion at that point.

### Remote-control design brief and work stages
{{p:1}} said the team would design a new remote control that should be original, trendy, and user-friendly, and asked everyone to note those requirements. She explained that functional, conceptual, and detailed design would each involve individual work followed by discussion at a meeting. {{p:4}} summarized these as three types of design: functional, conceptual, and detailed. During the discussion, {{p:1}} remarked that the writing implement was difficult to write with, and {{p:4}} joked that after finishing the remote control they would redesign it.

### Whiteboard tool practice
{{p:1}} proposed trying the whiteboard as tool training, with participants drawing a favorite animal so they would know how to use it if they needed to present something on it at the next meeting. She invited {{p:4}} to try it; {{p:4}} agreed to see what she could do and drew a cat, noting that she had a very fat cat that liked to sit in that position. {{p:1}} reminded her to press the control so the drawing would record. {{p:1}} then invited {{p:2}} to try the board, and {{p:2}} agreed and asked what to draw. {{p:3}} suggested a snake, which {{p:2}} drew. {{p:4}} hoped the cat would be hungry because she did not like snakes. {{p:1}} said they could discuss erasing the drawing later.

### Financial and market constraints
{{p:1}} presented the project finance figures: the selling price was to be 25 euros; the company’s profit aim was 50 million euros; the market range was unlimited, meaning international; and production cost should hopefully be less than 12.50 euros and must not exceed that amount. {{p:4}} observed that the targets would keep everyone challenged. {{p:1}} said the team should keep the budget in mind when choosing materials and designing the product.

### Initial ideas for the remote control
{{p:1}} asked whether anyone had experience using remote controls and invited ideas about what users disliked or would want changed, including size and button quantity or legibility. {{p:2}} said remotes should be compact, noting that current ones were very long, and suggested a multipurpose device that could control televisions, audio players, household temperature, air conditioners, and heating systems. {{p:1}} restated the concept as a multifunctional gadget for household appliances, and the others agreed. {{p:4}} said that, to market successfully, the product should do more things; {{p:1}} added that it should offer something new and different from existing remotes. The group also considered making it trendy and distinctive through different colors, materials, and shapes. {{p:1}} suggested a kidney-shaped form that might feel better in the hand, and {{p:4}} agreed that a friendly shape would help.

### Finding a misplaced remote
{{p:4}} suggested that the remote could beep when someone claps, because people often lose it and cannot find it. {{p:1}} agreed that remotes can be covered by a newspaper or hidden behind a plant, especially when someone wants to turn off the television and cannot locate it. {{p:1}}, {{p:3}}, and {{p:4}} discussed a sound or signal, such as a beep or blinking light, to help locate it. {{p:3}} said a light could make its location recognizable. In response to {{p:4}} asking what should trigger the signal, {{p:1}} proposed a light sensor that would activate when the remote was hidden in a dark spot, such as beneath a newspaper or sweater or behind a plant, and then emit a light signal or beep. {{p:4}} confirmed the idea as a light sensor activating the signal. {{p:1}} said some kind of sensor would be needed and considered voice or clapping insufficiently specific, noting that clap-operated lamps only work to a certain degree. {{p:4}} pointed out that a remote might be in an obvious place and still go unnoticed, for example on top of a bookcase when it is usually kept on a coffee table. {{p:1}} said they had good initial points but needed to move along.

The product should be an attractive, intuitive impulse purchase priced at 25 euros and available to market by September for Christmas; research cited 34% of complaints about remotes being difficult to learn and highlighted that they are often misplaced, motivating simple controls and find-it features such as light and a beep. Although {{p:4}}’s research suggested control of TVs, VCRs, stereos, and possibly an appliance could fit the budget, {{p:1}} relayed management’s constraints: focus on TV control, exclude teletext as outdated, protect the company’s corporate image and colours, and respect time-to-market requirements. {{p:3}} described how a battery-powered integrated circuit sends infrared signals, and suggested fluorescent or light-emitting buttons, a beep for unintended multiple presses, a child lock, varied shapes and colours, clear labels, a clock, and a holder; {{p:4}} and {{p:2}} discussed tactilely distinct buttons, while {{p:4}} emphasized that mode changes can be confusing, especially for older or less dexterous users. {{p:2}} proposed TV power and channel/volume controls, timers to switch programmes or the television on or off at chosen times, child locks, a compact T-shaped form, skin-safe materials, an alarm clock, illuminated buttons, and a child-safe shape; the group also discussed clock and alarm functionality and automatic shutoff at 10 o’clock. The group framed the target market broadly as everyone with a TV, while identifying children, older people, and people who find small buttons or controls difficult as possible subgroups; {{p:2}} suggested a core design for ages 10 to 40 with additional subgroup-friendly controls, and the team considered whether to offer different shapes or cosmetic cases using the same electronics, including replaceable colour covers. No final decision was made on subgroup-specific variants or button layouts: {{p:1}} concluded that subgroup features would depend on the budget, and {{p:3}} floated a 70%/30% split between a unique remote and another version, which was not clearly resolved; the meeting ended with a lunch break and plans to revisit points after further research."}

{"mom":"### Meeting setup and presentation order
{{p:1}} checked that everyone was ready and said the Marketing Manager should begin by addressing needs and desires. {{p:4}} asked to start and requested that the slides be shown while presenting; {{p:1}} brought up the slides in full-screen mode.

### Marketing approach, timing, and customer appeal
{{p:4}} said the group should first gather a wide range of suggestions, even ideas that might sound unrealistic, and then eliminate options according to design and budget feasibility. {{p:4}} would consult {{p:3}} about implementation difficulty, cost, and development time, and consult {{p:2}} about user-friendly features, priorities, appearance, and colour. Features should be prioritized for customer appeal as well as technical practicality.

{{p:4}} emphasized that timing mattered as much as money: the product should be an attractive impulse purchase, ideally bought as a Christmas present for 25 euros. It needed to be on the market by September, because products not already being shown around in September would not sell for Christmas. The product needed a compelling selling point, a short learning curve, intuitive operation, and as few buttons as possible to avoid confusion. {{p:4}} suggested the motto “fashion in electronics” for a marketing campaign.

### Product scope and management constraints
{{p:4}} reported that research after the first meeting suggested a whole-house control product would not fit the budget. The suggestions should therefore be specific enough to form a list that could be assessed and crossed off. {{p:4}} thought control of a TV, VCR, stereo, and perhaps a coffee pot or lamp might fit the budget and price point.

{{p:1}} relayed instructions from higher management: the product should control only the TV, partly because adding other devices was considered too complex and would affect time to market. Teletext should be excluded as outdated. The product also had to maintain the company’s corporate image, using its corporate colour and design so it would be clearly identifiable as the company’s product. {{p:1}} said these constraints meant the team should focus on TV control and eliminate teletext and other out-of-scope ideas.

### Research on existing remotes and discoverability
{{p:4}} said research found that 34 percent of complaints about existing remote controls concerned how long they took to learn. Another important complaint was that remotes were often lost somewhere in the room. The team should make the remote simple, obvious, and intuitive, and consider a light-emitting feature and a beep to help people find it.

### Industrial design and working principles
{{p:3}} presented the working design of a remote controller. The integrated circuit acts as the controller’s brain, receives power from a battery, and converts button inputs into infrared signals sent to a device such as a TV or air conditioner. {{p:3}} said a battery was preferable to a mains supply so the remote could be carried wherever needed. A remote is normally designed for a single device; controlling multiple devices would require compatibility with the same signal frequency. {{p:3}} considered multi-device control difficult, and {{p:4}} and {{p:1}} noted that management had already ruled it out.

{{p:3}} described the interface as buttons or a switch pad that tell the integrated circuit what action to send to the TV, such as changing the channel, adjusting volume, muting, or applying a child lock. {{p:3}} proposed fluorescent or light-emitting button labels so the remote could be found in the dark, a beep when many buttons were pressed at once to indicate that no action would be taken, and a child lock to prevent children’s button presses from operating it. {{p:3}} also suggested different, comfortable shapes that fit the hand, including animal shapes. {{p:3}} said changing the shape would not necessarily add much cost, while {{p:1}} noted that making one mould would limit the additional cost. Several shapes using the same electronics and buttons were considered possible, subject to checking the budget; {{p:4}} suggested an adult-oriented design and fun or animal-shaped versions for children, which could also help children remember where the remote was.

The participants discussed the trade-off between the number of buttons and the number of features. {{p:3}} said more buttons could make a remote more complicated, while too few features could make it less attractive; using buttons for multiple operations in different modes was possible but could add complexity. {{p:4}} said this needed discussion with {{p:2}}, noting that one button per feature could make the remote easier to learn. {{p:4}} and {{p:1}} pointed out that mode changes and small buttons could frustrate users, especially people with limited dexterity, who might press the wrong button. Differently shaped buttons—for example, a triangle for volume and a square for channel changes—could provide tactile cues. {{p:3}} added that button text should be clear and unambiguous.

{{p:3}} suggested including a clock, saying it could be added to the integrated circuit without extra cost. {{p:4}} supported the idea because people might want to check the time while watching the news or waiting for a favourite programme. {{p:2}} later also proposed an alarm clock, saying it could provide an alarm at 8 p.m. and should not cost much to include. {{p:3}} agreed that a clock could support an alarm. {{p:2}} suggested illuminated buttons that glow differently in the dark, a compact remote, human-friendly materials that would not cause skin disease or allergies for children or adults, and a design without sharp projections that might harm a child.

{{p:3}} listed components including buttons, switches beneath them, bulbs or lights, a battery, a chip, connecting wires, and a case or holder for the remote. {{p:3}} also said research on the company website had provided points about how the design works; {{p:4}} suggested looking at the site, and {{p:3}} clarified that it had been consulted for ideas and working-design information.

### User-interface research and proposed features
{{p:2}} said the primary purpose of a remote is to control a television from a distance. It should have an on/off switch and a signal system, such as radio waves, infrared light, or an LED, to change functions such as channels and volume. {{p:2}} proposed a timer that could switch on the TV at a selected time—for example, 9 o’clock for a particular programme—and a child lock that would let parents block a channel from children of a particular age. {{p:2}} also suggested a compact design, a T-shaped form as a personal preference, and an alarm clock that could be set for a chosen time, such as 8 p.m. {{p:2}} cited research indicating that remotes use different signal types, including infrared and radio waves.

{{p:2}} also proposed automatic shutoff at 10 o’clock to save electricity and prevent someone from continuing to watch later. {{p:3}} compared this with a timer that locks the television. {{p:2}} said the remote could serve both as a TV controller and as an alarm clock, and could use a child lock without adding many circuits.

### Target group and product variants
{{p:1}} said the decisions needed from the meeting were the target group and the product’s function or working design. The broad target group could be everyone who owns a TV, but it included subgroups such as elderly people with limited finger or hand function, people who felt nervous about pressing small buttons, and children. {{p:1}} asked whether to design one product for one target group or consider different shapes and buttons for different groups, and whether the 25-euro price point could support subgroup-specific options.

{{p:4}} noted the marketing appeal of a product that children would ask their parents to buy, while {{p:1}} suggested addressing children through shape and colour, such as pink, fluorescent, or banana-coloured designs. {{p:4}} suggested a banana-shaped version. {{p:2}} proposed a general design aimed mainly at people aged 10 to 40, with specific functional buttons added for children, elderly people, and people with nervous problems. {{p:3}} suggested larger buttons for elderly users, but {{p:2}} noted that a household would include people of different ages and would not want to buy three separate remotes; they would prefer one remote usable by everyone. {{p:3}} said a larger, dedicated design for elderly people or children could be considered, while the group also discussed whether such variations would meaningfully affect cost.

{{p:1}} framed the question as whether the budget allowed more than one design. The basic design and electronics could remain the same, with changes such as larger, illuminated, or differently shaped buttons, or different plastic cases. {{p:1}} compared this with portable phones that came with removable plastic cases, such as striped or fluorescent-blue cases, and suggested including an alternate colour or stripe in the package, with additional colours available separately. {{p:4}} and {{p:3}} agreed that different covers or cases could be an option. The cost of multiple designs remained to be assessed; {{p:1}} said, by way of example, that 40 percent of units might have large buttons and the rest regular buttons.

### Wrap-up and next steps
{{p:1}} summarized that the target group was basically everyone with a TV, and that subgroup features could be included if money allowed. {{p:3}} raised an unresolved possibility that 70 percent might be a unique remote controller and 30 percent another version; the discussion did not settle those proportions. {{p:1}} said the budget would determine whether subgroup features or multiple versions were feasible. {{p:4}} suggested returning to one or two points at the next meeting, and {{p:3}} recommended doing more research. The meeting then moved to a lunch break, with {{p:1}} saying the participants would meet again after lunch."}

{"summary":"{{p:4}} proposed an open idea-gathering process, followed by filtering for design and budget feasibility and prioritizing customer appeal. {{p:4}} said they would consult {{p:3}} about implementation difficulty, cost, and development time, and {{p:2}} about user-friendly features, priorities, appearance, and colour. The product should be an attractive, intuitive impulse purchase priced at 25 euros and available to market by September for Christmas; research cited 34% of complaints about remotes being difficult to learn and highlighted that they are often misplaced, motivating simple controls and find-it features such as light and a beep. Although {{p:4}}’s research suggested control of TVs, VCRs, stereos, and possibly an appliance could fit the budget, {{p:1}} relayed management’s constraints: focus on TV control, exclude teletext as outdated, protect the company’s corporate image and colours, and respect time-to-market requirements. {{p:3}} described how a battery-powered integrated circuit sends infrared signals, and suggested fluorescent or light-emitting buttons, a beep for unintended multiple presses, a child lock, varied shapes and colours, clear labels, a clock, and a holder; {{p:4}} and {{p:2}} discussed tactilely distinct buttons, while {{p:4}} emphasized that mode changes can be confusing, especially for older or less dexterous users. {{p:2}} proposed TV power and channel/volume controls, timers to switch programmes or the television on or off at chosen times, child locks, a compact T-shaped form, skin-safe materials, an alarm clock, illuminated buttons, and a child-safe shape; the group also discussed clock and alarm functionality and automatic shutoff at 10 o’clock. The group framed the target market broadly as everyone with a TV, while identifying children, older people, and people who find small buttons or controls difficult as possible subgroups; {{p:2}} suggested a core design for ages 10 to 40 with additional subgroup-friendly controls, and the team considered whether to offer different shapes or cosmetic cases using the same electronics, including replaceable colour covers. No final decision was made on subgroup-specific variants or button layouts: {{p:1}} concluded that subgroup features would depend on the budget, and {{p:3}} floated a 70%/30% split between a unique remote and another version, which was not clearly resolved. The meeting ended with a lunch break, plans to meet again after lunch, and a suggestion to revisit points after further research.","mom":"### Meeting setup and presentation order
{{p:1}} checked that everyone was ready and said the Marketing Manager should begin by addressing needs and desires. {{p:4}} asked to start and requested that the slides be shown while presenting; {{p:1}} brought up the slides in full-screen mode.

### Marketing approach, timing, and customer appeal
{{p:4}} said the group should first gather a wide range of suggestions, even ideas that might sound unrealistic, and then eliminate options according to design and budget feasibility. {{p:4}} would consult {{p:3}} about implementation difficulty, cost, and development time, and consult {{p:2}} about user-friendly features, priorities, appearance, and colour. Features should be prioritized for customer appeal as well as technical practicality.

{{p:4}} emphasized that timing mattered as much as money: the product should be an attractive impulse purchase, ideally bought as a Christmas present for 25 euros. It needed to be on the market by September, because products not already being shown around in September would not sell for Christmas. The product needed a compelling selling point, a short learning curve, intuitive operation, and as few buttons as possible to avoid confusion. {{p:4}} suggested the motto “fashion in electronics” for a marketing campaign.

### Product scope and management constraints
{{p:4}} reported that research after the first meeting suggested a whole-house control product would not fit the budget. The suggestions should therefore be specific enough to form a list that could be assessed and crossed off. {{p:4}} thought control of a TV, VCR, stereo, and perhaps a coffee pot or lamp might fit the budget and price point.

{{p:1}} relayed instructions from higher management: the product should control only the TV, partly because adding other devices was considered too complex and would affect time to market. Teletext should be excluded as outdated. The product also had to maintain the company’s corporate image, using its corporate colour and design so it would be clearly identifiable as the company’s product. {{p:1}} said these constraints meant the team should focus on TV control and eliminate teletext and other out-of-scope ideas.

### Research on existing remotes and discoverability
{{p:4}} said research found that 34 percent of complaints about existing remote controls concerned how long they took to learn. Another important complaint was that remotes were often lost somewhere in the room. The team should make the remote simple, obvious, and intuitive, and consider a light-emitting feature and a beep to help people find it.

### Industrial design and working principles
{{p:3}} presented the working design of a remote controller. The integrated circuit acts as the controller’s brain, receives power from a battery, and converts button inputs into infrared signals sent to a device such as a TV or air conditioner. {{p:3}} said a battery was preferable to a mains supply so the remote could be carried wherever needed. A remote is normally designed for a single device; controlling multiple devices would require compatibility with the same signal frequency. {{p:3}} considered multi-device control difficult, and {{p:4}} and {{p:1}} noted that management had already ruled it out.

{{p:3}} described the interface as buttons or a switch pad that tell the integrated circuit what action to send to the TV, such as changing the channel, adjusting volume, muting, or applying a child lock. {{p:3}} proposed fluorescent or light-emitting button labels so the remote could be found in the dark, a beep when many buttons were pressed at once to indicate that no action would be taken, and a child lock to prevent children’s button presses from operating it. {{p:3}} also suggested different, comfortable shapes that fit the hand, including animal shapes. {{p:3}} said changing the shape would not necessarily add much cost, while {{p:1}} noted that making one mould would limit the additional cost. Several shapes using the same electronics and buttons were considered possible, subject to checking the budget; {{p:4}} suggested an adult-oriented design and fun or animal-shaped versions for children, which could also help children remember where the remote was.

The participants discussed the trade-off between the number of buttons and the number of features. {{p:3}} said more buttons could make a remote more complicated, while too few features could make it less attractive; using buttons for multiple operations in different modes was possible but could add complexity. {{p:4}} said this needed discussion with {{p:2}}, noting that one button per feature could make the remote easier to learn. {{p:4}} and {{p:1}} pointed out that mode changes and small buttons could frustrate users, especially people with limited dexterity, who might press the wrong button. Differently shaped buttons—for example, a triangle for volume and a square for channel changes—could provide tactile cues. {{p:3}} added that button text should be clear and unambiguous.

{{p:3}} suggested including a clock, saying it could be added to the integrated circuit without extra cost. {{p:4}} supported the idea because people might want to check the time while watching the news or waiting for a favourite programme. {{p:2}} later also proposed an alarm clock, saying it could provide an alarm at 8 p.m. and should not cost much to include. {{p:3}} agreed that a clock could support an alarm. {{p:2}} suggested illuminated buttons that glow differently in the dark, a compact remote, human-friendly materials that would not cause skin disease or allergies for children or adults, and a design without sharp projections that might harm a child.

{{p:3}} listed components including buttons, switches beneath them, bulbs or lights, a battery, a chip, connecting wires, and a case or holder for the remote. {{p:3}} also said research on the company website had provided points about how the design works; {{p:4}} suggested looking at the site, and {{p:3}} clarified that it had been consulted for ideas and working-design information.

### User-interface research and proposed features
{{p:2}} said the primary purpose of a remote is to control a television from a distance. It should have an on/off switch and a signal system, such as radio waves, infrared light, or an LED, to change functions such as channels and volume. {{p:2}} proposed a timer that could switch on the TV at a selected time—for example, 9 o’clock for a particular programme—and a child lock that would let parents block a channel from children of a particular age. {{p:2}} also suggested a compact design, a T-shaped form as a personal preference, and an alarm clock that could be set for a chosen time, such as 8 p.m. {{p:2}} cited research indicating that remotes use different signal types, including infrared and radio waves.

{{p:2}} also proposed automatic shutoff at 10 o’clock to save electricity and prevent someone from continuing to watch later. {{p:3}} compared this with a timer that locks the television. {{p:2}} said the remote could serve both as a TV controller and as an alarm clock, and could use a child lock without adding many circuits.

### Target group and product variants
{{p:1}} said the decisions needed from the meeting were the target group and the product’s function or working design. The broad target group could be everyone who owns a TV, but it included subgroups such as elderly people with limited finger or hand function, people who felt nervous about pressing small buttons, and children. {{p:1}} asked whether to design one product for one target group or consider different shapes and buttons for different groups, and whether the 25-euro price point could support subgroup-specific options.

{{p:4}} noted the marketing appeal of a product that children would ask their parents to buy, while {{p:1}} suggested addressing children through shape and colour, such as pink, fluorescent, or banana-coloured designs. {{p:4}} suggested a banana-shaped version. {{p:2}} proposed a general design aimed mainly at people aged 10 to 40, with specific functional buttons added for children, elderly people, and people with nervous problems. {{p:3}} suggested larger buttons for elderly users, but {{p:2}} noted that a household would include people of different ages and would not want to buy three separate remotes; they would prefer one remote usable by everyone. {{p:3}} said a larger, dedicated design for elderly people or children could be considered, while the group also discussed whether such variations would meaningfully affect cost.

{{p:1}} framed the question as whether the budget allowed more than one design. The basic design and electronics could remain the same, with changes such as larger, illuminated, or differently shaped buttons, or different plastic cases. {{p:1}} compared this with portable phones that came with removable plastic cases, such as striped or fluorescent-blue cases, and suggested including an alternate colour or stripe in the package, with additional colours available separately. {{p:4}} and {{p:3}} agreed that different covers or cases could be an option. The cost of multiple designs remained to be assessed; {{p:1}} said, by way of example, that 40 percent of units might have large buttons and the rest regular buttons.

### Wrap-up and next steps
{{p:1}} summarized that the target group was basically everyone with a TV, and that subgroup features could be included if money allowed. {{p:3}} raised an unresolved possibility that 70 percent might be a unique remote controller and 30 percent another version; the discussion did not settle those proportions. {{p:1}} said the budget would determine whether subgroup features or multiple versions were feasible. {{p:4}} suggested returning to one or two points at the next meeting, and {{p:3}} recommended doing more research. {{p:1}} said the group would take a lunch break and meet again after lunch.

### Action items
- {{p:4}} will consult {{p:3}} about feature implementation difficulty, cost, and development time, and consult {{p:2}} about user-friendly features, priorities, appearance, and colour. Due: not specified.
- {{p:1}} and the team will assess whether the budget allows multiple designs or subgroup-oriented features, including possible button and case variations. Due: not specified.

The group agreed on battery power as the most cost-effective option, a chip on a printed board, and a bright, colorful, trendy, compact and strong case; push-buttons were preferred over scroll wheels because scrolling requires a more sophisticated, costly chip. The oversized remote was viewed as unwieldy rather than suitable as an impulse purchase, and the marketing presentation noted that the concept options still needed narrowing. The next meeting was scheduled for 30 minutes later: {{p:3}} would develop the look-and-feel design, {{p:2}} the user-interface design, and {{p:4}} the product evaluation; {{p:2}} and {{p:3}} were to collaborate on a modelling-clay prototype using instructions from their coaches."}

{"mom":"### Review of the previous meeting
{{p:1}} recapped the previous meeting and the ideas raised for the remote control. The marketing approach was to gather suggestions and find a way to market the product within the available budget. The product should be easy and simple to use, have a short learning curve, and address the fact that remotes are often lost. It should also be attractive enough to encourage impulse purchases, perhaps supported by a slogan. Suggested technical and functional features included an infrared chip and interface, lid buttons, a beep, a child lock, a clock display, different shapes, an on-off button, a channel lock to prevent children watching undesirable channels, a compact T-shaped design, an alarm clock, non-allergenic materials, energy saving, and a timer for programming a favourite television program. Possible systems were infrared or radio waves. Suggested components included buttons, infrared bulbs, a battery, chips, wires, and a holder. {{p:1}} also recalled that {{p:2}} had suggested an on-off button and channel lock, and that the technical manager had proposed the infrared chip and controls. The participants agreed that this broadly reflected the last discussion.

### User interface presentation
{{p:2}} presented interface concepts, emphasizing that the remote’s appearance should be attractive and saleable. The remote sends messages to the television, including power, channel changes, and selection of channels using number buttons from one to nine. Other proposed controls included swapping between channels, scrolling channels one by one, increasing or decreasing volume, subtitles (for example, English subtitles for a French program), picture colour, contrast, sharpness and brightness, memory, and mute. The mute button would let a viewer lower the sound while taking a telephone call and continue watching television.

{{p:2}} described speech recognition as a particularly important possible feature. A user could record their voice, and the television’s recognizer could respond to spoken commands—for example, saying “ninth channel” to switch to channel nine. {{p:2}} described this as a way to create a simple interface with the important features. The presentation contrasted that approach with existing remotes that have many buttons and can be difficult to understand; a simple, user-friendly design should be usable even by a child. Examples shown included a voice-recognition universal remote for television, cable or satellite, VCR, DVDs and audio; a child-friendly remote that was attractive, available in different colours and shapes, and had a small, compact body with a minimum of buttons; and an oversized universal remote intended to be difficult to misplace. {{p:2}} said their personal preference was to incorporate speech recognition for particular functions.

In response, {{p:4}} said there were many possible options and the group would need to narrow them down. The T-shape and child-oriented design were good possibilities, but the oversized design was funny, too unwieldy, and unlikely to be an impulse purchase at a checkout counter. {{p:4}} considered the presentation good and said it had explored the options. {{p:1}} clarified that the group would return to decision-making later.

### Components and technical design presentation
{{p:3}} said the presentation would focus on components and the technical side of remote-controller design. The casing could be hard plastic to hold the integrated circuit, battery and other components, withstand being dropped, and avoid breaking. It should be strong, use no harmful materials, and be recyclable. Colouring components could support blue, red and green versions.

{{p:3}} described the integrated circuit as the remote’s heart and said it should be highly sophisticated and efficient, as well as resistant to high and low temperatures. As an example, it should withstand outside temperatures of 38 or 40 degrees. The remote should also have a timer and alarm facility. Other listed electronic components were a resistor to regulate electricity flow, a capacitor, a diode, a transistor and a resonator. {{p:3}} suggested a rechargeable battery: even a lower-performance, lower-voltage battery could be used if rechargeable, allowing longer use and reducing cost. A circuit board would also be required.

{{p:3}} explained the operating sequence: pressing a button completes a specific connection in the small circuit beneath it; signals travel through the wires to the chip, which identifies the pressed button and generates a button-specific Morse-code-like signal. The transistor amplifies the signal, and the LED converts it into infrared light. The television sensor detects the infrared signal, identifies the required action, and performs it. In the example of channel one, the chip recognizes that button and generates its specific signal.

Discussing examples of existing remote construction, {{p:3}} pointed out a circuit board and electronic components, including an 18-pin chip, a capacitor, three resistors, a resonator, a diode and a transistor. The chip was labeled TA1835. {{p:3}} said printed circuit boards were easy and inexpensive to build in bulk: printed traces on the board act as wires and circuits, so separate wires are not needed. The board has contacts beneath the buttons; pressing a button activates the circuit and sends signals to the integrated circuit.

{{p:3}} compared push-buttons with scroll wheels. A push-button requires a simple chip, whereas a scroll wheel normally requires a more sophisticated, higher-priced chip. Possible energy sources included a basic battery, a hand-powered dynamo using kinetic energy from shaking the remote, or solar cells. The product could be supplied in different cases. Possible materials included plastic, rubber, wood and titanium, although {{p:3}} said titanium could not be used. Electronics could use a simple, regular or advanced chip on the printed circuit, with an infrared sender. {{p:3}} also mentioned developing samples and a speaker.

{{p:4}} asked whether repeated button presses could achieve scrolling. {{p:3}} distinguished scroll wheels from switches and said scroll wheels had been used about 10 years earlier but were no longer commonly used because they require a sophisticated chip. {{p:3}} recommended ordinary push-buttons instead; {{p:4}} agreed, citing cost, and {{p:2}} also confirmed push-buttons.

### Marketing presentation
{{p:4}} described a research method focused on competitors: reviewing press coverage and advertisements for other remote controllers, browsing the internet, and noticing the remotes people used at homes or meetings, asking about them when convenient. {{p:4}} encouraged the others to do the same. The findings were that small, hand-fitting products and simple designs were preferred. People do not want to squint at small print; they want buttons with obvious functions, as few buttons as possible, and no mode button that makes one button serve multiple purposes. Each button should do something, and appearance should be eye-catching, cute and appealing.

{{p:4}} said the product should reach the market before competitors, look good, and be available in time to sell before other companies released their Christmas items. The advertising campaign should focus on one or two features; highlighting too many features could confuse consumers. {{p:4}} also reported that fruit and vegetable shapes were popular that year and that consumers were moving away from hard plastic and metal toward soft, spongy-feeling materials, possibly with some cloth, as considerations for saleability.

### Concept decisions
After the presentations, {{p:1}} said the meeting needed to decide the remote’s concept. {{p:2}} proposed including voice recognition, describing it as a potentially saleable feature. {{p:4}} suggested it could be the product’s star feature and agreed it was a strong option. {{p:3}} expressed doubts about how well speech recognition would work, citing problems recognizing different people’s voices; {{p:1}} noted that users might need to teach the system. {{p:2}} explained an alternative based on recording users’ commands in advance: a user or family members could record a command such as “good morning” for around eight o’clock to turn on the television and show the news. {{p:2}} said the television could recognize the recorded user’s voice and switch on.

{{p:1}} redirected discussion to the concept’s components and asked what energy source to use. {{p:1}}, {{p:2}} and {{p:4}} named a battery, and {{p:4}} said the group had agreed on it as the most cost-effective and best choice. The group also agreed on a chip on a printed circuit. For the case, {{p:1}} proposed something bright and colourful; {{p:2}} added compactness, {{p:3}} added strength, and {{p:4}} suggested a trendy design. {{p:1}} summarized the case concept as trendy, compact and strong, with the group affirming it.

For the user-interface concept, {{p:3}} and {{p:2}} identified push-buttons as the switch type. The group discussed additional features, including a mute button, a channel-swapping button and speech recognition. {{p:4}} proposed listing speech recognition if possible, pending further research by the industrial engineer into its cost. The group agreed to this conditional inclusion.

### Actions and next meeting
{{p:1}} said the next meeting would be in 30 minutes. Until then, {{p:3}} was assigned the look-and-feel design, {{p:2}} the user-interface design, and {{p:4}} the product evaluation. {{p:3}} and {{p:2}} were to work together on a prototype using modelling clay; their coaches would send specific instructions. {{p:1}} said participants could contact the project manager or their coach with questions. The meeting concluded with the group due to reconvene in 30 minutes according to the timetable."}

{"summary":"### Review of the previous meeting
{{p:1}} recapped the previous meeting and the ideas raised for the remote control. The marketing approach was to gather suggestions and find a way to market the product within the available budget. The product should be easy and simple to use, have a short learning curve, and address the fact that remotes are often lost. It should also be attractive enough to encourage impulse purchases, perhaps supported by a slogan. Suggested technical and functional features included an infrared chip and interface, lid buttons, a beep, a child lock, a clock display, different shapes, an on-off button, a channel lock to prevent children watching undesirable channels, a compact T-shaped design, an alarm clock, non-allergenic materials, energy saving, and a timer for programming a favourite television program. Possible systems were infrared or radio waves. Suggested components included buttons, infrared bulbs, a battery, chips, wires, and a holder. {{p:1}} also recalled that {{p:2}} had suggested an on-off button and channel lock, and that the technical manager had proposed the infrared chip and controls. The participants agreed that this broadly reflected the last discussion.

### User interface presentation
{{p:2}} presented interface concepts, emphasizing that the remote’s appearance should be attractive and saleable. The remote sends messages to the television, including power, channel changes, and selection of channels using number buttons from one to nine. Other proposed controls included swapping between channels, scrolling channels one by one, increasing or decreasing volume, subtitles (for example, English subtitles for a French program), picture colour, contrast, sharpness and brightness, memory, and mute. The mute button would let a viewer lower the sound while taking a telephone call and continue watching television.

{{p:2}} described speech recognition as a particularly important possible feature. A user could record their voice, and the television’s recognizer could respond to spoken commands—for example, saying “ninth channel” to switch to channel nine. {{p:2}} described this as a way to create a simple interface with the important features. The presentation contrasted that approach with existing remotes that have many buttons and can be difficult to understand; a simple, user-friendly design should be usable even by a child. Examples shown included a voice-recognition universal remote for television, cable or satellite, VCR, DVDs and audio; a child-friendly remote that was attractive, available in different colours and shapes, and had a small, compact body with a minimum of buttons; and an oversized universal remote intended to be difficult to misplace. {{p:2}} said their personal preference was to incorporate speech recognition for particular functions.

In response, {{p:4}} said there were many possible options and the group would need to narrow them down. The T-shape and child-oriented design were good possibilities, but the oversized design was funny, too unwieldy, and unlikely to be an impulse purchase at a checkout counter. {{p:4}} considered the presentation good and said it had explored the options. {{p:1}} clarified that the group would return to decision-making later.

### Components and technical design presentation
{{p:3}} said the presentation would focus on components and the technical side of remote-controller design. The casing could be hard plastic to hold the integrated circuit, battery and other components, withstand being dropped, and avoid breaking. It should be strong, use no harmful materials, and be recyclable. Colouring components could support blue, red and green versions.

{{p:3}} described the integrated circuit as the remote’s heart and said it should be highly sophisticated and efficient, as well as resistant to high and low temperatures. As an example, it should withstand outside temperatures of 38 or 40 degrees. The remote should also have a timer and alarm facility. Other listed electronic components were a resistor to regulate electricity flow, a capacitor, a diode, a transistor and a resonator. {{p:3}} suggested a rechargeable battery: even a lower-performance, lower-voltage battery could be used if rechargeable, allowing longer use and reducing cost. A circuit board would also be required.

{{p:3}} explained the operating sequence: pressing a button completes a specific connection in the small circuit beneath it; signals travel through the wires to the chip, which identifies the pressed button and generates a button-specific Morse-code-like signal. The transistor amplifies the signal, and the LED converts it into infrared light. The television sensor detects the infrared signal, identifies the required action, and performs it. In the example of channel one, the chip recognizes that button and generates its specific signal.

Discussing examples of existing remote construction, {{p:3}} pointed out a circuit board and electronic components, including an 18-pin chip, a capacitor, three resistors, a resonator, a diode and a transistor. The chip was labeled TA1835. {{p:3}} said printed circuit boards were easy and inexpensive to build in bulk: printed traces on the board act as wires and circuits, so separate wires are not needed. The board has contacts beneath the buttons; pressing a button activates the circuit and sends signals to the integrated circuit.

{{p:3}} compared push-buttons with scroll wheels. A push-button requires a simple chip, whereas a scroll wheel normally requires a more sophisticated, higher-priced chip. Possible energy sources included a basic battery, a hand-powered dynamo using kinetic energy from shaking the remote, or solar cells. The product could be supplied in different cases. Possible materials included plastic, rubber, wood and titanium, although {{p:3}} said titanium could not be used. Electronics could use a simple, regular or advanced chip on the printed circuit, with an infrared sender. {{p:3}} also mentioned developing samples and a speaker.

{{p:4}} asked whether repeated button presses could achieve scrolling. {{p:3}} distinguished scroll wheels from switches and said scroll wheels had been used about 10 years earlier but were no longer commonly used because they require a sophisticated chip. {{p:3}} recommended ordinary push-buttons instead; {{p:4}} agreed, citing cost, and {{p:2}} also confirmed push-buttons.

### Marketing presentation
{{p:4}} described a research method focused on competitors: reviewing press coverage and advertisements for other remote controllers, browsing the internet, and noticing the remotes people used at homes or meetings, asking about them when convenient. {{p:4}} encouraged the others to do the same. The findings were that small, hand-fitting products and simple designs were preferred. People do not want to squint at small print; they want buttons with obvious functions, as few buttons as possible, and no mode button that makes one button serve multiple purposes. Each button should do something, and appearance should be eye-catching, cute and appealing.

{{p:4}} said the product should reach the market before competitors, look good, and be available in time to sell before other companies released their Christmas items. The advertising campaign should focus on one or two features; highlighting too many features could confuse consumers. {{p:4}} also reported that fruit and vegetable shapes were popular that year and that consumers were moving away from hard plastic and metal toward soft, spongy-feeling materials, possibly with some cloth, as considerations for saleability.

### Concept decisions
After the presentations, {{p:1}} said the meeting needed to decide the remote’s concept. {{p:2}} proposed including voice recognition, describing it as a potentially saleable feature. {{p:4}} suggested it could be the product’s star feature and agreed it was a strong option. {{p:3}} expressed doubts about how well speech recognition would work, citing problems recognizing different people’s voices; {{p:1}} noted that users might need to teach the system. {{p:2}} explained an alternative based on recording users’ commands in advance: a user or family members could record a command such as “good morning” for around eight o’clock to turn on the television and show the news. {{p:2}} said the television could recognize the recorded user’s voice and switch on.

{{p:1}} redirected discussion to the concept’s components and asked what energy source to use. {{p:1}}, {{p:2}} and {{p:4}} named a battery, and {{p:4}} said the group had agreed on it as the most cost-effective and best choice. The group also agreed on a chip on a printed circuit. For the case, {{p:1}} proposed something bright and colourful; {{p:2}} added compactness, {{p:3}} added strength, and {{p:4}} suggested a trendy design. {{p:1}} summarized the case concept as trendy, compact and strong, with the group affirming it.

For the user-interface concept, {{p:3}} and {{p:2}} identified push-buttons as the switch type. The group discussed additional features, including a mute button, a channel-swapping button and speech recognition. {{p:4}} proposed listing speech recognition if possible, pending further research by the industrial engineer into its cost. The group agreed to this conditional inclusion.

### Actions and next meeting
{{p:1}} said the next meeting would be in 30 minutes. Until then, {{p:3}} was assigned the look-and-feel design, {{p:2}} the user-interface design, and {{p:4}} the product evaluation. {{p:3}} and {{p:2}} were to work together on a prototype using modelling clay; their coaches would send specific instructions. {{p:1}} said participants could contact the project manager or their coach with questions. {{p:4}} asked whether repeated button presses could achieve scrolling. {{p:3}} distinguished scroll wheels from switches and said scroll wheels had been used about 10 years earlier but were no longer commonly used because they require a sophisticated chip. {{p:3}} recommended ordinary push-buttons instead; {{p:4}} agreed, citing cost, and {{p:2}} also confirmed push-buttons.

### Marketing presentation
{{p:4}} described a research method focused on competitors: reviewing press coverage and advertisements for other remote controllers, browsing the internet, and noticing the remotes people used at homes or meetings, asking about them when convenient. {{p:4}} encouraged the others to do the same. The findings were that small, hand-fitting products and simple designs were preferred. People do not want to squint at small print; they want buttons with obvious functions, as few buttons as possible, and no mode button that makes one button serve multiple purposes. Each button should do something, and appearance should be eye-catching, cute and appealing.

{{p:4}} said the product should reach the market before competitors, look good, and be available in time to sell before other companies released their Christmas items. The advertising campaign should focus on one or two features; highlighting too many features could confuse consumers. {{p:4}} also reported that fruit and vegetable shapes were popular that year and that consumers were moving away from hard plastic and metal toward soft, spongy-feeling materials, possibly with some cloth, as considerations for saleability.

### Concept decisions
After the presentations, {{p:1}} said the meeting needed to decide the remote’s concept. {{p:2}} proposed including voice recognition, describing it as a potentially saleable feature. {{p:4}} suggested it could be the product’s star feature and agreed it was a strong option. {{p:3}} expressed doubts about how well speech recognition would work, citing problems recognizing different people’s voices; {{p:1}} noted that users might need to teach the system. {{p:2}} explained an alternative based on recording users’ commands in advance: a user or family members could record a command such as “good morning” for around eight o’clock to turn on the television and show the news. {{p:2}} said the television could recognize the recorded user’s voice and switch on.

{{p:1}} redirected discussion to the concept’s components and asked what energy source to use. {{p:1}}, {{p:2}} and {{p:4}} named a battery, and {{p:4}} said the group had agreed on it as the most cost-effective and best choice. The group also agreed on a chip on a printed circuit. For the case, {{p:1}} proposed something bright and colourful; {{p:2}} added compactness, {{p:3}} added strength, and {{p:4}} suggested a trendy design. {{p:1}} summarized the case concept as trendy, compact and strong, with the group affirming it.

For the user-interface concept, {{p:3}} and {{p:2}} identified push-buttons as the switch type. The group discussed additional features, including a mute button, a channel-swapping button and speech recognition. {{p:4}} proposed listing speech recognition if possible, pending further research by the industrial engineer into its cost. The group agreed to this conditional inclusion.

The financing review identified battery power, a simple chip on a printed circuit board, a double-curved plastic case, rubber buttons, special colors and form, and push buttons; the estimate was €8.20, with about €4.00–€4.30 remaining, and the team said it was within budget but noted that voice-recognition costs were not included and its quality within the remaining amount was uncertain.
