{"mom":"### Review of the Previous Meeting
{{p:1}} said they needed to redo the previous meeting’s minutes, then recapped the discussion. The interface designer had proposed a remote control with nine channel buttons, next and volume buttons, subtitle and picture-control features (including colour contrast and sharpness), a memory switch, mute, and speech recognition. The design was to be child-friendly, colourful, and use few buttons; an oversized version had also been proposed, though that idea was challenged. The industrial designer’s proposals included a strong, recyclable plastic case made without harmful materials; a sophisticated, temperature-resistant circuit board; a timer or alarm; electronic components including a resistor, capacitor, diode, transistor and resonator; and, if possible, a rechargeable battery. The proposed operation involved pressing a button, a chip relaying a Morse-code-related signal to a generator for amplification, and an inexpensive circuit board. The design would use push buttons rather than a more expensive, less practical scrolling method, and be battery-operated. The marketing proposal was for a small, easy-to-use, eye-catching remote, with one or two features to focus the campaign on, and a fruit-and-vegetable design with a soft feel. The group’s previous decision was to focus on speech recognition, battery power, a chip, a trendy, compact and strong design, and buttons.

### Prototype Design and Features
{{p:3}} presented a model of the proposed remote, shaped like a snail. It was blue and bright, with yellow and other coloured buttons; {{p:3}} described it as attractive, compact, easy to hold, and easy to operate. Its case would be strong plastic and its buttons soft rubber, chosen because users would touch the buttons frequently. The light-emitting diode would be fluorescent green, with a bulb-like infrared feature. {{p:2}} explained that the remote included an infrared signal-emitting LED, an on/off switch, mute buttons on the side, number buttons from one to nine for channels, two volume buttons, and two buttons to scroll up and down through programme channels. A fluorescent green menu button at the centre would control picture colour, sharpness and brightness. An elongated, slightly flexible swapping button would return users to a channel they had previously watched: for example, a viewer could switch from channel two to channel ten and then swap back to channel two. The model also included an inbuilt voice recogniser that would recognise the user’s voice and act accordingly. The numeric buttons would carry numbers, while the other buttons would have symbols printed on the case so the controls could be recognised without language-dependent labels. {{p:2}} also described a holder shaped like an oyster or shell to fit the snail-shaped remote.

### Initial Marketing Feedback and Selling Points
{{p:4}} praised the remote because it could be held and operated with one hand, including by someone with a small hand, and the buttons could be reached without turning the remote over or using two hands. The buttons were raised; the prominent, raised on/off button was easy to locate, and {{p:4}} liked the attractive colours. The mute controls were on both sides, so either one could be pressed, making them suitable for left- or right-handed users. {{p:4}} said the model looked sellable. The group agreed that voice recognition was an unusual feature and a major selling point because competitors did not seem to offer it in the same price range. {{p:4}} recommended promoting two points: the appearance, particularly the snail image, and voice recognition. The snail’s reputation for being slow could also support a humorous campaign presenting it as a fast snail. {{p:1}} added practicality of use as another possible point, while {{p:4}} argued that the visual appearance should be emphasised because consumers would encounter the product in a shop before they could try it with a television.

### Financing and Product Configuration
{{p:1}} moved the discussion to financing and confirmed the energy source as a battery. The group selected one battery, a simple chip on print, one case, and a single-curved case shape; {{p:4}} initially suggested the model might be double-curved, and the group discussed that option. They confirmed plastic for the case and rubber for the soft buttons, with special colours, push buttons and a special form. They rejected a scroll wheel and an LCD display; {{p:4}} noted that they had not included a clock. The spreadsheet initially showed a total of 7.6, which the group checked and corrected to 8.2. {{p:1}} concluded that the product was within budget.

### Production Evaluation and Market Research
{{p:4}} proposed showing the prototype to people from different age and socioeconomic groups to find out whether it would sell and identify details that might need fine-tuning. The team would not need to accept every suggestion, but should gather some feedback. {{p:4}} also recommended consumer research to catch safety concerns, such as a button being toxic or a child swallowing it, before the product was sold. After gathering input, the team could rely on its best judgement and support the product if it believed the design was good.

{{p:4}} said the prototype fulfilled the desired biomorphic shape: rounded and comfortable rather than angular or square. It was small, bright and warm in colour, and its shape felt comfortable in the hand despite the hard plastic; the soft buttons would contribute to the feel. {{p:4}} considered look, feel and shape more important than functionality at the point of purchase, since shoppers could not try the remote with a television in the store. On a scale of one to seven, where one was good and seven was worst, the group rated the shape one across the team. For size, {{p:4}} gave four, calling it average; {{p:1}} gave at least two, while {{p:2}} and {{p:3}} each gave one, with {{p:3}} saying it was quite small. Everyone rated colour one, citing the bright, warm colours. For feel, {{p:1}} gave two, {{p:4}} gave three, {{p:2}} gave three, and {{p:3}} suggested two. For functionality, {{p:1}} gave three because the prototype could not really be tried out and the other qualities were more tangible; {{p:2}} gave two and {{p:3}} gave three. {{p:4}} had previously assessed functionality at five out of seven and said the team had a good product that could move forward, while noting that functionality might warrant further discussion.

### Voice Recognition, Budget and Possible Changes
{{p:1}} noticed that the financing did not include the voice recogniser and said the team did not know how to evaluate or account for its cost. The quoted cost was 8 euros 20, leaving about 4 euros to spend; {{p:1}} referred to a maximum of 4.30 euros remaining and cautioned that the team could not present the product to management as complete without knowing whether that amount would cover voice recognition. {{p:4}} said that technology could provide many options at different prices, but quality would be the challenge; the team might have to accept a lower quality that could still sell. {{p:1}} reiterated that the team needed to reserve money for voice recognition and avoid adding many more features while staying within budget.

The team considered whether there was room for more creativity. {{p:3}} suggested adding features and making some buttons smaller so more buttons could fit, since the current buttons seemed large. {{p:4}} noted that speech recognition might require additional buttons to record speech, and suggested removing one of the two mute buttons and possibly consolidating the volume controls into one button. {{p:4}} also proposed consolidating other controls. {{p:1}} cautioned that any changes had to leave enough budget for the voice recogniser.

### Team and Process Evaluation
{{p:1}} asked whether the team was satisfied with the project process, creativity and product. {{p:1}} and {{p:4}} said they were happy with the result; {{p:4}} thought it was something they could market. {{p:4}}, {{p:2}} and {{p:3}} praised {{p:1}}’s project leadership, and {{p:1}} said the teamwork had been very good. In reviewing the methods used, the team said it could have made more use of the whiteboard. {{p:1}} observed that the whiteboard was not ideally positioned for everyone to see, and {{p:4}} said the slide had been used because it was better positioned. {{p:1}} added that the slide presentations had made the work easier. The group felt it had found new ideas and done well.

### Conclusion
{{p:1}} confirmed that the costs were within budget and that the project had been evaluated. The group agreed to celebrate: {{p:4}} said they had apple juice that day and would have champagne after selling a million units. {{p:1}} thanked everyone and concluded that the team had developed a feasible new product from both production and marketing perspectives."}

{"summary":"### Review of the Previous Meeting
{{p:1}} recapped the prior meeting’s requirements and proposals. The interface designer wanted looks to matter because the remote sends messages to the TV, and proposed nine channel buttons, next, volume, subtitles and picture controls (colour contrast and sharpness), a memory switch, mute, and speech recognition; the design should be child-friendly, colourful, and have few buttons, while an oversized design was challenged. The industrial designer proposed a strong, colourful, recyclable plastic case without harmful materials; a sophisticated, temperature-resistant circuit board; a timer or alarm; electronic components including a resistor, capacitor, diode, transistor and resonator; and, if possible, a rechargeable battery. The proposed operation used a button and chip to relay a Morse-code-related signal to a generator for amplification, with an inexpensive circuit board. Push buttons were preferred to a more expensive, less practical scrolling method, and the remote would be battery-operated. Marketing wanted a small, easy-to-use, eye-catching remote, with one or two campaign features and a fruit-and-vegetable design with a soft feel. The previous meeting’s selected focus was speech recognition, battery power, a chip, a trendy, compact and strong design, and buttons.

### Prototype Design and Features
{{p:3}} presented a model of the remote shaped like a snail: blue, bright, with yellow and other coloured buttons, compact, attractive, easy to hold, and easy to operate. The case would be strong plastic and the frequently touched buttons soft rubber. The LED would be fluorescent green and include a bulb-like infrared feature. {{p:3}} said {{p:2}} would explain the buttons, naming her as Francina. {{p:2}} described an infrared signal-emitting LED, an on/off switch, mute buttons on the sides, number buttons one to nine for channels, two volume buttons, and two buttons to scroll programme channels up or down. A fluorescent-green central menu button would control picture colour, sharpness, and brightness. An elongated, slightly flexible swapping button would return to the previously watched channel—for example, from channel ten back to channel two. An inbuilt voice recogniser would recognise the user’s voice and act accordingly. The number buttons would show numbers, and the other buttons would have symbols printed on the case so users could identify them without language-dependent labels. {{p:2}} also described a matching oyster- or shell-shaped holder for the snail remote.

### Initial Marketing Feedback and Selling Points
{{p:4}} praised the one-thumb, one-handed layout: the whole remote could be reached even by someone with a small hand, without turning it over or needing two hands. The raised buttons and prominent raised on/off button were easy to locate, and {{p:4}} liked the colours. Mute buttons on both sides allowed either one to be pressed and suited left- or right-handed users. {{p:4}} thought the model looked sellable. The group identified voice recognition as unusual and a major selling point because competitors did not seem to offer it in the same price range. {{p:4}} recommended promoting the appearance and voice recognition as the two selling points, using the snail image and perhaps a humorous “rapid snail” campaign. {{p:1}} also mentioned practicality of use, while {{p:4}} said the visual appearance should be emphasised because shoppers would see the product in a shop before they could try it with a television.

### Financing and Product Configuration
{{p:1}} reviewed the financing: battery power, one battery, a simple chip on print, one case, plastic for the case, rubber for the soft buttons, special colours and form, and push buttons. The group discussed the case shape: {{p:4}} thought it might be double-curved, though the selection was initially described as single-curved. They rejected a scroll wheel and LCD display; {{p:4}} observed that they had left out a clock. The spreadsheet first showed 7.6, then the group checked and corrected the estimate to €8.20. {{p:1}} said it was within budget.

### Production Evaluation and Market Research
{{p:4}} proposed showing the prototype to people across age and socioeconomic groups to determine whether it would sell and identify details to fine-tune. The group need not accept every suggestion, but should gather some feedback. {{p:4}} also recommended consumer research to identify safety issues, such as a toxic button or a child swallowing one, before selling the product; afterward the team could use its best judgement and support the product if it believed the design was good.

{{p:4}} said the prototype achieved the desired biomorphic shape—rounded and comfortable rather than angular or square—and was small, bright, and warm in colour. Although the case would be hard plastic, it felt comfortable in the hand and the soft buttons would contribute to the feel. {{p:4}} considered look, feel, and shape more important than functionality at the point of purchase because shoppers could not try it with a television in the store. Ratings used a scale of 1 (best) to 7 (worst). Shape was rated 1 by everyone. Size received a 4 from {{p:4}}, at least 2 from {{p:1}}, and 1 each from {{p:2}} and {{p:3}}; {{p:3}} said it was quite small. Everyone rated colour 1. Feel received 2 from {{p:1}} and {{p:3}}, and 3 from {{p:4}} and {{p:2}}. Functionality received 3 from {{p:1}} and {{p:3}}, and 2 from {{p:2}}. {{p:1}} noted the prototype could not really be tried out and the other qualities were more tangible. {{p:4}} had earlier assessed functionality as 5 out of 7, but said the team had a good product that could move forward; functionality remained the main area for possible discussion or improvement.

### Voice Recognition, Budget and Possible Changes
{{p:1}} noticed that the financing excluded the voice recogniser and said its cost was not yet evaluated or included. The stated estimate was €8.20, leaving about €4 to spend; {{p:1}} cited a maximum remaining amount of €4.30 and cautioned that the team could not present the product to management as complete without knowing whether that would cover voice recognition. {{p:4}} said technology offered many options at different prices, but quality was the challenge; the team might need to accept a lower quality that could still sell. {{p:1}} said the team should reserve money for voice recognition and avoid adding many more features while staying within budget.

{{p:3}} proposed adding features and making some buttons smaller so more could fit, since the current buttons seemed large. {{p:4}} noted speech recognition might require additional buttons to record speech, and suggested removing one of the two mute buttons, possibly consolidating volume control into one button, and consolidating other controls. {{p:1}} cautioned that changes must leave enough money for the voice recogniser. The team discussed possible refinements, but did not settle on specific changes.

### Team and Process Evaluation
{{p:1}} asked whether the team was satisfied with the process, creativity, and product. {{p:1}} and {{p:4}} said they were happy with the result; {{p:4}} thought it was marketable. {{p:4}}, {{p:2}}, and {{p:3}} praised {{p:1}}’s project leadership, and {{p:1}} said teamwork had been very good. The team said it could have used the whiteboard more. {{p:1}} noted that the board was not ideally positioned for everyone to see; {{p:4}} said the slide was used because it was better positioned, and {{p:1}} said the slide presentations made the work easier. The group felt it had generated new ideas and done well.

### Conclusion
{{p:1}} confirmed the costs were within budget and the project had been evaluated. The group proposed celebrating: {{p:4}} said they had apple juice today and would have champagne after selling a million units. {{p:1}} thanked everyone and concluded that the team had developed a product feasible for both production and marketing.","mom":"### Review of the Previous Meeting

Its case would be strong plastic and its buttons soft rubber, chosen because users would touch the buttons frequently. The light-emitting diode would be fluorescent green, with a bulb-like infrared feature. {{p:3}} said {{p:2}} would explain the button layout, naming her as Francina. {{p:2}} explained that the remote included an infrared signal-emitting LED, an on/off switch, mute buttons on the side, number buttons from one to nine for channels, two volume buttons, and two buttons to scroll up and down through programme channels. A fluorescent green menu button at the centre would control picture colour, sharpness and brightness. An elongated, slightly flexible swapping button would return users to a channel they had previously watched: for example, a viewer could switch from channel two to channel ten and then swap back to channel two. The model also included an inbuilt voice recogniser that would recognise the user’s voice and act accordingly. The numeric buttons would carry numbers, while the other buttons would have symbols printed on the case so the controls could be recognised without language-dependent labels. {{p:2}} also described a holder shaped like an oyster or shell to fit the snail-shaped remote.

### Initial Marketing Feedback and Selling Points
{{p:4}} praised the remote because it could be held and operated with one hand, including by someone with a small hand, and the buttons could be reached without turning the remote over or using two hands. The buttons were raised; the prominent, raised on/off button was easy to locate, and {{p:4}} liked the attractive colours. The mute controls were on both sides, so either one could be pressed, making them suitable for left- or right-handed users. {{p:4}} said the model looked sellable. The group agreed that voice recognition was an unusual feature and a major selling point because competitors did not seem to offer it in the same price range. {{p:4}} recommended promoting two points: the appearance, particularly the snail image, and voice recognition. The snail’s reputation for being slow could also support a humorous campaign presenting it as a fast snail. {{p:1}} added practicality of use as another possible point, while {{p:4}} argued that the visual appearance should be emphasised because consumers would encounter the product in a shop before they could try it with a television.

### Financing and Product Configuration
{{p:1}} moved the discussion to financing and confirmed the energy source as a battery. The group selected one battery, a simple chip on print, one case, and a single-curved case shape; {{p:4}} initially suggested the model might be double-curved, and the group discussed that option. They confirmed plastic for the case and rubber for the soft buttons, with special colours, push buttons and a special form. They rejected a scroll wheel and an LCD display; {{p:4}} noted that they had not included a clock. The spreadsheet initially showed a total of 7.6, which the group checked and corrected to 8.2. {{p:1}} concluded that the product was within budget.

### Production Evaluation and Market Research
{{p:4}} proposed showing the prototype to people from different age and socioeconomic groups to find out whether it would sell and identify details that might need fine-tuning. The team would not need to accept every suggestion, but should gather some feedback. {{p:4}} also recommended consumer research to catch safety concerns, such as a button being toxic or a child swallowing it, before the product was sold. After gathering input, the team could rely on its best judgement and support the product if it believed the design was good.

{{p:4}} said the prototype fulfilled the desired biomorphic shape: rounded and comfortable rather than angular or square. It was small, bright and warm in colour, and its shape felt comfortable in the hand despite the hard plastic; the soft buttons would contribute to the feel. {{p:4}} considered look, feel and shape more important than functionality at the point of purchase, since shoppers could not try the remote with a television in the store. On a scale of one to seven, where one was good and seven was worst, the group rated the shape one across the team. For size, {{p:4}} gave four, calling it average; {{p:1}} gave at least two, while {{p:2}} and {{p:3}} each gave one, with {{p:3}} saying it was quite small. Everyone rated colour one, citing the bright, warm colours. For feel, {{p:1}} gave two, {{p:4}} gave three, {{p:2}} gave three, and {{p:3}} suggested two. For functionality, {{p:1}} gave three because the prototype could not really be tried out and the other qualities were more tangible; {{p:2}} gave two and {{p:3}} gave three. {{p:4}} had previously assessed functionality at five out of seven and said the team had a good product that could move forward, while noting that functionality might warrant further discussion.

### Voice Recognition, Budget and Possible Changes
{{p:1}} noticed that the financing did not include the voice recogniser and said the team did not know how to evaluate or account for its cost. The quoted cost was 8 euros 20, leaving about 4 euros to spend; {{p:1}} referred to a maximum of 4.30 euros remaining and cautioned that the team could not present the product to management as complete without knowing whether that amount would cover voice recognition. {{p:4}} said that technology could provide many options at different prices, but quality would be the challenge; the team might have to accept a lower quality that could still sell. {{p:1}} reiterated that the team needed to reserve money for voice recognition and avoid adding many more features while staying within budget.

The team considered whether there was room for more creativity. {{p:3}} suggested adding features and making some buttons smaller so more buttons could fit, since the current buttons seemed large. {{p:4}} noted that speech recognition might require additional buttons to record speech, and suggested removing one of the two mute buttons and possibly consolidating the volume controls into one button. {{p:4}} also proposed consolidating other controls. {{p:1}} cautioned that any changes had to leave enough budget for the voice recogniser.

### Team and Process Evaluation
{{p:1}} asked whether the team was satisfied with the project process, creativity and product. {{p:1}} and {{p:4}} said they were happy with the result; {{p:4}} thought it was something they could market. {{p:4}}, {{p:2}} and {{p:3}} praised {{p:1}}’s project leadership, and {{p:1}} said the teamwork had been very good. In reviewing the methods used, the team said it could have made more use of the whiteboard. {{p:1}} observed that the whiteboard was not ideally positioned for everyone to see, and {{p:4}} said the slide had been used because it was better positioned. {{p:1}} added that the slide presentations had made the work easier. The group felt it had found new ideas and done well.

### Conclusion
{{p:1}} confirmed that the costs were within budget and that the project had been evaluated. TS3003a: {"title":"Remote-control project kickoff and tool training","summary":"{{p:1}} (Bart) introduced the Real Reaction project to develop a new remote control that is original, trendy, and user-friendly, and outlined the agenda: introductions, tool training, project planning, and closing. The work will proceed through functional, conceptual, and detailed design; {{p:3}} will cover working and component design and some look-and-feel work, {{p:2}} technical function and user-interface design, and {{p:4}} user requirements, trend watching, and product evaluation. {"mom":"### Introductions and meeting setup
{{p:1}} welcomed everyone, introduced himself as Bart, the project manager, and opened with a short presentation. {{p:4}} introduced themself as Frank. {{p:1}} explained that cameras, wires, and microphones would record participants’ actions and voices, and noted that some microphones in the room could be ignored because they would disappear when not in use. The presentation kick-off document was being modified by the administrator, so {{p:1}} suggested reading it instead. {{p:1}} said the agenda was opening and introductions, tool training, project-plan description, and closing. {{p:1}} asked {{p:4}} to take minutes occasionally; {{p:4}} agreed.

### Company, project aim, and roles
{{p:1}} said the team was working for Real Reaction, an electronics company that combines fashion and electronics and puts substantial effort into design and the product itself. The project aim was a new remote control that should be original, trendy, and user-friendly. {{p:1}} said those qualities were why the team had hired a marketing expert, an industrial designer, and a user-interface designer: marketing would focus on a trendy, user-friendly look; industrial design on user-friendliness and originality; and user-interface design on the new remote control. {{p:1}} also pointed out an error in the corporate information: it said Real Remote instead of Real Reaction, which was not the company’s name.

{{p:1}} described three project phases: functional design, involving individual work and meetings; conceptual design; and detailed design. The industrial designer would work on working design, component design, and some look-and-feel design. The user-interface designer would handle technical function design, the user-interface concept, and user-interface design. The marketing expert would contribute to user-requirements specification, trend watching, and product evaluation. {{p:1}} said these responsibilities would be worked out further in other meetings.

### Smartboard and shared documents training
{{p:1}} said the team would use high-tech tools and that initial training would be useful. The room had smartboards, including a whiteboard with a toolbar. {{p:1}} explained that participants could save, undo a drawing, start a blank document for each person, select a pen or eraser, and choose a pen colour and line width; the capture function was not needed. The pen function had to be selected before drawing. A second toolbar allowed users to save, print, move back or forward one page, and switch between drawings. {{p:1}} said documents were in the shared project documents folder and could be opened on the smartboards for display.

To practise, the team took turns drawing animals and describing characteristics. {{p:1}} instructed participants to use different colours and line widths, hold the pen like a small child so the sensors would not be blocked, and draw slowly because the pen might not keep up with fast movement. {{p:1}} drew a dolphin, describing it as living for fun, and passed the pen to {{p:4}}. {{p:4}} chose a different line width and black ink, drew a sheep, and noted its blue marking. The user-interface designer drew a character identified by the others as Garfield. The industrial designer drew a cat, saying cats were independent. After the exercise, {{p:1}} asked whether everyone knew how to use the board; participants indicated that they did, and {{p:1}} invited them to ask before drawing on it.

### Project financial targets and international scope
{{p:1}} stated that the remote control’s selling price was €25 and the profit aim was €50 million, the minimum the project needed to achieve. The product could be sold internationally, so the team should consider different users, cultures, and trends, although that work would come later. Production cost could be no more than €12.50. {{p:1}} cautioned against adding expensive features, such as small televisions inside remote controls, and reiterated the targets: a €25 selling price, €50 million profit aim, international-market focus, and maximum production cost of €12.50.

### Discussion of remote-control needs and possible features
{{p:1}} opened a discussion, saying about five or ten minutes remained; a message indicated five minutes, which {{p:1}} accepted as good timing. Asked about experience with non-standard remote controls, {{p:4}} described having a broad television at home and a DVD player, with separate remotes for the television, video recorder, and DVD player. {{p:4}} suggested making one remote control that could operate them all. {{p:1}} said they had a remote at home that could be programmed for eight different devices. It used infrared with a small device in the room, allowing operation from another floor; {{p:1}} gave the example of a video recorder or DVD player downstairs and a television on the second floor. {{p:1}} agreed that combining different devices in one remote would make things easier.

{{p:1}} said the team wanted different functions and could investigate using infrared, but needed to find out whether that would exceed production costs. {{p:4}} said the remote should be shockproof because theirs tended to fall often. The user-interface designer raised waterproofing as another possibility. {{p:4}} also suggested a battery-status display to show how much charge remained, while noting that it could raise production costs; a small LED was offered as a possible simpler option. {{p:1}} agreed it was another idea and asked for further suggestions. The industrial designer said the ideas had already been mentioned. No one raised further questions about the kick-off presentation.

### Follow-up and close
{{p:1}} said the meeting minutes would be placed in the project folder. The team would then work on its individual projects, and {{p:1}} said they would meet again in about half an hour. {{p:1}} wished everyone good luck."}

{{p:1}} welcomed everyone, introduced himself as Bart, the project manager, and opened with a short presentation. {{p:4}} introduced themself as Frank. {{p:1}} explained that cameras, wires, and microphones would record participants’ actions and voices, and noted that some microphones in the room could be ignored because they would disappear when not in use. The presentation kick-off document was being modified by the administrator, so {{p:1}} suggested reading it instead. {{p:1}} said the agenda was opening and introductions, tool training, project-plan description, and closing. {{p:1}} asked {{p:4}} to take minutes occasionally; {{p:4}} agreed.

### Company, project aim, and roles
{{p:1}} said the team was working for Real Reaction, an electronics company that combines fashion and electronics and puts substantial effort into design and the product itself. The project aim was a new remote control that should be original, trendy, and user-friendly. {{p:1}} said those qualities were why the team had hired a marketing expert, an industrial designer, and a user-interface designer: marketing would focus on a trendy, user-friendly look; industrial design on user-friendliness and originality; and user-interface design on the new remote control. {{p:1}} also pointed out an error in the corporate information: it said Real Remote instead of Real Reaction, which was not the company’s name.

{{p:1}} described three project phases: functional design, involving individual work and meetings; conceptual design; and detailed design. The industrial designer would work on working design, component design, and some look-and-feel design. The user-interface designer would handle technical function design, the user-interface concept, and user-interface design. The marketing expert would contribute to user-requirements specification, trend watching, and product evaluation. {{p:1}} said these responsibilities would be worked out further in other meetings.

### Smartboard and shared documents training
{{p:1}} said the team would use high-tech tools and that initial training would be useful. The room had smartboards, including a whiteboard with a toolbar. {{p:1}} explained that participants could save, undo a drawing, start a blank document for each person, select a pen or eraser, and choose a pen colour and line width; the capture function was not needed. The pen function had to be selected before drawing. A second toolbar allowed users to save, print, move back or forward one page, and switch between drawings. {{p:1}} said documents were in the shared project documents folder and could be opened on the smartboards for display.

To practise, the team took turns drawing animals and describing characteristics. {{p:1}} instructed participants to use different colours and line widths, hold the pen like a small child so the sensors would not be blocked, and draw slowly because the pen might not keep up with fast movement. {{p:1}} drew a dolphin, describing it as living for fun, and passed the pen to {{p:4}}. {{p:4}} chose a different line width and black ink, drew a sheep, and noted its blue marking. The user-interface designer drew a character identified by the others as Garfield. The industrial designer drew a cat, saying cats were independent. After the exercise, {{p:1}} asked whether everyone knew how to use the board; participants indicated that they did, and {{p:1}} invited them to ask before drawing on it.

### Project financial targets and international scope
{{p:1}} stated that the remote control’s selling price was €25 and the profit aim was €50 million, the minimum the project needed to achieve. The product could be sold internationally, so the team should consider different users, cultures, and trends, although that work would come later. Production cost could be no more than €12.50. {{p:1}} cautioned against adding expensive features, such as small televisions inside remote controls, and reiterated the targets: a €25 selling price, €50 million profit aim, international-market focus, and maximum production cost of €12.50.

### Discussion of remote-control needs and possible features
{{p:1}} opened a discussion, saying about five or ten minutes remained; a message indicated five minutes, which {{p:1}} accepted as good timing. Asked about experience with non-standard remote controls, {{p:4}} described having a broad television at home and a DVD player, with separate remotes for the television, video recorder, and DVD player. {{p:4}} suggested making one remote control that could operate them all. {{p:1}} said they had a remote at home that could be programmed for eight different devices. It used infrared with a small device in the room, allowing operation from another floor; {{p:1}} gave the example of a video recorder or DVD player downstairs and a television on the second floor. {{p:1}} agreed that combining different devices in one remote would make things easier.

{{p:1}} said the team wanted different functions and could investigate using infrared, but needed to find out whether that would exceed production costs. {{p:4}} said the remote should be shockproof because theirs tended to fall often. {"mom":"### Meeting purpose and agenda
{{p:1}} opened the second meeting and said the team was entering the functional-design phase. The goal was to agree on user requirements, technical functional design, and working design before moving to the second phase. {{p:1}} would take the minutes. Everyone was to present, with about 7 minutes per presentation within a total of 40 minutes; the group would then discuss new project requirements already sent to {{p:1}} and decide which control functions to include. {{p:1}} also announced a small air-conditioning-system adjustment affecting wings C and E, which could cause temporary cooling problems for a couple of days; it should then be over, and the weather was expected to be cold anyway.

### Market research and design proposal
{{p:4}} presented research from a usability lab, where users were observed operating remote controls and completed a questionnaire. The study included 100 test subjects, alongside market research on market composition and ages. {{p:4}} reported that 75% of respondents considered their remote control ugly, while an additional 80% said they would spend more for a fancy-looking remote. Half said they used only about 10% of the buttons, and half said their remote tended to get lost in their room. On a 1-to-10 relevance scale, channel selection and volume selection each scored 10, the power button scored 9, and teletext scored 6.5. Audio, video, and channel-settings buttons were described as infrequently used but still somewhat important. Channel selection was reportedly used 168 times per hour.

{{p:4}} said 60% of the market consisted of people aged 16–46, who were critical of remote controls, liked new functions, and did not spend money easily. People aged 46–65 made up 40% of the market; they were less interested in features but spent more readily. {{p:4}} therefore recommended designing a remote for the future and focusing on ages 16–45, which {{p:4}} described as the largest market segment and the main source of potential profit. The design should be fancy-looking, account for the finding that about one quarter of respondents thought remote controls caused RSI, and be easy to learn, since 34% found it difficult to learn to operate a new remote. {{p:4}} recommended having few buttons and emphasizing the most frequently used buttons, particularly channel and audio selection, which should be robust and not break easily.

{{p:4}} suggested a docking station that could receive a button press and send a signal to make the remote beep, helping locate it in the room; it could also recharge the remote’s batteries. {{p:4}} also said many respondents preferred an LCD screen, particularly those aged 16–25, and that the preference remained feasible up to age 45. Both the docking station and screen could considerably increase production costs, but {{p:4}} offered them as ideas to consider. No questions were raised about the presentation’s functional requirements.

### User-interface concept and touchscreen discussion
{{p:2}} said the concept should combine general remote-control functions in a user-friendly way, since people use devices such as DVD players, televisions, and stereos but too many functions in one remote would be difficult to use. {{p:2}} proposed retaining familiar general controls, such as a red on/off button, and using a touchscreen display for device-specific functions. Physical buttons would select the device, with a separate set of display buttons for each device rather than showing every device’s controls at once. {{p:2}} also recommended keeping the physical buttons simple and large enough for both older and younger users.

{{p:3}} cautioned that a touchscreen would push the cost well above €12.50. {{p:2}} disagreed that it was necessarily unaffordable, saying a simple, single-colour touchscreen could be inexpensive; {{p:2}} had seen one online a few weeks earlier priced at €20 or less. {{p:4}} noted that a touchscreen could make the design look fancy. {{p:3}} warned that it would be fragile and prone to scratches, and {{p:4}} agreed the team would need to investigate that concern.

### Working-design presentation
{{p:3}} explained that a user presses a button, the remote identifies it, and infrared sends a signal to the TV, which switches to the corresponding frequency or function. The plate has conductive disks for each button; pressing one sends a signal to the LED, which transmits it to the TV. In the schematic, the buttons and power source connect to a chip that controls the infrared bulb, and the pressed button can be seen. {{p:3}} recommended standard plastic materials and simple internal workings for robustness, while concentrating investment on aesthetics, design, and user interface: high-tech materials would sharply raise the price and their cost would recur in every product, whereas the remote needed to be designed only once.

### Product requirements and target market
{{p:1}} set the requirement that the remote operate televisions only, because supporting more functions would make it too complex and increase time to market; it therefore had to be simple. {{p:1}} initially proposed omitting teletext, reasoning that it would become obsolete as internet access became available on televisions. {{p:1}} also said the target should be customers aged 40 and over, since the company was developing a separate new product specifically for younger customers. The team would need to find a market above 40 that suited the remote, and the corporate image had to be clearly reflected in the product’s design and operation.

{{p:4}} objected to omitting teletext: although new TVs would have internet access, {{p:4}} considered it unlikely that people over 40 would have internet-enabled TVs within the next 20 years. {{p:4}} also cited the research finding that respondents considered teletext important and said the over-40 market seemed small, favoring a standard rather than innovative remote. {{p:1}} argued that people aged 40 and over represented 40% of the market and that, in the Netherlands, the 40-plus and 50-plus generations together formed the largest share of the population. {{p:4}} countered that they were not the largest part of the market and were less critical: they wanted a remote that worked and would accept one that looked acceptable, whereas people aged 16–45 were more likely to want a fancy design. {{p:3}} suggested that good marketing could make a remote for older people successful, comparing the opportunity with a successful mobile phone for elderly users, and said the team should shift its focus to functionality. {{p:1}} reiterated that younger users were already the focus of another product and proposed exploring requirements for older users.

The discussion established that teletext should remain under consideration rather than be ruled out. {{p:2}} said deaf people need teletext subtitles, and {{p:4}} agreed. No one objected when {{p:1}} asked whether anyone was against keeping teletext. {{p:1}} proposed making large subtitles an advantage, with a dedicated remote button that would immediately turn on large subtitles for older users; {{p:3}} supported the idea. The group also endorsed keeping the controls simple and using few buttons. {{p:4}} observed that a TV-only remote would already require relatively few buttons, including number buttons 1–0, channel up and down, volume up and down, and some teletext buttons. {{p:4}} questioned whether reducing buttons further would create a competitive advantage, since many existing TV-only remotes already had few buttons. {{p:1}} maintained that button placement and design still mattered.

{{p:4}} said the team should not spend too much time optimizing button count, but suggested researching what older people would like as extras in a new remote. Recalling that 50% of respondents said their remote tended to get lost, {{p:4}} supported a locating feature. {{p:1}} and {{p:3}} discussed an audible signal, similar to a key-chain finder that sounds when whistled. {{p:4}} noted that some phones with docking stations can be made to ring by pressing a button. {{p:1}} considered an audio signal feasible and not too expensive, and said a docking station could be a useful point of difference. {{p:3}} said the docking station should be possible within the budget if it was not too fancy and the remote remained fairly small; {{p:1}} agreed and said a fancy-looking station could be an advantage. The group agreed to focus on extras, including further research into older users’ preferences.

### Display, materials, and age range
{{p:1}} raised the LCD screen as a possible extra and questioned whether it would raise costs too much. {{p:3}} said the team might have to choose between the docking station and screen because both could be too much. {{p:4}} recommended a small, non-touchscreen display that would explain what a button does when pressed, because respondents had found new remotes hard to learn and older users might have difficulty understanding new devices. {{p:1}} supported the idea as a source of extra information, while {{p:4}} was unsure whether the small screen would fit the costs.

{{p:1}} summarized the emerging requirements as a fancy design, ease of learning, few buttons, a possible docking station and LCD, and general functions. {{p:3}} had recommended default plastic materials; {{p:1}} supported this, saying older users would not care whether the cover was titanium or plastic. {{p:4}} suggested that older users might be more careful with their remotes than younger users. {{p:1}} asked the team to clarify the target age range, distinguishing elderly users from people aged 40–80 and suggesting that the design might be for people over 60. {{p:4}} said a product for genuinely elderly users could strengthen the company’s image and that there could be a good market for it if it were innovative, but said further research was needed to settle the age range. The group also discussed cultural differences; {{p:3}} said television sets were not different in every country. {{p:4}} suggested that a small display explaining the buttons would make the product easier to adapt across cultures and languages. {{p:1}} agreed that language adaptation would help, while a dedicated language-selection button might be unnecessary.

### Next meeting and close
{{p:1}} said the minutes would be placed in the project document folder. For the next meeting, {{p:3}} would prepare the components concept, {{p:2}} the user-interface concept, and the trend-watching. {{p:1}} asked them to keep the target group, requirements, and current trends in mind; specific instructions would be sent by the personal coach. {{p:1}} thanked everyone and said the meeting was followed by a lunch break."}

{{p:1}} opened the second meeting and said the team was entering the functional-design phase. The goal was to agree on user requirements, technical functional design, and working design before moving to the second phase. {{p:1}} said they would take the minutes. Everyone was to present, with about seven minutes per presentation within a total of 40 minutes; the group would then discuss new project requirements sent to {{p:1}} and decide which control functions to include. {{p:1}} announced an air-conditioning-system adjustment affecting wings C and E, which could cause temporary trouble for a couple of days; it should then be over, and the weather was expected to be cold anyway.

### Market research and design proposal
{{p:4}} presented research from a usability lab, where users were observed operating remote controls and completed a questionnaire. The study included 100 test subjects, alongside market research on market composition and ages. {{p:4}} reported that 75% of respondents considered their remote control ugly, while an additional 80% said they would spend more for a fancy-looking remote. Half said they used only about 10% of the buttons, and half said their remote tended to get lost in their room. On a 1-to-10 relevance scale, channel selection and volume selection each scored 10, the power button scored 9, and teletext scored 6.5. Audio, video, and channel-settings buttons were described as infrequently used but still somewhat important. Channel selection was reportedly used 168 times per hour.

{{p:4}} said 60% of the market consisted of people aged 16–46, who were critical of remote controls, liked new functions, and did not spend money easily. People aged 46–65 made up 40% of the market; they were less interested in features but spent more readily. {{p:4}} therefore recommended designing a remote for the future and focusing on ages 16–45, which {{p:4}} described as the largest market segment and the main source of potential profit. The design should be fancy-looking, account for the finding that about one quarter of respondents thought remote controls caused RSI, and be easy to learn, since 34% found it difficult to learn to operate a new remote. {{p:4}} recommended having few buttons and emphasizing the most frequently used buttons, particularly channel and audio selection, which should be robust and not break easily.

{{p:4}} suggested a docking station that could receive a button press and send a signal to make the remote beep, helping locate it in the room; it could also recharge the remote’s batteries. {{p:4}} also said many respondents preferred an LCD screen, particularly those aged 16–25, and that the preference remained feasible up to age 45. Both the docking station and screen could considerably increase production costs, but {{p:4}} offered them as ideas to consider. No questions were raised about the presentation’s functional requirements.

### User-interface concept and touchscreen discussion
{{p:2}} said the concept should combine general remote-control functions in a user-friendly way, since people use devices such as DVD players, televisions, and stereos but too many functions in one remote would be difficult to use. {{p:2}} proposed retaining familiar general controls, such as a red on/off button, and using a touchscreen display for device-specific functions. Physical buttons would select the device, with a separate set of display buttons for each device rather than showing every device’s controls at once. {{p:2}} also recommended keeping the physical buttons simple and large enough for both older and younger users.

{{p:3}} cautioned that a touchscreen would push the cost well above €12.50. {{p:2}} disagreed that it was necessarily unaffordable, saying a simple, single-colour touchscreen could be inexpensive; {{p:2}} had seen one online a few weeks earlier priced at €20 or less. {{p:4}} noted that a touchscreen could make the design look fancy. {{p:3}} warned that it would be fragile and prone to scratches, and {{p:4}} said the team would need to investigate that concern.

### Working-design presentation
{{p:3}} explained that a user presses a button, the remote identifies it, and infrared sends a signal to the TV, which switches to the corresponding frequency or function. The plate has conductive disks for each button; pressing one sends a signal to the LED, which transmits it to the TV. In the schematic, the buttons and power source connect to a chip that controls the infrared bulb, and the pressed button can be seen. {{p:3}} recommended standard plastic materials and simple internal workings for robustness, while concentrating investment on aesthetics, design, and user interface: high-tech materials would sharply raise the price and their cost would recur in every product, whereas the remote needed to be designed only once.

### Product requirements and target market
{{p:1}} set the requirement that the remote operate televisions only, because supporting more functions would make it too complex and increase time to market; it therefore had to be simple. {{p:1}} initially proposed omitting teletext, reasoning that it would become obsolete as internet access became available on televisions. {{p:1}} also said the target should be customers aged 40 and over, since the company was developing a separate new product specifically for younger customers. The team would need to find a market above 40 that suited the remote, and the corporate image had to be clearly reflected in the product’s design and operation.

{{p:4}} objected to omitting teletext: although new TVs would have internet access, {{p:4}} considered it unlikely that people over 40 would have internet-enabled TVs within the next 20 years. {{p:4}} also cited the research finding that respondents considered teletext important and said the over-40 market seemed small, favoring a standard rather than innovative remote. {{p:1}} argued that people aged 40 and over represented 40% of the market and that, in the Netherlands, the 40-plus and 50-plus generations together formed the largest share of the population. {{p:4}} countered that they were not the largest part of the market and were less critical: they wanted a remote that worked and would accept one that looked acceptable, whereas people aged 16–45 were more likely to want a fancy design. {{p:3}} suggested that good marketing could make a remote for older people successful, comparing the opportunity with a successful mobile phone for elderly users, and said the team should shift its focus to functionality. {{p:1}} reiterated that younger users were already the focus of another product and proposed exploring requirements for older users.

The discussion established that teletext should remain under consideration rather than be ruled out. {{p:2}} said deaf people need teletext subtitles, and {{p:4}} agreed. No one objected when {{p:1}} asked whether anyone was against keeping teletext. {{p:1}} proposed making large subtitles an advantage, with a dedicated remote button that would immediately turn on large subtitles for older users; {{p:3}} supported the idea. The group also endorsed keeping the controls simple and using few buttons. {{p:4}} observed that a TV-only remote would already require relatively few buttons, including number buttons 1–0, channel up and down, volume up and down, and some teletext buttons. {{p:4}} questioned whether reducing buttons further would create a competitive advantage, since many existing TV-only remotes already had few buttons. {{p:1}} maintained that button placement and design still mattered.

{{p:4}} said the team should not spend too much time optimizing button count, but suggested researching what older people would like as extras in a new remote. Recalling that 50% of respondents said their remote tended to get lost, {{p:4}} supported a locating feature. {{p:1}} and {{p:3}} discussed an audible signal, similar to a key-chain finder that sounds when whistled. {{p:4}} noted that some phones with docking stations can be made to ring by pressing a button. {{p:1}} considered an audio signal feasible and not too expensive, and said a docking station could be a useful point of difference. {{p:3}} said the docking station should be possible within the budget if it was not too fancy and the remote remained fairly small; {{p:1}} agreed and said a fancy-looking station could be an advantage. The group agreed to focus on extras, including further research into older users’ preferences.

### Display, materials, and age range
{{p:1}} raised the LCD screen as a possible extra and questioned whether it would raise costs too much. {{p:3}} said the team might have to choose between the docking station and screen because both could be too much. {{p:4}} recommended a small, non-touchscreen display that would explain what a button does when pressed, because respondents had found new remotes hard to learn and older users might have difficulty understanding new devices. {{p:1}} supported the idea as a source of extra information, while {{p:4}} was unsure whether the small screen would fit the costs.

{{p:1}} summarized the emerging requirements as a fancy design, ease of learning, few buttons, a possible docking station and LCD, and general functions. {{p:3}} had recommended default plastic materials; {{p:1}} supported this, saying older users would not care whether the cover was titanium or plastic. {{p:4}} suggested that older users might be more careful with their remotes than younger users. {{p:1}} asked the team to clarify the target age range, distinguishing elderly users from people aged 40–80 and suggesting that the design might be for people over 60. {{p:4}} said a product for genuinely elderly users could strengthen the company’s image and that there could be a good market for it if it were innovative, but said further research was needed to settle the age range. The group also discussed cultural differences; {{p:3}} said television sets were not different in every country. {{p:4}} suggested that a small display explaining the buttons would make the product easier to adapt across cultures and languages. {{p:1}} agreed that language adaptation would help, while a dedicated language-selection button might be unnecessary.

### Next meeting and close
{{p:1}} said the minutes would be placed in the project document folder. For the next meeting, {{p:3}} would prepare the components concept, {{p:2}} the user-interface concept, and the team would cover trend-watching. {{p:1}} asked them to keep the target group, requirements, and current trends in mind; {{p:1}} raised the LCD screen as a possible extra and questioned whether it would raise costs too much. {{p:3}} said the team might have to choose between the docking station and screen because both could be too much. {{p:4}} recommended a small, non-touchscreen display that would explain what a button does when pressed, because respondents had found new remotes hard to learn and older users might have difficulty understanding new devices. {{p:1}} supported the idea as a source of extra information, while {{p:4}} was unsure whether the small screen would fit the costs.

{"mom":"### Opening, agenda, and recap
{{p:1}} opened the third meeting, identified it as the conceptual design meeting in the second phase, and said the meeting would cover conceptual component and design specifications and trend-watching. The agenda was an opening, three presentations, a decision on remote-control concepts, and a closing; about 40 minutes were available. {{p:1}} asked whether anyone had encountered preparation problems; {{p:2}} said no. Recapping the previous meeting, {{p:1}} listed the agreed requirements: teletext, a docking station, an audio signal, a small screen, button information as an extra, and default materials. The target market was customers aged 60 to 80. No one raised additional requirements. The group kept the same presentation order as last time, and {{p:4}} volunteered to start.

### Trend research and target-market preferences
{{p:4}} reported conducting market research over the past few days, distributing additional questionnaires, sending trend-watchers to Milan and Paris, and consulting additional trend-watchers after the original team returned. The research ranked fancy design as the most important factor, innovativeness at about half as important, and ease of use at about half the importance of innovativeness. Innovativeness meant functions not found on other remote controls. For the 60-to-80-year-old target group, those factors were more evenly balanced. {{p:4}} said older people preferred dark colors, recognizable shapes, and familiar materials; surveys particularly indicated wood as a suitable material. The remote and docking station should blend into a room rather than be eye-catching, and the design should be simple. The docking station and small screen were identified as key innovative features to include. Trend-watchers recommended a telephone-like shape, but {{p:4}} said older customers would find an upright remote in its dock unfamiliar and would prefer it to lie flat. {{p:4}} recommended two editions: a wood-like color and feel for more affluent customers, and a gray-black color for people with less means. {{p:2}} had no questions about the trends.

### User-interface concepts
{{p:2}} presented interface research, building on the previous meeting’s discussion of using a few buttons. The proposed approach focused on primary functions and a user-friendly design with large buttons: on/off, sound control, channel up and down, and number buttons from 0 to 9. Suggested additional features were speech recognition and a dedicated subtitle button. A single press on the subtitle button would show small subtitles; a double press would show large subtitles for people unable to read small text. {{p:2}} proposed a small display showing button functions and the television channel, with the on/off button in a familiar corner and the display near the top where people would look. Channel controls would be placed where the thumb could reach them easily. Speech recognition could also help locate a lost remote by making it emit a signal, or allow spoken commands such as turning the sound off. {{p:2}} said a simple speech-recognition system might be inexpensive, and estimated that one battery could power the small display for six months or more. The design’s form remained to be discussed.

### Component and material options
{{p:3}} outlined component choices. The energy source could be a basic battery or optional kinetic energy, generated by shaking the remote like a watch; kinetic power would make the docking station obsolete, so {{p:3}} initially regarded it as unsuitable. The casing could be flat, single-curved, or double-curved, with no technical restrictions; a rubber anti-slip belt could be added. Buttons could be plastic or rubber. The chipset needed to be advanced because the design included an LCD screen. Although trend research found that people liked wood, {{p:3}} noted that it raised the price and might not suit the product image unless the team made two product lines. Overall, form should follow function.

### Energy source and voice recognition decision
{{p:1}} began the concept discussion with the energy source because it affected production price and product image, and asked whether kinetic power could fit the budget. {{p:3}} listed four possibilities: a normal battery, a hand dynamo, solar cells, or kinetic energy. {{p:3}} dismissed the hand dynamo because users would not want to wind it before watching television, and solar cells because rooms might not be bright enough. Asked by {{p:4}} how kinetic power worked, {{p:3}} explained that shaking the remote powered it up. {{p:4}} objected that older users might not want to shake the remote before use and argued that the docking station could be a marketing advantage and a place to recharge batteries or locate a lost remote. {{p:2}} said the small display would use little energy and that one battery could last six months or more. {{p:1}} added that older people like to keep things in place and may not want remotes left around their rooms; a dock would give the remote a designated place. {{p:1}} suggested making a lost-remote beeper part of the docking station, which could be cheaper and more efficient than putting it in the remote, while retaining voice recognition only for channel commands if appropriate.

{{p:4}} asked what speech recognition would add to production cost. {{p:3}} had no pricing information and said they would ask the manufacturing department. Referring to earlier market research, {{p:4}} said the target group would not pay more for speech recognition in the remote and advised against it if it increased the selling price; the feature might be better suited to a product for younger people. {{p:4}} clarified that the research question asked whether people preferred the feature, not whether they would pay extra, and argued that an LCD screen could make the remote easier to use, whereas speech recognition would not. The researched LCD was relatively large, like a screen on an advanced mobile phone. {{p:1}} said the screen with extra information could be included because users could ignore it, but proposed discarding speech recognition because it would significantly increase cost without making the remote much easier to use. With speech recognition removed, {{p:1}} concluded that a rechargeable battery in the docking station was sufficient, cheaper than kinetic power, and selected the battery. {{p:3}} agreed it was the best choice.

### Chipset and changeable case covers
{{p:1}} and {{p:3}} agreed that the LCD required an advanced chipset, leaving no practical alternative. The discussion then turned to casing and color. {{p:1}} said real wood would cost more to produce but could attract older customers seeking an exclusive item to show their grandchildren. {{p:4}} suggested that the important feature might be the wood color rather than actual wood, so a wood-colored case could achieve the look. {{p:3}} did not know whether colored material would cost more and said they would need to research it; {{p:1}} noted that wood would be harder to work and shape. {{p:2}} proposed one standard remote with separately sold changeable cases, similar to mobile-phone covers. {{p:1}} supported the idea as a distinctive product feature that could be advertised as a new case for a grandparent’s remote. {{p:4}} cautioned that the design needed to accommodate both wood-like and plastic covers, but recommended designing one remote rather than two different models. The group supported changeable covers and considered black, gray, and other colors, while noting that design costs and compatibility required careful review.

### Casing shape and docking arrangement
{{p:4}} asked for clarification of the flat, single-curved, and double-curved case options. {{p:3}} explained that flat cases were straight like many older remotes, while the manufacturing department could also supply single- or double-curved cases. These choices affected form only, not price or functionality, so the design team could choose. {{p:1}} favored a single curve because it could help position the screen at an angle that older users could see while operating the remote. {{p:3}} said a single-curved shape might also help prevent repetitive strain injury; the three available options were flat, single-curved, and double-curved. The discussion favored a remote that lay flat in its dock rather than standing upright. The docking station could sit on or beside the television, with the remote clicked into it.

### Interface layout and ergonomics
{{p:1}} invited ideas for the remote’s form. {{p:2}} said a conventional shape was possible but not especially distinctive. {{p:4}} recalled the proposal to put channel controls on the right, within easy thumb reach, and said this could help address repetitive strain injury, which many remotes caused. {{p:4}} suggested matching controls on both sides for left- and right-handed users and said paired controls could allow a symmetrical design. {{p:2}} asked whether channel controls could be on one side and volume controls on the other. {{p:4}} and {{p:1}} cautioned that extra controls could make the remote harder to use and confuse people, especially if the buttons had the same labels. {{p:1}} considered a reversible remote but found the proposed plus-and-minus arrangement impractical; the group felt the basic functions were simple enough that left-handed users would not have trouble using a normal-shaped remote. {{p:1}} nevertheless suggested making the design more distinctive in another way. {{p:3}} recommended choosing the case first as the basis for the rest of the design, then sketched the flat, single-curved, and double-curved options. {{p:1}} favored the single-curved case, with the display at the top so users could see it while holding the remote. {{p:2}} explored shaping the casing to fit the hand and placing channel buttons within thumb reach. The discussion settled on putting the display on top, retaining an on/off button at the top, and arranging controls so the layout could serve both left- and right-handed users. {{p:4}} preferred rounded corners, which {{p:1}} said would look friendlier.

### Next steps and close
{{p:1}} said the team now had a general concept for the design and materials. For the next meeting, the team would work on the look-and-feel design, incorporate the corporate design image into the remote, and consider the corporate website. User-interface design and product evaluation were also next steps; {{p:1}} assigned the Industrial Designer and User Interface Designer to work together on product evaluation and said their instructions would be sent by the coach. {{p:1}} would put the minutes in the folder. The team would continue the project toward a design for older customers; {{p:1}} was unsure whether the designers would begin working together immediately or first complete questionnaires, and said they would receive a message. The minutes and design material were saved in the projects folder for the group to review. {{p:1}} said the next session would start again in 30 minutes."}

{"summary":"{{p:1}} opened the third meeting in the project’s second phase, a conceptual-design session, and said the team would discuss component and design specifications and trend-watching today. The agenda included an opening, three presentations, deciding on remote-control concepts, and a closing, with about 40 minutes available. The agreed requirements from the previous meeting were teletext, a docking station, an audio signal, a small screen, button information, and default materials; the target market was customers aged 60–80. The group kept the previous presentation lineup, and {{p:4}} volunteered to start. Market research, questionnaires, and trend-watchers sent to Milan and Paris found fancy design most important, innovativeness about half as important, and ease of use about half as important again. For older customers these factors were more evenly weighted; preferences included dark colours, familiar shapes and materials, and especially wood. The remote and dock should be simple and blend into a room; the trend-watchers recommended a telephone-like shape, but older users would prefer it to lie flat in its dock. Marketing proposed wood-like and grey-black editions for different budgets, and identified the dock and small screen as innovative features. {{p:2}} proposed primary controls, large buttons, a small display showing button functions and the current channel, speech recognition, and one subtitle button: one press for small subtitles and a double press for larger subtitles. {{p:3}} outlined battery or kinetic power, flat or curved casings, plastic or rubber buttons, a rubber anti-slip belt, and an advanced chipset for an LCD screen. The group rejected speech recognition because it could significantly raise cost without making the remote much easier to use, and chose a rechargeable battery in the docking station as cheaper and adequate; {{p:2}} estimated one battery could last six months or more. The group selected an advanced chipset for the display and supported one standard remote with interchangeable case covers rather than separate models. Wood-coloured covers could provide a premium look, but the team noted that production cost, material, design, and compatibility required further consideration; {{p:3}} said they would research the cost of coloured material. The group favoured a single-curved casing to angle the screen for easier viewing, a display on top, a conventional overall shape with a more appealing design, and channel controls within thumb reach. Extra mirrored controls were considered potentially confusing; left- and right-handed use, round corners, and a flat dock arrangement were also discussed. For the next meeting, the Industrial Designer and User Interface Designer were to work together on look-and-feel, corporate design, user-interface design, and product evaluation. {{p:1}} said their instructions would come from the coach, that the minutes would be put in the folder, and that the designers might first complete questionnaires and then receive a message. Meeting materials were saved in the projects folder, and {{p:1}} expected the group to start again in 30 minutes.","mom":"### Opening, agenda, and recap
{{p:1}} opened the third meeting, identified it as the conceptual-design meeting in the second phase, and said the team would discuss conceptual specifications for components and design and trend-watching today. The agenda was an opening, three presentations, a decision on remote-control concepts, and a closing; about 40 minutes were available. {{p:1}} asked whether anyone had encountered preparation problems; {{p:2}} said no. Recapping the previous meeting, {{p:1}} listed the agreed requirements: teletext, a docking station, an audio signal, a small screen, button information as an extra, and default materials. The target market was customers aged 60 to 80. No one raised additional requirements. The group kept the same presentation order as last time, and {{p:4}} volunteered to start.

### Trend research and target-market preferences
{{p:4}} reported conducting market research over the past few days, distributing additional questionnaires, sending trend-watchers to Milan and Paris, and consulting additional trend-watchers after the original team returned. The research ranked fancy design as the most important factor, innovativeness at about half as important, and ease of use at about half the importance of innovativeness. Innovativeness meant functions not found on other remote controls. For the 60-to-80-year-old target group, those factors were more evenly balanced. {{p:4}} said older people preferred dark colours, recognisable shapes, and familiar materials; surveys particularly indicated wood as a suitable material. The remote and docking station should blend into a room rather than be eye-catching, and the design should be simple. The docking station and small screen were identified as key innovative features to include. Trend-watchers recommended a telephone-like shape, but {{p:4}} said older customers would find an upright remote in its dock unfamiliar and would prefer it to lie flat. {{p:4}} recommended two editions: a wood-like colour and feel for more affluent customers, and a grey-black colour for people with less means. {{p:2}} had no questions about the trends.

### User-interface concepts
{{p:2}} presented interface research, building on the previous meeting’s discussion of using a few buttons. The proposed approach focused on primary functions and a user-friendly design with large buttons: on/off, sound control, channel up and down, and number buttons from 0 to 9. Suggested additional features were speech recognition and a dedicated subtitle button. A single press on the subtitle button would show small subtitles; a double press would show large subtitles for people unable to read small text. {{p:2}} proposed a small display showing button functions and the television channel, with the on/off button in a familiar corner and the display near the top where people would look. Channel controls would be placed where the thumb could reach them easily. Speech recognition could also help locate a lost remote by making it emit a signal, or allow spoken commands such as turning the sound off. {{p:2}} said a simple speech-recognition system might be inexpensive, and estimated that one battery could power the small display for six months or more. The design’s form remained to be discussed.

### Component and material options
{{p:3}} outlined component choices. The energy source could be a basic battery or optional kinetic energy, generated by shaking the remote like a watch; kinetic power would make the docking station obsolete, so {{p:3}} initially regarded it as unsuitable. The casing could be flat, single-curved, or double-curved, with no technical restrictions; a rubber anti-slip belt could be added. Buttons could be plastic or rubber. The chipset needed to be advanced because the design included an LCD screen. Although trend research found that people liked wood, {{p:3}} noted that it raised the price and might not suit the product image unless the team made two product lines. Overall, form should follow function.

### Energy source and voice recognition decision
{{p:1}} began the concept discussion with the energy source because it affected production price and product image, and asked whether kinetic power could fit the budget. {{p:3}} listed four possibilities: a normal battery, a hand dynamo, solar cells, or kinetic energy. {{p:3}} dismissed the hand dynamo because users would not want to wind it before watching television, and solar cells because rooms might not be bright enough. Asked by {{p:4}} how kinetic power worked, {{p:3}} explained that shaking the remote powered it up. {{p:4}} objected that older users might not want to shake the remote before use and argued that the docking station could be a marketing advantage and a place to recharge batteries or locate a lost remote. {{p:2}} said the small display would use little energy and that one battery could last six months or more. {{p:1}} added that older people like to keep things in place and may not want remotes left around their rooms; a dock would give the remote a designated place. {{p:1}} suggested making a lost-remote beeper part of the docking station, which could be cheaper and more efficient than putting it in the remote, while retaining voice recognition only for channel commands if appropriate.

{{p:4}} asked what speech recognition would add to production cost. {{p:3}} had no pricing information and said they would ask the manufacturing department. Referring to earlier market research, {{p:4}} said the target group would not pay more for speech recognition in the remote and advised against it if it increased the selling price; the feature might be better suited to a product for younger people. {{p:4}} clarified that the research question asked whether people preferred the feature, not whether they would pay extra, and argued that an LCD screen could make the remote easier to use, whereas speech recognition would not. The researched LCD was relatively large, like a screen on an advanced mobile phone. {{p:1}} said the screen with extra information could be included because users could ignore it, but proposed discarding speech recognition because it would significantly increase cost without making the remote much easier to use. With speech recognition removed, {{p:1}} concluded that a rechargeable battery in the docking station was sufficient, cheaper than kinetic power, and selected the battery. {{p:3}} agreed it was the best choice.

### Chipset and changeable case covers
{{p:1}} and {{p:3}} agreed that the LCD required an advanced chipset, leaving no practical alternative. The docking station and small screen were identified as key innovative features to include. Trend-watchers recommended a telephone-like shape, but {{p:4}} said older customers would find an upright remote in its dock unfamiliar and would prefer it to lie flat. {{p:4}} recommended two editions: a wood-like colour and feel for more affluent customers, and a grey-black colour for people with less means. {{p:2}} had no questions about the trends.

{{p:2}} presented interface research, building on the previous meeting’s discussion of using a few buttons. The proposed approach focused on primary functions and a user-friendly design with large buttons: on/off, sound control, channel up and down, and number buttons from 0 to 9. Suggested additional features were speech recognition and a dedicated subtitle button. Channel controls would be placed where the thumb could reach them easily. Speech recognition could also help locate a lost remote by making it emit a signal, or allow spoken commands such as turning the sound off. {{p:2}} said a simple speech-recognition system might be inexpensive, and estimated that one battery could power the small display for six months or more. The chipset needed to be advanced because the design included an LCD screen.
