They discussed whether to broaden the target market to younger users, potentially using interchangeable or fashion-oriented front covers, and {{p:1}} planned to prepare a final presentation, return in about ten minutes, and provide questionnaires for participants to complete in their rooms."}

{"mom":"### Welcome and meeting plan
{{p:1}} opened the fourth and last meeting, which started at 3:00, and said the group would discuss the final design, evaluate both the product and the project, and close the project that day. The detailed-design discussion would cover the design’s look and feel, interface usability, and product evaluation. The agenda was to present the prototype, set evaluation criteria, review whether the design could be delivered within the budget of €12.50 per remote control, evaluate the project, and close. {{p:1}} said they had 40 minutes and expected to finish at 3:30. {{p:4}} apologized for arriving late because of traffic; {{p:1}} said it was understandable at that time of day.

### Prototype: functions and button layout
{{p:3}} presented the prototype developed with Richard. Its proposed controls included an on/off button, a mute button below it, volume and channel selectors, a simple plus/minus control, a help button that would show guidance on the LCD when held while another button was pressed, number buttons from 0 to 9, teletext and subtitle buttons, and the company logo. {{p:3}} described it as a simple prototype and said user testing would show how people responded. {{p:4}} asked whether questions about functionality were welcome; {{p:3}} invited questions at any time.

{{p:4}} asked how the teletext control would move between pages. {{p:2}} explained that users could enter a page number with the number buttons or use the channel-shifting control to move up and down through teletext. {{p:1}} recalled that earlier meetings had aimed for a simple design with only a few large buttons, and questioned whether all the proposed buttons were needed. {{p:3}} said the on/off button was essential, as were volume and channel controls; mute could potentially be replaced by pressing volume-down twice. {{p:3}} considered help necessary because otherwise users would have no way to find out what a button did. {{p:2}} and {{p:1}} discussed using a long press as an alternative, but {{p:2}} cautioned that older users might not know about that option. The participants also treated the number buttons, teletext, and subtitles as necessary. {{p:4}} said a remote intended only for television would have little to gain from the proposed additional controls.

{{p:3}} said the buttons would be equal-sized and round, with small identifying marks, such as a triangle for volume, to aid recognition. {{p:2}} said the small display meant LEDs would not be needed. {{p:3}} proposed rubber buttons in a different colour from the case so they would stand out.

### Cost review and design trade-offs
{{p:1}} moved to the finance review, noting that only 30 minutes remained and that producing the design for €12.50 would be difficult. The initial estimate assumed two batteries, though the group discussed whether one rechargeable battery might suffice; {{p:1}} said using one would save €2. The advanced chip was needed, leaving little scope for savings there. A single-curved case cost €1 more than an uncurved case, but {{p:1}} favored the single curve for the design and to give the display a prominent place. Plastic was already the cheapest case material, while the buttons were the biggest cost. The group counted the proposed layout as 16 or 17 buttons and discussed an estimate of €18, above the €12.50 target.

{{p:1}} proposed removing the help and mute buttons by assigning their functions to long presses, which would save €1 and bring the count to 15. {{p:4}} objected that this approach would not be suitable. The group clarified whether the combined volume and channel controls counted as one or two buttons; {{p:2}} explained that they could be large controls but were more expensive than small buttons. {{p:4}} suggested integrating three number buttons into one control to reduce cost, and {{p:1}} agreed that this was possible and could also benefit the design. The participants discussed whether the advanced chip allowed the grouped controls to count as one button, but {{p:4}} maintained that the proposed cross-shaped control was effectively four buttons.

The group considered removing the LCD to save on both the display and the chip. {{p:3}} pointed out that omitting the display would remove a major feature, and {{p:4}} suggested the docking station might then be the remote’s only distinctive advantage. {{p:3}} noted that the docking station was not included in the schematic or its price. {{p:4}} raised changing suppliers, and {{p:1}} mentioned a possible Polish supplier. {{p:3}} questioned whether combining controls would make the remote less usable for older people, citing {{p:3}}’s mother’s difficulty sending an SMS. {{p:4}} said market research indicated that older people were more willing to spend, and suggested raising the remote’s price slightly; {{p:1}} responded that the team had to stay within the €12.50 budget and had no additional development budget.

The team explored replacing the ten number buttons with a scroll wheel for program numbers. {{p:1}} explained that users could scroll until the desired number appeared on the LCD, then press the wheel; {{p:4}} noted that an integrated scroll-and-push control would also cost more. {{p:3}} suggested that a pause of half a second after scrolling could select the channel without a press, and {{p:1}} said that would cut costs substantially. {{p:4}} warned that this could undermine usability, particularly for older people who might not know what a scroll wheel was or expect a remote to have ten number buttons. {{p:1}} proposed explaining the wheel in television advertising and the guide, keeping the LCD to provide usage help, and using it as part of the innovative design. {{p:4}} observed that the wheel looked large.

{{p:3}} then proposed using the scroll wheel for volume after pressing a volume button, and likewise for channel selection, which could save two buttons and make the wheel’s purpose clearer. {{p:1}} endorsed the idea. The emerging layout used separate volume and channel buttons plus the scroll wheel; the group discussed retaining teletext and reducing the layout to four or five buttons. {{p:3}} suggested a flat case and a smaller overall remote if more buttons were removed, arranging volume and channel controls level with the on/off button, with the screen behind and the scroll control beneath. {{p:2}} noted that a larger remote could cost the same as a smaller one if the cost difference was only in the single- or double-curved case. {{p:1}} explained that case moulds and manufacturing equipment affected the price: a single-curved case was straightforward to produce, while a single curve required a different machine from a flat case.

Asked to choose between a flat and single-curved design, {{p:4}} favored the single curve, while acknowledging that the changes and cost pressure were difficult. {{p:4}} suggested asking the board for more money or doing market research on the options, including an €18 remote. {{p:1}} said they could keep the single curve to emphasize the LCD and support help functions, which would be useful alongside the scroll control. The group also discussed whether the unusual design would be unfamiliar or confusing to older users and require substantial marketing. {{p:2}} pointed out that older people might recognize scroll controls from radios. {{p:1}} suggested giving the controls a familiar appearance. The team did not settle on a final cost figure in this discussion, but continued developing the reduced-button concept while keeping the €12.50 target in view.

### Product evaluation criteria and ratings
{{p:4}} said the evaluation criteria had been developed from a literature study and analysis of earlier requirements. The criteria covered whether the remote was fancy in its shape and look and feel; whether it was innovative and what new functions it offered; ease of use and learnability; functionality, including whether there were too many functions and whether the included functions were useful; cost; fit with the target group; and recognizability as a product from the company. {{p:4}} noted that preparing the evaluation had been difficult because the previous meeting’s minutes were unavailable. {{p:1}} explained that the digital pen had failed to upload its data and downloading its software was producing errors.

On a scale of 1 to 7, the group rated the design’s fanciness 6. For innovation, {{p:1}} proposed 7, citing the subtitles, LCD, docking station, and scroll controls. {{p:4}} agreed that the LCD, docking station, and scroll buttons made it innovative. The group then discussed usability: {{p:1}} described it as somewhat uncertain, and the participants settled on a rating between 4 and 5, with {{p:4}} choosing 4. The group agreed the design included the functions they wanted and did not have too many; {{p:4}} called it slim and assigned a score of 7. The discussion also raised unresolved frustrations such as remotes getting lost and repetitive strain injury, which {{p:3}} said the team had not considered. The group judged production costs to be within the preset limits in the current evaluation. On fit with the focus group, ratings diverged: {{p:3}} suggested 3, while {{p:1}} and {{p:4}} questioned whether the design fit older users, citing the unfamiliar radio-style control; {{p:1}} rated it 4, {{p:4}} 2, and {{p:2}} 3, and the group recorded 3. On company recognizability, participants said the logo, the company’s fashion-oriented slogan, and removable front cases helped identify the product.

{{p:4}} calculated the evaluation as seven factors multiplied by seven, giving a maximum of 49. After deductions of 1, 3, and 4, the group arrived at 41 out of 49. {{p:1}} first called this around 80 percent, then calculated the score as 84 percent and described it as a good result.

### Project-process evaluation
{{p:1}} asked whether the project had moved through the right phases. Participants agreed, while {{p:4}} said the finance review should have happened much earlier, during the design phase, because the team lacked price information. {{p:1}} agreed that the process had suffered from insufficient price information.

Asked whether there had been room for creativity, {{p:4}} said there had not been much, attributing this to the finance sheet. {{p:3}} agreed that there had been room, but that finance constrained it. {{p:4}} said they would have liked to include younger users and provide internet access and more individualized options. {{p:1}} noted internet access as a restriction. On leadership and role clarity, participants agreed that everyone had understood what they needed to do. They also said teamwork, including the collaboration between {{p:2}} and {{p:3}} in the final phase, had worked well. {{p:3}} said the tasks were structured step by step and therefore easy to carry out.

On whether the means provided were sufficient, {{p:3}} said drawing on the smartboard was difficult but the digital pen was useful. {{p:1}} noted that the pen had failed to download its data and described the smartboard as irritating. Participants suggested a flip chart or another easier, more precise drawing method. {{p:2}} observed that digital presentation materials could be saved and shared online or in a shared folder, though {{p:4}} said an attempt to open the file on a laptop had not worked. {{p:1}} said the smartboard application might be required and that exporting the work as an image should be possible. The group concluded that sharing information over the network was possible, although the file-sharing process had caused difficulty. {{p:2}} suggested that ratings and similar tasks might be easier on a computer, where each participant could enter an individual score and the results could be combined.

### Budget, target market, and project close
In the final budget discussion, participants said the costs were within budget, taking account of the decision not to make a docking station. {{p:1}} said the docking station might allow the remote’s price to be slightly higher and could compensate for some costs, while noting that the station itself was inexpensive to make. The group discussed a funding figure, correcting the amount to €15 million, and {{p:1}} said the project could attract that amount if the product were exported, especially to America, because it was innovative.

{{p:4}} suggested refocusing the product toward younger users, since a scroll button might appeal more to them than to older users. {{p:1}} proposed marketing the remote to everyone or targeting different markets by changing the removable front covers, including testing more fashionable covers for younger consumers. {{p:4}} agreed that such covers could make the product more popular with younger people. {{p:1}} then said the group could celebrate, but noted that one more questionnaire still had to be completed. The participants were told to complete it in their own rooms; {{p:1}} planned to return with a final presentation in about 10 minutes and said the project summary would be prepared."}

{"summary":"{{p:1}} opened the fourth and final meeting, scheduled from 3:00 to 3:30, to review the final design, evaluate the product and project, and close the project that day. {{p:3}} presented the prototype developed with Richard: on/off, mute, volume and channel controls, help shown on the LCD when held with another button, number buttons, teletext, subtitles, and the company logo. The proposed interface used equal-sized round buttons with recognition marks and contrasting rubber buttons; the LCD meant no LEDs were needed. The team explored reducing controls and meeting the €12.50-per-remote target: one rechargeable battery could save €2, the advanced chip was needed for the LCD, and the single-curved case cost €1 more than a flat one but was favored to emphasize the display. They discussed replacing number buttons with a scroll wheel and using it for both channel and volume control, retaining key functions, and making the wheel understandable to older users through advertising and LCD help. {{p:1}} supported keeping the single-curved design while cutting costs.

Product evaluation criteria included appearance, innovation, usability and learnability, functionality, cost, target-group fit, and company recognition. Ratings included 6/7 for appearance, 7 for innovation, 4 for ease of use, 7 for functionality, and 3 for fit with the target group. The overall score was 41/49 (about 84%). The project review found that finance and pricing should have been considered earlier in the design phase and that the finance sheet restricted creativity. Roles, teamwork, and structured tasks were clear and effective; the digital pen was useful, but smart-board drawing and software/data download problems were frustrating, with a flip-over suggested as an alternative. The group also considered widening the target market to younger users, including fashion-oriented or interchangeable front covers. {{p:1}} planned to prepare and present the final presentation, return in about ten minutes, and provide questionnaires for participants to complete in their rooms.","mom":"### Welcome and meeting plan
{{p:1}} opened the fourth and last meeting, beginning at 3:00, and said the group would discuss the final design, evaluate both the product and the project, and close the project that day. The detailed-design discussion would cover the design’s look and feel, interface usability, and product evaluation. The agenda was to present the prototype, set evaluation criteria, review whether the design could be delivered within the budget of €12.50 per remote control, evaluate the project, and close. {{p:1}} said they had 40 minutes and expected to finish at 3:30. {{p:4}} apologized for arriving late because of traffic; {{p:1}} said it was understandable at that time of day.

### Prototype: functions and button layout
{{p:3}} presented the prototype developed with Richard. Its proposed controls included an on/off button, a mute button below it, volume and channel selectors, a simple plus/minus control, a help button that would show guidance on the LCD when held while another button was pressed, number buttons from 0 to 9, teletext and subtitle buttons, and the company logo. {{p:3}} described it as a simple prototype and said user testing would show how people responded. {{p:4}} asked whether questions about functionality were welcome; {{p:3}} invited questions at any time.

{{p:4}} asked how the teletext control would move between pages. {{p:2}} explained that users could enter a page number with the number buttons or use the channel-shifting control to move up and down through teletext. {{p:1}} recalled that earlier meetings had aimed for a simple design with only a few large buttons, and questioned whether all the proposed buttons were needed. {{p:3}} said the on/off button was essential, as were volume and channel controls; mute could potentially be replaced by pressing volume-down twice. {{p:3}} considered help necessary because otherwise users would have no way to find out what a button did. {{p:2}} and {{p:1}} discussed using a long press as an alternative, but {{p:2}} cautioned that older users might not know about that option. The participants also treated the number buttons, teletext, and subtitles as necessary. {{p:4}} said a remote intended only for television would have little to gain from the proposed additional controls.

{{p:3}} said the buttons would be equal-sized and round, with small identifying marks, such as a triangle for volume, to aid recognition. {{p:2}} said the small display meant LEDs would not be needed. {{p:3}} proposed rubber buttons in a different colour from the case so they would stand out.

### Cost review and design trade-offs
{{p:1}} moved to the finance review, noting that only 30 minutes remained and that producing the design for €12.50 would be difficult. The initial estimate assumed two batteries, though the group discussed whether one rechargeable battery might suffice; {{p:1}} said using one would save €2. The advanced chip was needed, leaving little scope for savings there. A single-curved case cost €1 more than an uncurved case, but {{p:1}} favored the single curve for the design and to give the display a prominent place. Plastic was already the cheapest case material, while the buttons were the biggest cost. The group counted the proposed layout as 16 or 17 buttons and discussed an estimate of €18, above the €12.50 target.

{{p:1}} proposed removing the help and mute buttons by assigning their functions to long presses, which would save €1 and bring the count to 15. {{p:4}} objected that this approach would not be suitable. The group clarified whether the combined volume and channel controls counted as one or two buttons; {{p:2}} explained that they could be large controls but were more expensive than small buttons. {{p:4}} suggested integrating three number buttons into one control to reduce cost, and {{p:1}} agreed that this was possible and could also benefit the design. The participants discussed whether the advanced chip allowed the grouped controls to count as one button, but {{p:4}} maintained that the proposed cross-shaped control was effectively four buttons.

The group considered removing the LCD to save on both the display and the chip. {{p:3}} pointed out that omitting the display would remove a major feature, and {{p:4}} suggested the docking station might then be the remote’s only distinctive advantage. {{p:3}} noted that the docking station was not included in the schematic or its price. {{p:4}} raised changing suppliers, and {{p:1}} mentioned a possible Polish supplier. {{p:3}} questioned whether combining controls would make the remote less usable for older people, citing {{p:3}}’s mother’s difficulty sending an SMS. {{p:4}} said market research indicated that older people were more willing to spend, and suggested raising the remote’s price slightly; {{p:1}} responded that the team had to stay within the €12.50 budget and had no additional development budget.

The team explored replacing the ten number buttons with a scroll wheel for program numbers. {{p:1}} explained that users could scroll until the desired number appeared on the LCD, then press the wheel; {{p:4}} noted that an integrated scroll-and-push control would also cost more. {{p:3}} suggested that a pause of half a second after scrolling could select the channel without a press, and {{p:1}} said that would cut costs substantially. {{p:4}} warned that this could undermine usability, particularly for older people who might not know what a scroll wheel was or expect a remote to have ten number buttons. {{p:1}} proposed explaining the wheel in television advertising and the guide, keeping the LCD to provide usage help, and using it as part of the innovative design. {{p:4}} observed that the wheel looked large.

{{p:3}} then proposed using the scroll wheel for volume after pressing a volume button, and likewise for channel selection, which could save two buttons and make the wheel’s purpose clearer. {{p:1}} endorsed the idea. The emerging layout used separate volume and channel buttons plus the scroll wheel; the group discussed retaining teletext and reducing the layout to four or five buttons. {{p:3}} suggested a flat case and a smaller overall remote if more buttons were removed, arranging volume and channel controls level with the on/off button, with the screen behind and the scroll control beneath. {{p:2}} noted that a larger remote could cost the same as a smaller one if the cost difference was only in the single- or double-curved case. {{p:1}} explained that case moulds and manufacturing equipment affected the price: a single-curved case was straightforward to produce, while a single curve required a different machine from a flat case.

Asked to choose between a flat and single-curved design, {{p:4}} favored the single curve, while acknowledging that the changes and cost pressure were difficult. {{p:4}} suggested asking the board for more money or doing market research on the options, including an €18 remote. {{p:1}} said they could keep the single curve to emphasize the LCD and support help functions, which would be useful alongside the scroll control. The group also discussed whether the unusual design would be unfamiliar or confusing to older users and require substantial marketing. {{p:2}} pointed out that older people might recognize scroll controls from radios. {{p:1}} suggested giving the controls a familiar appearance. The team did not settle on a final cost figure in this discussion, but continued developing the reduced-button concept while keeping the €12.50 target in view.

### Product evaluation criteria and ratings
{{p:4}} said the evaluation criteria had been developed from a literature study and analysis of earlier requirements. The criteria covered whether the remote was fancy in its shape and look and feel; whether it was innovative and what new functions it offered; ease of use and learnability; functionality, including whether there were too many functions and whether the included functions were useful; cost; fit with the target group; and recognizability as a product from the company. {{p:4}} noted that preparing the evaluation had been difficult because the previous meeting’s minutes were unavailable. {{p:1}} explained that the digital pen had failed to upload its data and downloading its software was producing errors.

On a scale of 1 to 7, the group rated the design’s fanciness 6. For innovation, {{p:1}} proposed 7, citing the subtitles, LCD, docking station, and scroll controls. {{p:4}} agreed that the LCD, docking station, and scroll buttons made it innovative. The group then discussed usability: {{p:1}} described it as somewhat uncertain, and the participants settled on a rating between 4 and 5, with {{p:4}} choosing 4. The group agreed the design included the functions they wanted and did not have too many; {{p:4}} called it slim and assigned a score of 7. The discussion also raised unresolved frustrations such as remotes getting lost and repetitive strain injury, which {{p:3}} said the team had not considered. The group judged production costs to be within the preset limits in the current evaluation. On fit with the focus group, ratings diverged: {{p:3}} suggested 3, while {{p:1}} and {{p:4}} questioned whether the design fit older users, citing the unfamiliar radio-style control; {{p:1}} rated it 4, {{p:4}} 2, and {{p:2}} 3, and the group recorded 3. On company recognizability, participants said the logo, the company’s fashion-oriented slogan, and removable front cases helped identify the product.

{{p:4}} calculated the evaluation as seven factors multiplied by seven, giving a maximum of 49. After deductions of 1, 3, and 4, the group arrived at 41 out of 49. {{p:1}} first called this around 80 percent, then calculated the score as 84 percent and described it as a good result.

### Project-process evaluation
{{p:1}} asked whether the project had moved through the right phases. Participants agreed, while {{p:4}} said the finance review should have happened much earlier, during the design phase, because the team lacked price information. {{p:1}} agreed that the process had suffered from insufficient price information.

Asked whether there had been room for creativity, {{p:4}} said there had not been much, attributing this to the finance sheet. {{p:3}} agreed that there had been room, but that finance constrained it. {{p:4}} said they would have liked to include younger users and provide internet access and more individualized options. {{p:1}} noted internet access as a restriction. On leadership and role clarity, participants agreed that everyone had understood what they needed to do. They also said teamwork, including the collaboration between {{p:2}} and {{p:3}} in the final phase, had worked well. {{p:3}} said the tasks were structured step by step and therefore easy to carry out.

On whether the means provided were sufficient, {{p:3}} said drawing on the smartboard was difficult but the digital pen was useful. {{p:1}} noted that the pen had failed to download its data and described the smartboard as irritating. Participants suggested a flip chart or another easier, more precise drawing method. {{p:2}} observed that digital presentation materials could be saved and shared online or in a shared folder, though {{p:4}} said an attempt to open the file on a laptop had not worked. {{p:1}} said the smartboard application might be required and that exporting the work as an image should be possible. The group concluded that sharing information over the network was possible, although the file-sharing process had caused difficulty. {{p:2}} suggested that ratings and similar tasks might be easier on a computer, where each participant could enter an individual score and the results could be combined.

### Budget, target market, and project close
In the final budget discussion, participants said the costs were within budget, taking account of the decision not to make a docking station. {{p:1}} said the docking station might allow the remote’s price to be slightly higher and could compensate for some costs, while noting that the station itself was inexpensive to make. The group discussed a funding figure, correcting the amount to €15 million, and {{p:1}} said the project could attract that amount if the product were exported, especially to America, because it was innovative.

{{p:4}} suggested refocusing the product toward younger users, since a scroll button might appeal more to them than to older users. {{p:1}} proposed marketing the remote to everyone or targeting different markets by changing the removable front covers, including testing more fashionable covers for younger consumers. {{p:4}} agreed that such covers could make the product more popular with younger people. {{p:1}} then said the group could celebrate, but noted that one more questionnaire still had to be completed. {"mom":"### Opening and meeting agenda
{{p:1}} welcomed the group to the kick-off meeting, introduced himself as Danny Wolfs, the Project Manager, and outlined the agenda: introductions, getting acquainted through training on the two smart boards, reviewing the project plan and how to carry it out, discussion, and a closing. {{p:1}} also explained the room’s cameras and microphones, asked everyone to keep laptops in the designated positions so they would not block the cameras, and reminded them that the cameras needed to see participants’ faces. The attendees introduced themselves: {{p:2}} said he was Juergen Toffs, the User Interface Designer; {{p:3}} introduced himself as the Industrial Designer but did not state his name in the transcript; and {{p:4}} said he was Tim, the Marketing Expert.

### Project aim and stages
{{p:1}} said the project aim was to create a new remote control that was original, trendy, and user-friendly. He described three stages: functional design, deciding what functions to include and why; conceptual design, deciding broadly how to implement them; and detailed design, examining technical feasibility. Each stage would be split into individual work and a meeting.

### Smart-board training
{{p:1}} explained that one of the two smart boards was for presentations, including PowerPoint or Word presentations, while the other was for drawing. Documents intended for display needed to be saved in the shared folder, not My Documents. He reviewed the board’s save, print, undo, blank, select, and pen controls, and stressed that everything drawn on the board must be saved and nothing deleted. The drawing board was not fully real-time, so users should press firmly and wait a few seconds for their strokes to appear. {{p:1}} described the program as easy to use.

### Introductions exercise and drawing-tool practice
{{p:1}} asked everyone to draw a favorite animal on the whiteboard on the left and explain why they chose it, using different colors and pen widths. In response to {{p:4}} asking whether the company board had assigned the exercise, {{p:1}} said it was part of his introduction: the group did not know one another, so a short, fun exercise would help them get acquainted before tackling the harder work. {{p:1}} demonstrated how to use the drawing tool and explained that users should avoid touching a small part of it with their hand. During the exercise, {{p:1}} noted that the board had a 25-minute limit and urged the group to speed up. Participants reminded one another to use different colors and pen widths and to save their drawings. {{p:1}} said the pen-width setting he had used was five; {{p:4}} later said the larger lines were about nine.

{{p:1}} drew a cat and explained that his cat at home was named Simba because it looked like the lion from The Lion King; he said he had drawn only the face because they had 25 minutes. He chose red because his cat was red at home and he had red hair. {{p:4}} drew a turtle, explaining that he liked Teenage Mutant Hero Turtles. {{p:2}} drew a dog, saying he had chosen the easiest animal; he had had a dog a few years earlier, and they did not get another after it died. {{p:3}} drew a rabbit, identified by {{p:1}} as the white rabbit from The Matrix; {{p:3}} agreed and said he thought it was a good impression of a rabbit. The group joked about the drawings and compared which looked most artistic. {{p:1}} then moved the group on to the serious discussion.

### Price, production cost, and sales target
{{p:1}} said the remote’s selling price would be 25 euros and production cost must not exceed 20.50 euros. He said the required profit was 50 million euros, so the company would need to sell many units. In response to questions about the quantity, {{p:1}} calculated that at a selling price of 25 euros, the target would mean selling 2 million remotes. He added that the market was international, covering virtually the whole world, at least countries with television.

### Remote-control features and product direction
{{p:1}} invited the group to consider their experiences using remote controls at home, useful new features, and what could distinguish this product from other remotes. {{p:2}} said the most important function was changing channels and argued for keeping the remote as basic as possible, rather than combining control of a television, DVD player, radio, and other devices. {{p:4}} agreed with keeping it simple but presented marketing considerations: it should be intuitive, small, fairly cheap, and brand-independent, so the television’s brand would not matter. The stated price was 25 euros.

{{p:4}} also proposed making the remote multi-purpose, since most current remotes served only one purpose; this could add a new feature and distinguish the product from existing products. He suggested considering technology other than infrared because it was annoying when someone standing in front of the television prevented channel changes, and mentioned radio waves or Bluetooth as alternatives, while noting that they might be more expensive. He also proposed an LCD screen that could show upcoming programs for the channel being watched. {{p:4}} said the company was good at developing innovative products and that a new entrant seeking market share needed to do something special. {{p:1}} agreed that the product should add something to the market, while cautioning that the team must not lose sight of user-friendliness. {{p:2}} also raised price as a consideration. {{p:4}} clarified that these were marketing views and said he did not know about user-interface or design matters; the other participants noted that the team included specialists for those areas.

### Work between meetings and decisions for the next meeting
{{p:1}} said the next meeting would start in 30 minutes. Before it, participants would have individual tasks and would presumably provide feedback by email: the Industrial Designer should examine the working design, and the User Interface Designer should examine the technical functions. {{p:2}} said the team first needed to agree what it was going to make, including whether it would support multiple systems, before proceeding with technical-function work. {{p:4}} and {{p:3}} suggested postponing that decision until the next meeting, after preparing mock-ups and general ideas; the group could then plan further and edit or remove obsolete details. {{p:1}} said each person should independently consider what mattered most from their own perspective, then the group would bring the pieces together at the next meeting. He also proposed reaching an initial consensus on the project’s direction so user requirements would fit the technical functions. {{p:2}} agreed that technical functions depended on knowing what kinds of machines the remote would serve, while noting that details such as a text screen or Bluetooth were a step further. {{p:4}} suggested that each person prepare a list of required features and that the group decide together at the next meeting. {{p:1}} said participants would receive specific instructions from their personal coach and that he would see them in 30 minutes."}

{"summary":"### Opening and meeting agenda
{{p:1}}, who introduced himself as Danny Wolfs and Project Manager, welcomed the group to the kickoff meeting and outlined the agenda: introductions, getting acquainted through smart-board training, reviewing the project plan, discussion, and closing. He explained that the room was being watched by “Big Brother” via cameras and microphones, and that laptops were positioned so cameras could see participants’ faces. He said the agenda was for today and that he would introduce himself, then asked everyone to introduce themselves. {{p:2}} said he was Juergen Toffs, the User Interface Designer; {{p:3}} introduced himself as the Industrial Designer but did not state his name; and {{p:4}} said he was Tim, the Marketing Expert.

### Project aim and stages
{{p:1}} said the aim was to make a new remote control that was original, trendy, and user-friendly. The work would proceed through functional design (what functions to include and why), conceptual design (broadly how to implement them), and detailed design (examining technical feasibility). Each stage would include individual work and a meeting.

### Smart-board training
{{p:1}} explained that one of the two smart boards was for presentations such as PowerPoint or Word, and the other for drawing. Documents intended for display needed to be saved in the shared folder, rather than My Documents. He reviewed save, print, undo, blank, select, and pen controls, and stressed that all drawings must be saved and nothing deleted. The drawing board was not fully real-time, so users should press firmly and wait a few seconds for strokes to appear. He described the program as easy to use.

### Introductions exercise and drawing-tool practice
{{p:1}} asked everyone to draw a favorite animal on the whiteboard on the left and explain the choice, using different colors and pen widths. When {{p:4}} asked whether the company had assigned the exercise, {{p:1}} explained that it was part of his introduction: the group did not know one another, so a short, fun exercise would help them get acquainted before the harder work. He demonstrated the drawing tool and cautioned users not to touch a small part of it with their hand. {{p:4}} compared the exercise to Pictionary. During the exercise, {{p:1}} noted the 25-minute limit and urged the group to speed up. Participants reminded one another to use different colors and pen widths and to save drawings. {{p:1}} said his pen-width setting was five; {{p:4}} said the larger lines were about nine.

{{p:1}} drew his cat Simba, named because it looked like the lion from The Lion King. He drew only the face because they had 25 minutes and chose red because his cat at home was red and he had red hair. {{p:4}} drew a turtle because he liked Teenage Mutant Hero Turtles. {{p:2}} chose a dog as the easiest animal; he had had a dog a few years earlier, and they did not get another after it died. {{p:3}} drew a rabbit, which {{p:1}} identified as the white rabbit from The Matrix; {{p:3}} agreed and said he thought it was a good impression of a rabbit. The group joked about the drawings and compared which looked most artistic. {{p:1}} then moved the group on to the serious discussion.

### Price, production cost, and sales target
{{p:1}} said the selling price would be €25 and production cost must not exceed €20.50. The required profit was €50 million, which would require selling a large number of units. In response to questions, {{p:1}} estimated that at a €25 selling price the target meant selling two million remotes. He said the market was international—virtually the whole world, at least countries that have television. He added that, in his view, the product should not be an ultra-modern, high-definition, high-tech remote at a production cost of €12.50.

### Remote-control features and product direction
{{p:1}} invited the group to consider their experiences using remote controls at home, useful new features, and what could distinguish the product from competing remotes. {{p:2}} said the most important function was switching channels and argued for keeping the remote as basic as possible, rather than combining control of a television, DVD player, radio, and other devices. {{p:4}} agreed with simplicity but said the product should be intuitive, small, fairly cheap, and brand-independent, so the television brand would not matter. He noted the stated price of €25.

{{p:4}} also proposed a multi-purpose remote, since most current remotes served only one purpose; this could add a new feature and distinguish it from existing products. He suggested considering alternatives to infrared because someone standing in front of the television could prevent channel changes, mentioning radio waves or Bluetooth while noting these might be more expensive. He also proposed an LCD screen to show upcoming programs for the channel being watched. {{p:4}} said the company was good at developing innovative products and that a new entrant seeking market share needed to do something special. {{p:1}} agreed that the product should add something to the market, while cautioning against losing sight of user-friendliness. {{p:2}} also raised price as a consideration. {{p:4}} clarified that these were marketing views and that he did not know about user-interface or design matters; the other participants noted that the team included specialists for those areas.

### Work between meetings and decisions for the next meeting
{{p:1}} said the next meeting would start in 30 minutes. Participants would have individual tasks, with feedback expected by email: the Industrial Designer should examine the working design, and the User Interface Designer should review the technical functions. {{p:2}} said the team first needed to agree what it was going to make, including whether it would support multiple systems, before proceeding with technical-function work. {{p:4}} said they did not need to decide that yet; {{p:4}} and {{p:3}} suggested returning to it at the next meeting after preparing mock-ups and general ideas. They could then plan further and edit or remove obsolete details. {{p:1}} said each person should independently consider what mattered most from their own perspective, then the group would bring the pieces together at the next meeting. He proposed reaching an initial consensus on the project’s direction so user requirements would fit the technical functions. {{p:2}} agreed that technical functions depended on knowing what kinds of machines the remote would serve, while noting that matters such as a text screen or Bluetooth were a step further. {{p:4}} suggested that everyone prepare a list of required features and decide together at the next meeting. {{p:1}} said participants would receive specific instructions from their personal coach and that he would see them in 30 minutes.","actionItems":[{"id":"a1","text":"Save all drawings made on the smart board; TS3007b: {"title":"Remote-control design: research findings and interface direction","summary":"{{p:1}} opened the functional design meeting by assigning each participant a presentation on work from the previous half hour, saying the minutes would be placed in the shared folder and noting that minutes from the previous session were already there. The management board’s four points were that teletext was becoming outdated as internet became the main focus; the remote should control only the television, not serve multiple purposes; the intended audience should shift from current customers aged 40 and older to users younger than 40; and the slogan and logo should become more recognizable on the remote. {{p:4}} presented a questionnaire conducted by the usability lab with 100 respondents: the two age groups were 16–45 and 46–65, with market shares reported as about 65% and 35%; younger users favored newer technology such as LCD screens and speech recognition, while interest declined with age. The research also found that 75% considered current remotes ugly and 80% would pay more for a fancy-looking one; the most important, frequently used functions were channel switching, teletext, and volume control. {{p:4}} recommended targeting ages 16–45, improving those core functions, making their buttons larger, reducing unused buttons so the remote would be quicker to learn, and considering a TV-side holder; the participants agreed the remote should emphasize commonly used buttons rather than add functions indiscriminately. {{p:3}} reported that current remotes use infrared and have simple, low-cost structures, arguing against Bluetooth or a receiver because these would require compatible TV equipment or add cost and complexity; a replaceable standard battery and an indicator light to confirm button presses were also described. The group discussed reducing clutter through a simple layout, multifunction buttons or concealed options, while keeping core controls readily accessible and avoiding reliance on TV menus that vary or may not exist; a touch screen with permanent primary controls and a separate area for additional options was favored, with larger, familiar visual controls considered helpful for older users. The group also explored parental controls using a PIN and TV-specific profiles or stored settings, but {{p:1}} said such ideas could be addressed at a later stage; for updating remote profiles or firmware, participants considered USB or FireWire downloads and a TV-side connection, then favored updates at a shop or service center, potentially through a docking station, as the simpler approach. {{p:1}} said the meeting minutes were updated in the shared folder, announced a 30-minute lunch break followed by 30 minutes of individual work, and said instructions for the next meeting would arrive by email; after a brief discussion of whether the break should be 30 or 45 minutes, the group settled on 30 minutes, and the questionnaire was to be completed after lunch."}

{"mom":"### Meeting format and management-board guidance
{{p:1}} said the functional-design meeting would consist of presentations by each team member, except {{p:1}}, on the work completed during the previous half hour. {{p:1}} would take minutes and place them in the shared folder after the session; minutes from the previous session were already there. The group had 40 minutes, with presentations intended to last no more than 10 minutes each, and presenters could use the SMARTboards, Word files, or other facilities. {{p:1}} relayed four management-board points: teletext was considered outdated as the internet would be the main focus; the remote should be for television only, not a multipurpose controller; current customers were aged 40 and older, while the new remote should reach people younger than 40; and, as a future consideration rather than an immediate priority, the slogan and logo should be more recognizable on the remote.

### Marketing research findings and recommendations
{{p:4}} presented marketing research based on a questionnaire conducted by the usability lab with 100 respondents, with a report prepared by the marketing department. The findings divided the audience into ages 16–45 and 46–65. The younger group represented about 60–65% of the market, and the older group 35%. Younger users showed interest in advanced features such as an LCD screen on the remote and speech recognition, while interest in such technology declined among older respondents. On current remotes, 75% of users considered most models very ugly, and 80% said they would spend more for a fancy-looking remote. A frequency-of-use-versus-importance assessment identified channel switching, teletext, and volume controls as the most important buttons. {{p:1}} noted the apparent conflict between teletext’s measured importance and the board’s view that it would become outdated as internet access developed. {{p:4}} responded that teletext was currently the best way to get information on television, and respondents used it rather than internet features on a remote because the newer technology was not yet incorporated. {{p:4}} recommended targeting ages 16–45 because they represented the largest audience, at 65%, and were expected to generate more revenue because they watched more television than older people. The team should improve the most-used functions and make the most-used buttons larger or otherwise easier to use; many buttons on existing remotes went unused, so reducing their number could make the remote quicker and easier to learn. {{p:4}} also suggested a television-side holder for putting the remote away. In discussion, {{p:3}} asked what improving functions meant; {{p:4}} clarified that the focus should be on functionality and the buttons people actually used, with minor functions potentially consolidated onto shared buttons.

### Industrial-design review and component choices
{{p:3}} described examining current remote controls, how they look and work, their components and connections, and mapping their organization. Current remotes predominantly use infrared, matching the receivers in televisions and stereos. A Bluetooth remote would require Bluetooth capability in the television too, adding cost for the user; {{p:3}} therefore considered infrared more suitable for a relatively inexpensive design and doubted Bluetooth or radio would fit the budget, while leaving that question for marketing to investigate. In response to {{p:4}}’s suggestion of placing a Bluetooth or radio receiver in the television-side holder, {{p:3}} said it might be attractive but would still shift the problem and retain the need for infrared. {{p:3}} also proposed exploring a speech-activated locator: when someone asked where the remote was, it could beep, though the cost was unknown. The proposed basic components were an easily available replaceable battery, a chip and switch, and an infrared transmitter. Pressing a button would light a bulb immediately to show the user that the press registered; the chip would translate and process the signal before it was sent by the infrared bulb to the television. {{p:3}} favored a simple design, infrared transmission without a receiver, and no television input, arguing that teletext feedback would require a receiver and add cost and development time. {{p:4}} observed that current televisions could send infrared; {{p:3}} agreed this was possible but questioned the extra components, design work, and larger remote that a receiver would require. {{p:3}} recommended focusing on design and functionality, using one button for multiple functions or concealing less-used controls, and avoiding an oversized remote for simple functions.

### User-interface principles and touch-screen concepts
{{p:2}} said the design should balance technical feasibility, appearance, and user-friendliness. Too many functions make a remote harder to use, so functions should be limited or organized hierarchically rather than displayed all at once; {{p:2}} used the example of not wanting to see 50 links on an internet page or 50 remote buttons. The remote should have clear, easy-to-use buttons and keep essential actions such as play, back, stop, channel switching, and volume directly accessible. Although an earlier discussion had considered easy switching between multiple machines, {{p:2}} said that was no longer applicable because the remote was intended for television only. {{p:2}} cautioned that combining functions can conflict with simplicity: the team had to weigh a small number of options against a larger set of buttons. {{p:4}} proposed an LCD or touch screen with core controls in the middle and menus such as settings at the top or bottom. {{p:2}} asked whether menus should appear on the television or be contained in the remote, and recommended displaying menus on the television if one button opened several options; combinations of buttons or holding buttons for several seconds could be too complicated. {{p:4}} pointed out that television menus differ between models, so a remote’s menu might not match the television’s. {{p:3}} added that some televisions have no menu structure or only a very simple one, limiting compatibility. {{p:2}} stressed that the design had to reflect current market technology, with large, clear buttons and fewer options if necessary. Advanced functions could be placed out of the way, while power, channel, and volume actions should work directly without first navigating menus. The remote should give feedback so users could tell the television or remote had responded, rather than assume the batteries were low.

{{p:4}} supported a touch screen, citing a television news item about telephones for older people that used a touch screen with large call and hang-up images; enlarging the displayed images could make a remote more suitable for older users. {{p:2}} suggested keeping primary buttons visible, making the remote comfortable to hold, and including a logo and an aesthetic form. A flip-open design, like some older telephones, could reveal additional options if a touch screen proved too difficult. When {{p:4}} asked what the touch screen would show, {{p:2}} proposed menus for system or teletext functions, with the user selecting a menu and scrolling through the options. {{p:3}} suggested one large touch screen, possibly organized into three menus with sub-items or sub-functions. {{p:2}} proposed keeping the same essential buttons always available and using the lower part of a large touch screen for other functions; {{p:3}} compared this to an iPod-style arrangement with a few selected buttons and menus that could later be improved. {{p:1}} asked whether the group favored a fully touch-screen design. {{p:4}} and {{p:3}} supported it, while {{p:2}} agreed on the condition that the same essential buttons remained accessible and only special options used part of the screen. {{p:2}} emphasized that a user should still be able to turn off the television or change channels without navigating a menu. {{p:1}} raised the concern that older people might not be accustomed to touch screens and suggested retaining familiar physical controls for teletext and volume, with more difficult functions on the screen. {{p:4}} replied that an LCD could display very large numbers, and {{p:2}} said it could present buttons in the familiar style of an older remote. {{p:3}} noted that touching a screen does not feel the same as pressing a physical button, but the team should consider its target audience: people under 40. {{p:4}} cited the research showing younger users liked fancy new technology and said Microsoft had already developed touch-screen technology for multimedia applications.

### Parental controls and television compatibility
{{p:4}} proposed a parental-control feature using a PIN code that would let parents access all channels while preventing children without the code from switching to violent channels. {{p:3}} said feasibility depended on the television. The discussion clarified that channel assignments differ between television models and are not necessarily in a preset order: channel 15 on one television might not be channel 15 on another. {{p:2}} suggested matching the remote to the television first, then using passwords to restrict children from changing television settings such as color and volume. {{p:4}} described a parent logging in and assigning restrictions to channels—for example, marking channel 15 as a violent channel that their children should not watch and setting access to parents only. {{p:2}} suggested making parental control a separate menu option. {{p:1}} said the feature was an interesting idea but should not take the meeting too far off topic and might be addressed at a later stage.

The team also discussed how to make a remote work with different televisions and their different menu systems. {{p:2}} suggested storing television-model information in the remote so it could identify a brand, such as Philips, and offer the functions that model supports. {{p:1}} noted the international market and wide range of televisions. {{p:2}} said universal remotes already support many televisions; manuals may list 300–400 models, including old and new televisions. {{p:3}} cautioned that universal remotes have to be programmed to fit a particular television, which can be troublesome, and that synchronization or other features requiring the television to send information would need a receiver in the remote. {{p:4}} described current universal remotes as requiring users to look up and enter codes from a book; {{p:2}} gave the example of a Philips H55 television and code 455. As an alternative, {{p:4}} proposed matching a television type to a set of options stored in remote memory, with a model or profile selection—such as entering 1410—bringing up the corresponding options. {{p:3}} and {{p:2}} considered this possible, and {{p:4}} thought it would not take much storage space. {{p:2}} said the number of television models represented in universal-remote manuals suggested that storing the options was feasible. {{p:4}} observed that a newly purchased television might not be included in an older remote, prompting discussion of replacing the remote or updating its software or firmware.

### Updates and closing arrangements
{{p:4}} suggested adding a USB or FireWire connection so the remote could connect to a PC and download the latest firmware from the internet. {{p:3}} cautioned that not everyone had a PC. {{p:2}} suggested going to a shop or service center to have an update installed; {{p:4}} agreed that updating at a service center or shop would likely be cheapest. {{p:3}} also suggested using the proposed television-side holder as a possible connection point, including a telephone-line or internet connection, but noted that receiving information would again require extra components and cost. {{p:4}} proposed a docking station: place the remote in it, press start, and update it. The group agreed that this could be a practical approach, particularly because people do not buy a television every week. In a vote between two displayed concepts, {{p:3}} voted for the right-hand option, {{p:4}} also voted for it, and {{p:2}} said the discussion had persuaded them that displaying buttons in a familiar arrangement would help older users understand the controls. The group also noted a flip-open device as a possible way to reveal more options, although {{p:4}} worried it could be easy to break and {{p:1}} remarked that the design was very sensitive.

{{p:1}} said the meeting was nearly over and announced a lunch break, followed by 30 minutes of individual work. The minutes were updated and would be available in the shared folder. {{p:4}} asked when to return; the group clarified that lunch would be 30 minutes, with {{p:2}} suggesting a quarter to one. {{p:1}} said the next meeting’s specific instructions would arrive by email and hoped the work could be completed during the 30 minutes after lunch. {{p:1}} said the questionnaire would be completed after lunch because they were hungry. The team discussed saving the meeting material: {{p:1}} said the files were stored as SMART Board XDK, and participants considered saving or exporting an image, including JPEG, in the project documents. {{p:3}} said they had saved their material in their own documents and messenger. The meeting ended with thanks."}

{"summary":"{{p:1}} opened the functional-design meeting by asking each participant except {{p:1}} to present work from the previous half hour. {{p:1}} said the minutes would be placed in the shared folder after the session, and that minutes from the previous session were already there. The meeting had 40 minutes, with presentations intended to last no more than 10 minutes each; presenters could use the SMARTboards, Word files, or other facilities. The management board’s four points were that teletext was becoming outdated as internet became the main focus; the remote should control only the television, not serve multiple purposes; the intended audience should shift from current customers aged 40 and older to users younger than 40; and the slogan and logo should become more recognizable on the remote, although this was not an immediate priority. {{p:4}} presented a questionnaire conducted by the usability lab with 100 respondents and reported by the marketing department: the two age groups were 16–45 and 46–65, with market shares of about 65% and 35%. Younger users favored newer technology such as LCD screens and speech recognition, while interest declined with age. Research found that 75% considered current remotes very ugly and 80% would pay more for a fancy-looking one. Channel switching, teletext, and volume controls ranked highest for importance and frequency of use. {{p:1}} noted teletext’s apparent conflict with the board’s view that internet would make it outdated; {{p:4}} said teletext was currently the best way to get information on television and that internet features were not yet incorporated into remotes. {{p:4}} recommended targeting ages 16–45, improving core functions, making commonly used buttons larger or easier to use, and reducing unused buttons so the remote would be quicker to learn. {{p:4}} also suggested a television-side holder to put the remote away. {{p:3}} asked what improving functions meant; {{p:4}} clarified that the focus should be on functionality and the buttons people actually used, with minor functions potentially consolidated onto shared buttons.

{{p:3}} reported examining current remotes, their appearance, operation, components, connections, and organization. Current remotes use infrared and simple, low-cost structures. Bluetooth would require compatible television equipment and add cost; {{p:3}} therefore favored infrared and doubted Bluetooth or radio would fit the budget, leaving the budget question for marketing to investigate. A television-side holder with a Bluetooth or radio receiver was discussed, but {{p:3}} said it would move the problem and still retain the need for infrared. {{p:3}} floated a speech-activated locator that would beep when someone asked where the remote was, though the cost was unknown. The basic design described included an easily available replaceable battery, chip, switch, and infrared transmitter. A light would confirm button presses; the chip would process the signal before it was sent to the television. {{p:3}} favored a simple design, infrared transmission without a receiver, and no television input, arguing that teletext feedback would require a receiver and add cost and development time. {{p:4}} observed that current televisions could send infrared; {{p:3}} agreed this was possible but questioned the extra components, design work, and larger remote a receiver would require. {{p:3}} recommended focusing on design and functionality, using one button for multiple functions or concealing less-used controls, and avoiding an oversized remote for simple functions.

{{p:2}} said the design should balance technical feasibility, appearance, and user-friendliness. Too many functions make a remote harder to use, so functions should be limited or organized hierarchically rather than all displayed at once; {{p:2}} compared this to not wanting 50 links on an internet page or 50 buttons on a remote. Clear, easy-to-use controls should keep essential actions such as play, back, stop, channel switching, and volume directly accessible. Switching between multiple machines was no longer applicable because the remote was intended for television only. The team discussed the trade-off between combining functions and keeping the controls simple. {{p:4}} proposed an LCD or touch screen with core controls in the middle and menus such as settings at the top or bottom. {{p:2}} recommended that if one button opened several options, menus should appear on the television rather than using complicated button combinations or holding buttons. {{p:4}} and {{p:3}} noted that television menus vary and some televisions have no menu structure or only a simple one, limiting compatibility. {{p:2}} stressed working within current market technology, using large, clear buttons and fewer options if necessary, and keeping power, channel, and volume actions direct rather than behind menus. Users should receive feedback that the remote or television responded, rather than assume the batteries were low. {{p:4}} supported a touch screen, citing telephones for older people with large call and hang-up images; enlarged images could make controls more suitable for older users. {{p:2}} suggested keeping primary buttons visible, making the remote comfortable to hold, and including a logo and an aesthetic form. A flip-open design could reveal additional options if a touch screen proved too difficult. The screen could display system or teletext menus with scrollable options; {{p:3}} suggested one large touch screen organized into menus and sub-functions. {{p:2}} proposed keeping the same essential buttons always available and using the lower part of the screen for other functions, similar to an iPod-style arrangement. {{p:1}} asked whether the group favored a fully touch-screen design: {{p:4}} and {{p:3}} supported it, while {{p:2}} agreed only if the same essential buttons remained accessible and special options used part of the screen. {{p:1}} raised concern that older people might not be accustomed to touch screens and suggested familiar physical controls for teletext and volume with more difficult functions on screen. {{p:4}} said an LCD could show very large numbers, and {{p:2}} said the screen could display buttons in a familiar older-remote style. {{p:3}} noted that a touch screen does not feel like a physical button, but said the target audience was people under 40. {{p:4}} cited research that younger users liked fancy new technology and said Microsoft had already developed touch-screen technology for multimedia applications.

{"mom":"### Meeting purpose and agenda
{{p:1}} opened the conceptual design meeting for Real Reaction. The format was the same as at the previous meeting, with three presentations this time and a decision to be reached on the remote-control concepts. {{p:1}} said the concepts were in two groups: component concepts and user-interface concepts. The component package included a touch screen protected by a case to make it less breakable, with a choice between rechargeable power and replaceable batteries; the interface questions included the screen type and supplementary controls, including button placement. {{p:1}} would take notes, and the minutes would be placed in the shared folder. {{p:1}} asked {{p:3}} to begin with the component presentation.

### Component concepts: target users and styling
{{p:3}} said the component review compared products used by two age groups, people below 45 and people above 45, to assess their differences and identify how to target the product. The older group preferred traditional materials such as wood and chrome, straightforward shapes, and luxurious styles. Younger, dynamic users preferred soft materials, with Teletubbies offered as an example, as well as soft, fluffy, colorful materials and curved, rounded forms. {{p:3}} added that sports and gaming conveyed vitality for younger users. When {{p:1}} asked whether a soft material was appropriate for a remote, {{p:3}} said the material choice would be discussed later.

### Power source
{{p:3}} compared batteries with kinetic power, explaining that kinetic energy could be generated by movement, such as picking up the remote, and that a user could shake it if it needed more power. {{p:3}} considered kinetic power high-tech and attractive, with costs not much higher than a normal battery, but {{p:1}} questioned whether a remote would be moved enough to maintain its charge. {{p:3}} said picking it up and pressing buttons should provide enough movement, and suggested combining a battery with kinetic recharging. {{p:2}} proposed solar power; {{p:3}} said it would need light, preferably sunlight, and that normal light would provide less energy than a battery. Integrating solar panels into the remote would also take up interface space. {{p:3}} considered using light from the television but said it would still consume space and would not provide the full power needed. In the discussion, {{p:2}} favored kinetic power as a backup, {{p:4}} suggested a combination, and {{p:1}} said they preferred combining the sources too. The group endorsed a battery charged by kinetic movement, with {{p:1}} comparing it to a Seiko watch. {{p:3}} acknowledged the combination would add some cost; {{p:2}} joked about buying a battery for fifty cents.

### Case shape, material, and screen
{{p:3}} described a basic square case as boring and proposed single-curve or double-curve designs. A double curve would add dimensions and, in {{p:3}}’s view, create a younger, more high-tech, dynamic look; {{p:3}} offered to draw the concept in three dimensions. {{p:3}} said designers need not stick to a standard shape, because a deeper or more varied back would leave more room for creativity. For case material, {{p:3}} preferred rubber over plastic because it felt soft, while associating plastic with a cheap feel. {{p:1}} connected softness with younger users. The participants supported rubber, while {{p:2}} cautioned that it should remain firm and not be bendable; {{p:3}} said the chipset would hold it in place, and {{p:2}} noted that it might bounce if dropped. {{p:4}} added that rubber should be fairly hard, as on regular mobile phones, both to fit market trends and to improve safety if the remote were dropped. For the screen and controls, {{p:3}} recalled that the earlier meeting had already covered traditional buttons versus an LCD and proposed leaving the decision at LCD. An LCD would require a more advanced chipset and bring additional costs, whereas traditional buttons could use a simple chipset; {{p:3}} said the LCD option should be manageable and supported choosing the advanced chipset if the group selected LCD. {{p:4}} estimated sales of ten million units and suggested that a large company in Korea or Taiwan, such as Samsung, could offer a substantial chip discount; {{p:4}} added that chips usually cost no more than one dollar. {{p:2}} asked whether the touch screen itself had to be square. {{p:4}} said touch screens were generally square but suggested shaping the surrounding case, for example with features that cover part of the LCD, to customize the appearance.

### Marketing research and audience preferences
{{p:4}} reported that the marketing and research-and-development departments had visited Paris and Milan the previous week for trend-watching. They asked people of different ages and incomes about spending, design, and materials. For the main audience—people below 40—{{p:4}} reported a preference for fresh fruit-like colors, including green, red or strawberry red, and yellow or banana yellow, as well as spongy, soft materials. {{p:4}} said these findings were consistent with {{p:3}}’s observations. The secondary audience, people above 40, preferred dark, traditional colors and materials such as wood. After discussion about whether wood could be used for a remote, the participants considered a wooden appearance or wooden-looking case instead. {{p:4}} said the group had decided to target people below 40, so the secondary-audience findings would not apply. {{p:4}} summarized broader expectations for new remotes: they should look fancy, be technological and innovative, and be easy to use. To customize color, {{p:4}} proposed removable covers, like those used for mobile phones, giving the example of replacing a red cover with a green one. {{p:4}} also recommended rubber for market fit and drop safety, while emphasizing that it should be fairly hard. {{p:3}} observed that phones and remotes had a lot in common and mentioned having seen a phone that could be used as a remote.

### Additional feature proposals
{{p:4}} proposed reconsidering speech recognition, describing it as innovative and saying the market was calling for new technologies, but also warned that it could be very expensive. {{p:1}} gave an example of saying a command to trigger a function. {{p:4}} also suggested games such as Snake or Tetris to entertain younger users and noted a possible link between remote controls and mobile phones. {{p:1}} questioned whether people would use games while watching television; {{p:2}} said they could be useful when parents were watching a boring program, and participants also discussed taking the remote to college. {{p:4}} presented parental control with the slogan of taking parental control to a new dimension. The group discussed using a log-in or profile system, including parent and child profiles. {{p:2}} stressed that it would need to be fast: users should not have to wait twenty seconds for a log-in screen, remember a code, and navigate numerous settings when turning on the television to watch the news at eight o’clock. {{p:1}} countered that many parents would consider preventing children from seeing sex or violence on television more important than waiting an extra ten or fifteen seconds. {{p:2}} suggested a simple log-in, such as pressing one, two, or three for a profile, with children limited to children’s channels. {{p:3}} questioned whether the feature was worth the development time and resources, since it would require programming profiles. {{p:1}} said there was a significant market, noting concerns reported in magazines and on the news that children were influenced by television; {{p:1}} added that many people below 40 had young children and would want to restrict violent content. {{p:2}} proposed keeping the remote simple by making profiles an optional menu feature, so a grandparent would not have to use them. {{p:4}} said the remote should be simple when sold, with users able to install the feature personally; {{p:4}} would choose a remote with parental control if they had children. {{p:2}} raised the question of restricting programs by time as well as by channel, including violent films after ten o’clock. {{p:1}} suggested using television program guide information to block programs identified as violent, but {{p:2}} noted that someone would have to provide and maintain the program data. {{p:3}} pointed out that children could bypass the remote’s restrictions by pressing buttons on the television itself. {{p:2}} suggested that the remote could incorporate a clock and stop transmitting after a set time, but {{p:4}} noted that some televisions have buttons behind a compartment. The participants agreed that controlling access through the remote could not prevent every workaround.

### Decisions on features and interface
{{p:1}} summarized the discussion: games would be included, voice recognition would not, and parental control would be incorporated but kept uncomplicated. {{p:2}} supported placing parental control in the menu structure, while {{p:4}} described a parent-and-child log-in screen. The group discussed whether parental control should be a standard or optional feature; {{p:2}} preferred an always-available menu option that could be selected when the product was purchased, including a password or personal preference. {{p:3}} suggested separate basic and deluxe models, with a receiver in the model that included parental control, but acknowledged that this would cost more. {{p:2}} suggested limiting restrictions to selected channels and viewing times. The group’s final discussion treated parental control as included but not overly complex, while recognizing that the detailed implementation still needed work. On the main interface, {{p:2}} proposed one large touch screen with primary buttons always clearly visible, a changeable menu structure, and limited on-screen options at any one time. They advised against too many menu levels or repeated button presses, and suggested keeping teletext and other less-used functions in the menu. {{p:2}} described a one-handed form that would fit into the hand, slightly broader than remotes meant to be operated by thumb alone, with the thumb used for main buttons and the other hand for menus. They identified program buttons, volume and program controls, and a large LCD for the menu. {{p:4}} suggested a back-and-forth channel button like the one in Internet Explorer. {{p:2}} agreed it could be useful but preferred placing it in the menu, so the screen could still display it without making it a primary control. {{p:4}} illustrated the need by describing someone switching between channels two and seventeen; {{p:2}} agreed it was a good idea.

### Concept decisions and remaining interface discussion
{{p:1}} recapped the agreed direction: a battery-and-kinetic power combination; a double-curved case; rubber; a flashy, fruity color with a removable cover; a touch screen; and a menu structure with few levels that was easy to use. Parental control would be incorporated without making the product too complex, and games would be included. The group reached consensus on these points. {{p:4}} then suggested adding expert and simple views. {{p:2}} said the existing concept already provided a simple interface when the menu was not in use, with system properties and more programmable options available when selected. {{p:3}} proposed allowing advanced users to customize which buttons were included, such as adding a back-forward button for people who mainly watched two channels. The participants agreed to carry this idea to the next meeting.

### Follow-up information and next meeting
{{p:1}} shared two points from a master class attended during lunch. First, knowledge management and knowledge engineering were current topics, including sharing knowledge and learning from other companies; {{p:1}} connected this to examining how other companies handled marketing campaigns when introducing a new remote. The discussion identified benchmarking and import-export as relevant concepts. Second, {{p:1}} said a survey found that people preferred buying from one large provider rather than from companies partnering with it. {{p:1}} therefore said Real Reaction should present itself as a large, trustworthy company that could stand on its own. {{p:4}} proposed the name “R to the third power,” or “R3,” for “Real Reaction Remote.” {{p:1}} suggested a single brand and a short animation or logo when the remote was turned on, with the motto “We put fashion in electronics.” {{p:4}} said a code would also need to be entered; {{p:2}} argued that even a logo displayed for 0.5 seconds could be remembered. {{p:3}} suggested a small logo at the bottom of the LCD that could remain visible. {{p:1}} said the next meeting would start in 30 minutes and said participants could return to Paris and Milan once again. {{p:1}} identified the master class as Franz Mehler’s. For the next session, {{p:1}} said the industrial-development and user-interface teams would work together on a prototype and draw it on the SMARTboard; the marketing expert would work on product evaluation. Specific instructions would be sent by email."}
