The next meeting was in 30 minutes.","mom":"### Meeting purpose and agenda
{{p:1}} opened the conceptual design meeting for Real Reaction. The format was the same as at the previous meeting, with three presentations this time and a decision to be reached on the remote-control concepts. {{p:1}} said the concepts were in two groups: component concepts and user-interface concepts. The component package included a touch screen protected by a case to make it less breakable, with a choice between rechargeable power and replaceable batteries; the interface questions included the screen type and supplementary controls, including button placement. {{p:1}} would take notes, and the minutes would be placed in the shared folder. {{p:1}} asked {{p:3}} to begin with the component presentation. At the start, {{p:2}} reported that the laptop had problems and that there had been less time to complete the preparation.

### Component concepts: target users and styling
{{p:3}} said the component review compared products used by two age groups, people below 45 and people above 45, to assess their differences and identify how to target the product. The older group preferred traditional materials such as wood and chrome, straightforward shapes, and luxurious styles. Younger, dynamic users preferred soft materials, with Teletubbies offered as an example, as well as soft, fluffy, colorful materials and curved, rounded forms. {{p:3}} added that sports and gaming conveyed vitality for younger users. When {{p:1}} asked whether a soft material was appropriate for a remote, {{p:3}} said the material choice would be discussed later.

### Power source
{{p:3}} compared batteries with kinetic power, explaining that kinetic energy could be generated by movement, such as picking up the remote, and that a user could shake it if it needed more power. {{p:3}} considered kinetic power high-tech and attractive, with costs not much higher than a normal battery, but {{p:1}} questioned whether a remote would be moved enough to maintain its charge. {{p:3}} said picking it up and pressing buttons should provide enough movement, and suggested combining a battery with kinetic recharging. {{p:2}} proposed solar power; {{p:3}} said it would need light, preferably sunlight, and that normal light would provide less energy than a battery. Integrating solar panels into the remote would also take up interface space. {{p:3}} considered using light from the television but said it would still consume space and would not provide the full power needed. In the discussion, {{p:2}} favored kinetic power as a backup, {{p:4}} suggested a combination, and {{p:1}} said they preferred combining the sources too. The group endorsed a battery charged by kinetic movement, with {{p:1}} comparing it to a Seiko watch. {{p:3}} acknowledged the combination would add some cost; {{p:2}} joked about buying a battery for fifty cents.

### Case shape, material, and screen
{{p:3}} described a basic square case as boring and proposed single-curve or double-curve designs. A double curve would add dimensions and, in {{p:3}}’s view, create a younger, more high-tech, dynamic look; {{p:3}} offered to draw the concept in three dimensions. {{p:3}} said designers need not stick to a standard shape, because a deeper or more varied back would leave more room for creativity. For case material, {{p:3}} preferred rubber over plastic because it felt soft, while associating plastic with a cheap feel. {{p:1}} connected softness with younger users. The participants supported rubber, while {{p:2}} cautioned that it should remain firm and not be bendable; {{p:3}} said the chipset would hold it in place, and {{p:2}} noted that it might bounce if dropped. {{p:4}} added that rubber should be fairly hard, as on regular mobile phones, both to fit market trends and to improve safety if the remote were dropped. For the screen and controls, {{p:3}} recalled that the earlier meeting had already covered traditional buttons versus an LCD and proposed leaving the decision at LCD. An LCD would require a more advanced chipset and bring additional costs, whereas traditional buttons could use a simple chipset; {{p:3}} said the LCD option should be manageable and supported choosing the advanced chipset if the group selected LCD. {{p:4}} estimated sales of ten million units and suggested that a large company in Korea or Taiwan, such as Samsung, could offer a substantial chip discount; {{p:4}} added that chips usually cost no more than one dollar. No final budget figure was set. {{p:2}} asked whether the touch screen itself had to be square. {{p:4}} said touch screens were generally square but suggested shaping the surrounding case, for example with features that cover part of the LCD, to customize the appearance.

### Marketing research and audience preferences
{{p:4}} reported that the marketing and research-and-development departments had visited Paris and Milan the previous week for trend-watching. They asked people of different ages and incomes about spending, design, and materials. For the main audience—people below 40—{{p:4}} reported a preference for fresh fruit-like colors, including green, red or strawberry red, and yellow or banana yellow, as well as spongy, soft materials. {{p:4}} said these findings were consistent with {{p:3}}’s observations. The secondary audience, people above 40, preferred dark, traditional colors and materials such as wood. After discussion about whether wood could be used for a remote, the participants considered a wooden appearance or wooden-looking case instead. {{p:4}} said the group had decided to target people below 40, so the secondary-audience findings would not apply. {{p:4}} summarized broader expectations for new remotes: they should look fancy, be technological and innovative, and be easy to use. To customize color, {{p:4}} proposed removable covers, like those used for mobile phones, giving the example of replacing a red cover with a green one. {{p:4}} also recommended rubber for market fit and drop safety, while emphasizing that it should be fairly hard. {{p:3}} observed that phones and remotes had a lot in common and mentioned having seen a phone that could be used as a remote.

### Additional feature proposals
{{p:4}} proposed reconsidering speech recognition, describing it as innovative and saying the market was calling for new technologies, but also warned that it could be very expensive. {{p:1}} gave an example of saying a command to trigger a function. {{p:4}} also suggested games such as Snake or Tetris to entertain younger users and noted a possible link between remote controls and mobile phones. {{p:1}} questioned whether people would use games while watching television; {{p:2}} said they could be useful when parents were watching a boring program, and participants also discussed taking the remote to college. {{p:4}} presented parental control with the slogan of taking parental control to a new dimension. The group discussed using a log-in or profile system, including parent and child profiles. {{p:2}} stressed that it would need to be fast: users should not have to wait twenty seconds for a log-in screen, remember a code, and navigate numerous settings when turning on the television to watch the news at eight o’clock. {{p:1}} countered that many parents would consider preventing children from seeing sex or violence on television more important than waiting an extra ten or fifteen seconds. {{p:2}} suggested a simple log-in, such as pressing one, two, or three for a profile, with children limited to children’s channels. {{p:3}} questioned whether the feature was worth the development time and resources, since it would require programming profiles. {{p:1}} said there was a significant market, noting concerns reported in magazines and on the news that children were influenced by television; {{p:1}} added that many people below 40 had young children and would want to restrict violent content. {{p:2}} proposed keeping the remote simple by making profiles an optional menu feature, so a grandparent would not have to use them. {{p:4}} said the remote should be simple when sold, with users able to install the feature personally; {{p:4}} would choose a remote with parental control if they had children. {{p:2}} raised the question of restricting programs by time as well as by channel, including violent films after ten o’clock. {{p:1}} suggested using television program guide information to block programs identified as violent, but {{p:2}} noted that someone would have to provide and maintain the program data. {{p:3}} pointed out that children could bypass the remote’s restrictions by pressing buttons on the television itself. {{p:2}} suggested that the remote could incorporate a clock and stop transmitting after a set time, but {{p:4}} noted that some televisions have buttons behind a compartment. The participants agreed that controlling access through the remote could not prevent every workaround.

### Decisions on features and interface
{{p:1}} summarized the discussion: games would be included, voice recognition would not, and parental control would be incorporated but kept uncomplicated. {{p:2}} supported placing parental control in the menu structure, while {{p:4}} described a parent-and-child log-in screen. The group discussed whether parental control should be a standard or optional feature; {{p:2}} preferred an always-available menu option that could be selected when the product was purchased, including a password or personal preference. {{p:3}} suggested separate basic and deluxe models, with a receiver in the model that included parental control, but acknowledged that this would cost more. {{p:2}} suggested limiting restrictions to selected channels and viewing times. The group’s final discussion treated parental control as included but not overly complex, while recognizing that the detailed implementation still needed work. On the main interface, {{p:2}} proposed one large touch screen with primary buttons always clearly visible, a changeable menu structure, and limited on-screen options at any one time. They advised against too many menu levels or repeated button presses, and suggested keeping teletext and other less-used functions in the menu. {{p:2}} described a one-handed form that would fit into the hand, slightly broader than remotes meant to be operated by thumb alone, with the thumb used for main buttons and the other hand for menus. They identified program buttons, volume and program controls, and a large LCD for the menu. {{p:4}} suggested a back-and-forth channel button like the one in Internet Explorer. {{p:2}} agreed it could be useful but preferred placing it in the menu, so the screen could still display it without making it a primary control. {{p:4}} illustrated the need by describing someone switching between channels two and seventeen; {{p:2}} agreed it was a good idea.

### Concept decisions and remaining interface discussion
{{p:1}} recapped the agreed direction: a battery-and-kinetic power combination; a double-curved case; rubber; a flashy, fruity color with a removable cover; a touch screen; and a menu structure with few levels that was easy to use. Parental control would be incorporated without making the product too complex, and games would be included. The group reached consensus on these points. {{p:4}} then suggested adding expert and simple views. {{p:2}} said the existing concept already provided a simple interface when the menu was not in use, with system properties and more programmable options available when selected. {{p:3}} proposed allowing advanced users to customize which buttons were included, such as adding a back-forward button for people who mainly watched two channels. The participants agreed to carry this idea to the next meeting.

### Follow-up information and next meeting
{{p:1}} shared two points from a master class attended during lunch. First, knowledge management and knowledge engineering were current topics, including sharing knowledge and learning from other companies; {{p:1}} connected this to examining how other companies handled marketing campaigns when introducing a new remote. The discussion identified benchmarking and import-export as relevant concepts. Second, {{p:1}} said a survey found that people preferred buying from one large provider rather than from companies partnering with it. {{p:1}} therefore said Real Reaction should present itself as a large, trustworthy company that could stand on its own. {{p:4}} proposed the name “R to the third power,” or “R3,” for “Real Reaction Remote.” {{p:1}} suggested a single brand and a short animation or logo when the remote was turned on, with the motto “We put fashion in electronics.” {{p:4}} said a code would also need to be entered; {{p:2}} argued that even a logo displayed for 0.5 seconds could be remembered. {{p:3}} suggested a small logo at the bottom of the LCD that could remain visible. {{p:1}} said the next meeting would start in 30 minutes and said participants could return to Paris and Milan once again. {{p:1}} identified the master class as Franz Mehler’s. For the next session, {{p:1}} said the industrial-development and user-interface teams would work together on a prototype and draw it on the SMARTboard; the marketing expert would work on product evaluation. The next meeting was in 30 minutes.","mom":"### Meeting purpose and agenda
{{p:1}} opened the conceptual design meeting for Real Reaction. The format was the same as at the previous meeting, with three presentations this time and a decision to be reached on the remote-control concepts. {{p:1}} said the concepts were in two groups: component concepts and user-interface concepts. The component package included a touch screen protected by a case to make it less breakable, with a choice between rechargeable power and replaceable batteries; the interface questions included the screen type and supplementary controls, including button placement. {{p:1}} would take notes, and the minutes would be placed in the shared folder. {{p:1}} asked {{p:3}} to begin with the component presentation. At the start, {{p:2}} reported that the laptop had problems and that there had been less time to complete the preparation.

### Component concepts: target users and styling
{{p:3}} said the component review compared products used by two age groups, people below 45 and people above 45, to assess their differences and identify how to target the product. The older group preferred traditional materials such as wood and chrome, straightforward shapes, and luxurious styles. Younger, dynamic users preferred soft materials, with Teletubbies offered as an example, as well as soft, fluffy, colorful materials and curved, rounded forms. {{p:3}} added that sports and gaming conveyed vitality for younger users. When {{p:1}} asked whether a soft material was appropriate for a remote, {{p:3}} said the material choice would be discussed later.

### Power source
{{p:3}} compared batteries with kinetic power, explaining that kinetic energy could be generated by movement, such as picking up the remote, and that a user could shake it if it needed more power. {{p:3}} considered kinetic power high-tech and attractive, with costs not much higher than a normal battery, but {{p:1}} questioned whether a remote would be moved enough to maintain its charge. {{p:3}} said picking it up and pressing buttons should provide enough movement, and suggested combining a battery with kinetic recharging. {{p:2}} proposed solar power; {{p:3}} said it would need light, preferably sunlight, and that normal light would provide less energy than a battery. Integrating solar panels into the remote would also take up interface space. {{p:3}} considered using light from the television but said it would still consume space and would not provide the full power needed. In the discussion, {{p:2}} favored kinetic power as a backup, {{p:4}} suggested a combination, and {{p:1}} said they preferred combining the sources too. The group endorsed a battery charged by kinetic movement, with {{p:1}} comparing it to a Seiko watch. {{p:3}} acknowledged the combination would add some cost; {{p:2}} joked about buying a battery for fifty cents.

### Case shape, material, and screen
{{p:3}} described a basic square case as boring and proposed single-curve or double-curve designs. A double curve would add dimensions and, in {{p:3}}’s view, create a younger, more high-tech, dynamic look; {{p:3}} offered to draw the concept in three dimensions. {{p:3}} said designers need not stick to a standard shape, because a deeper or more varied back would leave more room for creativity. For case material, {{p:3}} preferred rubber over plastic because it felt soft, while associating plastic with a cheap feel. {{p:1}} connected softness with younger users. The participants supported rubber, while {{p:2}} cautioned that it should remain firm and not be bendable; {{p:3}} said the chipset would hold it in place, and {{p:2}} noted that it might bounce if dropped. {{p:4}} added that rubber should be fairly hard, as on regular mobile phones, both to fit market trends and to improve safety if the remote were dropped. For the screen and controls, {{p:3}} recalled that the earlier meeting had already covered traditional buttons versus an LCD and proposed leaving the decision at LCD. An LCD would require a more advanced chipset and bring additional costs, whereas traditional buttons could use a simple chipset; {{p:3}} said the LCD option should be manageable and supported choosing the advanced chipset if the group selected LCD. {{p:4}} estimated sales of ten million units and suggested that a large company in Korea or Taiwan, such as Samsung, could offer a substantial chip discount; {{p:4}} added that chips usually cost no more than one dollar. No final budget figure was set. {{p:2}} asked whether the touch screen itself had to be square. {{p:4}} said touch screens were generally square but suggested shaping the surrounding case, for example with features that cover part of the LCD, to customize the appearance.

### Marketing research and audience preferences
{{p:4}} reported that the marketing and research-and-development departments had visited Paris and Milan the previous week for trend-watching. They asked people of different ages and incomes about spending, design, and materials. For the main audience—people below 40—{{p:4}} reported a preference for fresh fruit-like colors, including green, red or strawberry red, and yellow or banana yellow, as well as spongy, soft materials. {{p:4}} said these findings were consistent with {{p:3}}’s observations. The secondary audience, people above 40, preferred dark, traditional colors and materials such as wood. After discussion about whether wood could be used for a remote, the participants considered a wooden appearance or wooden-looking case instead. {{p:4}} said the group had decided to target people below 40, so the secondary-audience findings would not apply. {{p:4}} summarized broader expectations for new remotes: they should look fancy, be technological and innovative, and be easy to use. To customize color, {{p:4}} proposed removable covers, like those used for mobile phones, giving the example of replacing a red cover with a green one. {{p:4}} also recommended rubber for market fit and drop safety, while emphasizing that it should be fairly hard. {{p:3}} observed that phones and remotes had a lot in common and mentioned having seen a phone that could be used as a remote.

### Additional feature proposals
{{p:4}} proposed reconsidering speech recognition, describing it as innovative and saying the market was calling for new technologies, but also warned that it could be very expensive. {{p:1}} gave an example of saying a command to trigger a function. {{p:4}} also suggested games such as Snake or Tetris to entertain younger users and noted a possible link between remote controls and mobile phones. {{p:1}} questioned whether people would use games while watching television; {{p:2}} said they could be useful when parents were watching a boring program, and participants also discussed taking the remote to college. {{p:4}} presented parental control with the slogan of taking parental control to a new dimension. The group discussed using a log-in or profile system, including parent and child profiles. {{p:2}} stressed that it would need to be fast: users should not have to wait twenty seconds for a log-in screen, remember a code, and navigate numerous settings when turning on the television to watch the news at eight o’clock. {{p:1}} countered that many parents would consider preventing children from seeing sex or violence on television more important than waiting an extra ten or fifteen seconds. {{p:2}} suggested a simple log-in, such as pressing one, two, or three for a profile, with children limited to children’s channels. {{p:3}} questioned whether the feature was worth the development time and resources, since it would require programming profiles. {{p:1}} said there was a significant market, noting concerns reported in magazines and on the news that children were influenced by television; {{p:1}} added that many people below 40 had young children and would want to restrict violent content. {{p:2}} proposed keeping the remote simple by making profiles an optional menu feature, so a grandparent would not have to use them. {{p:4}} said the remote should be simple when sold, with users able to install the feature personally; {{p:4}} would choose a remote with parental control if they had children. {{p:2}} raised the question of restricting programs by time as well as by channel, including violent films after ten o’clock. {{p:1}} suggested using television program guide information to block programs identified as violent, but {{p:2}} noted that someone would have to provide and maintain the program data. {{p:3}} pointed out that children could bypass the remote’s restrictions by pressing buttons on the television itself. {{p:2}} suggested that the remote could incorporate a clock and stop transmitting after a set time, but {{p:4}} noted that some televisions have buttons behind a compartment. The participants agreed that controlling access through the remote could not prevent every workaround.

### Decisions on features and interface
{{p:1}} summarized the discussion: games would be included, voice recognition would not, and parental control would be incorporated but kept uncomplicated. {{p:2}} supported placing parental control in the menu structure, while {{p:4}} described a parent-and-child log-in screen. The group discussed whether parental control should be a standard or optional feature; {{p:2}} preferred an always-available menu option that could be selected when the product was purchased, including a password or personal preference. {{p:3}} suggested separate basic and deluxe models, with a receiver in the model that included parental control, but acknowledged that this would cost more. {{p:2}} suggested limiting restrictions to selected channels and viewing times. The group’s final discussion treated parental control as included but not overly complex, while recognizing that the detailed implementation still needed work. On the main interface, {{p:2}} proposed one large touch screen with primary buttons always clearly visible, a changeable menu structure, and limited on-screen options at any one time. They advised against too many menu levels or repeated button presses, and suggested keeping teletext and other less-used functions in the menu. {{p:2}} described a one-handed form that would fit into the hand, slightly broader than remotes meant to be operated by thumb alone, with the thumb used for main buttons and the other hand for menus. They identified program buttons, volume and program controls, and a large LCD for the menu. {{p:4}} suggested a back-and-forth channel button like the one in Internet Explorer. {{p:2}} agreed it could be useful but preferred placing it in the menu, so the screen could still display it without making it a primary control. {{p:4}} illustrated the need by describing someone switching between channels two and seventeen; {{p:2}} agreed it was a good idea.

### Concept decisions and remaining interface discussion
{{p:1}} recapped the agreed direction: a battery-and-kinetic power combination; a double-curved case; rubber; a flashy, fruity color with a removable cover; a touch screen; and a menu structure with few levels that was easy to use. Parental control would be incorporated without making the product too complex, and games would be included. The group reached consensus on these points. {{p:4}} then suggested adding expert and simple views. {{p:2}} said the existing concept already provided a simple interface when the menu was not in use, with system properties and more programmable options available when selected. {{p:3}} proposed allowing advanced users to customize which buttons were included, such as adding a back-forward button for people who mainly watched two channels. The participants agreed to carry this idea to the next meeting.

### Follow-up information and next meeting
{{p:1}} shared two points from a master class attended during lunch. First, knowledge management and knowledge engineering were current topics, including sharing knowledge and learning from other companies; {{p:1}} connected this to examining how other companies handled marketing campaigns when introducing a new remote. The discussion identified benchmarking and import-export as relevant concepts. Second, {{p:1}} said a survey found that people preferred buying from one large provider rather than from companies partnering with it. {{p:1}} therefore said Real Reaction should present itself as a large, trustworthy company that could stand on its own. {{p:4}} proposed the name “R to the third power,” or “R3,” for “Real Reaction Remote.” {{p:1}} suggested a single brand and a short animation or logo when the remote was turned on, with the motto “We put fashion in electronics.” {{p:4}} said a code would also need to be entered; {{p:2}} argued that even a logo displayed for 0.5 seconds could be remembered. {{p:3}} suggested a small logo at the bottom of the LCD that could remain visible. {{p:1}} said the next meeting would start in 30 minutes and said participants could return to Paris and Milan once again. {{p:1}} identified the master class as Franz Mehler’s. For the next session, {{p:1}} said the industrial-development and user-interface teams would work together on a prototype and draw it on the SMARTboard; the marketing expert would work on product evaluation. The prototype was a single-touch-screen remote designed for one-handed use by either hand, with thumb-accessible primary buttons, a menu for the other hand, an LCD, customizable profiles, a curved overlay, rubber layers, and shaped bumps intended to improve balance and give a youthful, dynamic appearance; the bumps could accommodate electronics and help keep the device stable on a table. The group discussed a standard white or metallic-grey finish versus youthful fruity colors and optional covers; {{p:1}} cited a survey in Milan and Paris indicating older users were more willing to pay for extras, and the group considered a standard restrained fruity color with removable colorful covers and a wood-style cover as an add-on. {{p:4}} led a consensus-based seven-point evaluation of the prototype against prior user requirements and trend analysis; ratings discussed included 1 for age suitability, 1 for beauty, 3 for appeal across age groups, 3 for a fancy appearance, and 4–6 for teletext-button clarity, with volume buttons judged important and teletext located in a menu. The group also considered ease of finding the remote, freshness of its colors, soft rubber material, ease of use, big clear channel buttons, innovation, speech recognition, built-in games, and parental-advisory functions; the transcript records ratings including 2 for ease of use and 1 for innovation, while other ratings were debated rather than consistently resolved. For production costs, {{p:1}} set a €12.50 ceiling: the initial component estimate reached €11 before all costs were accounted for, and the team found it was €4 over budget; they therefore agreed to redesign the double-curved body as single-curved, with a flat back, to bring the estimate to €12.50, while keeping the appearance and core features in view. They discussed battery power and kinetic energy, but the kinetic option would raise the cost to €13.50 and require a flat design; {{p:1}} favored the single-curve compromise, and the group treated the kinetic feature as a possible promotion or cost-reduction alternative rather than settling on it. In the project retrospective, participants said the first meeting was poorly structured and constrained by fixed information, while later meetings produced better consensus; they also praised the design work’s creative freedom and noted that the SMARTboard digital pen was slow, imprecise, difficult to use, and had an oversized eraser. The group suggested improving the software with faster operation, easier handwriting and text entry, shape tools, image insertion, and a simple voting or group-decision application; {{p:1}} noted that the end report still needed completion, and {{p:4}} said ten minutes remained at one point and later noted five minutes for finishing."}

{"mom":"### Meeting agenda and prototype presentation
{{p:1}} took the minutes and said there would be no presentation from them. The agenda was a prototype presentation by two presenters, followed by an evaluation and completion of an Excel file received in connection with finance. The team needed to check whether costs stayed below €12.50; the evaluation would require substantial calculation time. A process evaluation would follow, covering how the team had worked with the SMARTboard, laptops, and other tools. {{p:1}} said the meeting would take 40 minutes and then invited the presenters to begin.

### Prototype design and features
{{p:2}} and {{p:3}} presented a first concept for a single-touchscreen remote. They described its form, button placement, and menu structure, aiming for a shape that could be held in either the left or right hand, with reduced thickness and an artistic element. Buttons on top would be usable by the thumb, while the menu could be operated with the other hand; the design should remain accessible to either hand. The basic remote would have an LCD screen and main buttons, with users able to change buttons later through their profiles; an advanced menu and submenus were also proposed. The back view included two raised contours intended to give the design a youthful, dynamic appearance and artistic character, help it sit stably on a table without rolling, and make it sit comfortably in the hand. Additional electronics could be housed in the raised areas, allowing a thinner central grip. The team discussed rubber layers to create a fluid, rounded surface over the panel. {{p:2}} said the maximum thickness for holding the device was 1.5 centimetres, leaving room for a battery and possibly other electronic chips; wiring and the touchscreen layer could keep the middle as thin as possible for grip.

{{p:3}} said the concept should be a more adult version of a children’s remote control, which {{p:1}} identified as a Weemote. The proposed initial colors included white or metallic grey, described as technological colors. {{p:2}} recommended interchangeable covers to appeal to different buyers: younger users might choose orange, red, blue, or purple covers, while older buyers might prefer white. {{p:4}} suggested selling the remote without a cover so customers could choose one in the shop; {{p:2}} responded that a cheap standard cover, perhaps white, would be needed to avoid exposing the LCD screen, with additional covers providing an extra source of revenue. {{p:1}} emphasized that the target was younger people and recalled a survey from Milan and Paris indicating older people were more willing to spend on extra features. {{p:1}} therefore favored flashy, fruity colors as standard and more traditional or luxurious finishes as paid extras; {{p:3}} agreed that this sounded logical. {{p:4}} suggested a wood-style cover for older users, and the group discussed a palette including wood-style and white covers plus a few restrained, hip fruit colors such as banana and mango. The standard color should be attractive and somewhat flashy but not overly bright. The team also considered whether the buttons should be standard, and agreed that something like the shown button arrangement would work.

### Evaluation method and design criteria
{{p:4}} began evaluating the prototype against requirements and trend analysis established during the design life cycle, using a seven-point scale. {{p:4}} said judgments should be made by consensus as group decisions. The first criterion was whether the remote was designed for people under 40. Participants noted that the design was also intended for people over 40, so the group settled around 3 rather than 1; {{p:2}} said it would primarily appeal to people under 40 but could appeal to older users too. For the criterion that the remote was beautiful, participants considered a low score, with {{p:2}} and {{p:3}} agreeing that the marketing angle was relevant. For whether it looked fancy, the group discussed a score of 3. The team agreed that the channel-switching buttons were big and clear. They judged the claim that the remote had teletext buttons false because teletext was in the menu, while volume buttons were present and important. They considered how findable the remote would be if lost under a bed or around the house: its fruity colors and unusual shape might make it stand out, but participants differed on how much difference this would make. {{p:1}} suggested that it could glow in the dark; the group discussed scores around 4 and 5. For the claim that the remote was made of soft material, they noted that it would use rubber, but should not be too soft, and gave a score of 3. On ease of use, participants said the design was not the easiest to use: primary buttons would remain visible, but adding many buttons could compromise functionality and the intended appearance. They settled on a score of 2. The group also evaluated innovation: they considered the removable feature and built-in games, while confirming that speech recognition was not included. They discussed the parental advisory function and proceeded to calculate the evaluation results.

### Production-cost calculation and redesign
{{p:1}} said the team needed to calculate production costs and could proceed with project evaluation if costs were under €12.50; otherwise, a redesign would be required. The group began listing components and amounts: a hand dynamo was not included and was assigned zero; a battery and kinetic mechanism were each counted as one; solar cells were zero; the advanced chip was discussed at €3, with disagreement over whether it was one component or several; and the sample sensor and speaker were not included. The team also discussed whether the device was flat or curved, concluding that its form was double-curved at that point. When the running total reached €11, {{p:1}} noted there was still a budget problem and {{p:3}} said they should continue to see how far over budget they were. They found they were €4 over budget. {{p:3}} proposed making the casing single-curved or uncurved; {{p:1}} also suggested removing the kinetic feature, noting that it required shaking and was not very innovative. The group discussed replacing it with a good battery, and {{p:4}} proposed selling rechargeable batteries, covers, and a docking station separately. {{p:2}} observed that rechargeable batteries could already be used, but would need to be recharged manually; {{p:1}} said omitting the kinetic feature could reduce costs. The team considered moving from a double-curved design to a single curve, flattening the back, and retaining the main design look. They also discussed using a regular chip rather than an advanced chip. {{p:1}} said the revised option would bring the cost to €12.50, the budget limit. Participants noted that wood was cheaper than rubber, contrary to their earlier expectation that it would be more expensive. The team treated the kinetic feature as a possible marketing promotion, though it would take the cost to €13.50 and require a flatter design; they decided the single-curve compromise was preferable. {{p:3}} noted that titanium could not use double curves. The discussion concluded with a single-curved design rather than a double-curved one.

### Project process, teamwork, and SMARTboard feedback
{{p:1}} asked whether there had been room for creativity in group or individual meetings. {{p:4}} said there had not been much room, mainly because the team had received fixed information and was expected to work from it, without searching independently online. {{p:3}} said {{p:4}} and {{p:2}} had less creative roles, while {{p:3}} and Jeroen had more design freedom. {{p:2}} said their role did allow creativity, including the possibility of selecting a remote design. On leadership, {{p:4}} called the first meeting somewhat unstructured and said it could have been organized better; they had spoken for much of that meeting. {{p:1}} agreed and said they too had been dissatisfied with the first meeting. {{p:3}} said the later meetings improved and produced good decisions through more consensus; {{p:2}} also described them as more constructive. The group said teamwork went well, while noting that members worked together on the project but each had their own task. {{p:3}} said their pair had some trouble with the digital pen. Participants found the pen difficult to use: it took time to draw or write, was not precise, and required adapting to the technology. {{p:2}} said writing with a normal pen and scanning the page would be simpler; the SMARTboard concept was good, but the pen did not work properly and added little value. {{p:1}} likewise said the SMARTboard was useful but the pen was not user-friendly. They also mentioned that the eraser was large and made erasing lines difficult. The group noted that the SMARTboard’s functionality existed but was not ideal and took too much time; for a larger group, participants might have only two minutes each to present their case, making advance preparation in PowerPoint and use of a flip-board for quick drawings more practical. {{p:4}} suggested a decision or voting application for group evaluations, allowing people to enter scores from 1 to 7. {{p:1}} supported a voting mechanism. {{p:3}} cautioned that individual voting could reduce discussion, while {{p:4}} said the group could still discuss scores and that processing the results digitally would be easier. They also considered one person entering a score while the rest discussed it.

### Evaluation results and final report
{{p:4}} reported that the mean evaluation score was 1.86 and considered that fairly good; {{p:1}} said the requirements averaged between 1 and 2, or very true. {{p:2}} said the software concept was acceptable but needed improvement: it was slow, opened a program that nearly locked up the computer, and took too long, so users would prefer to write quickly on a page rather than download and save their work. They wanted a more user-friendly process, such as writing on a screen and having the result placed elsewhere without adapting to the technology. {{p:2}} said users had to keep in mind that they were drawing on the screen, calling this a poor concept, though {{p:4}} considered it better than regular flip-overs because it could be saved more easily. Participants suggested adding text entry, circles and squares, and the ability to insert pictures; {{p:4}} mentioned scanner images and clip art, and {{p:3}} said a text function would be excellent. {{p:1}} said some predefined shapes were already available.

{{p:1}} said the project costs were within budget and the project had been evaluated, but an end report still had to be completed. The report would summarize the meetings and decisions made; {{p:1}} was working on it and suggested reviewing it together. {{p:4}} noted there were 10 minutes left to finish the report, and later said there were 5 minutes left for finishing. The report was described as about 75 pages and read-only at that stage; {{p:4}} suggested saving it under another name. {{p:1}} said it covered the functional design and needed the correct role labels, including Management Expert and Marketing Expert. The final design summary covered the most-used functions that should be immediately visible on the remote, the requirement that it be simple and clear to use, and its younger target users. {{p:4}} said channel switching should be at the top because it was the most-used function, with teletext second and volume changing also noted. The group discussed the order of functions and the conceptual design. {{p:1}} summarized the decisions, including batteries as the energy source, a single-curved form, rubber, fruity colors, removable covers, and buttons; {{p:3}} clarified that the final form was no longer double-curved. The added functions included Tetris and Snake under parental control, along with the touchscreen. The group discussed whether the added functions were included in the cost; {{p:4}} said parental control could be developed internally, though it would still have some cost. {{p:1}} said this could be discussed with the board of directors at Real Reaction. {"summary":"{{p:1}} opened the meeting by assigning minutes and setting a 40-minute agenda: a prototype presentation by {{p:2}} and {{p:3}}, an evaluation against criteria and completion of a finance Excel file, a process review, and a close. The team needed to check whether production costs stayed below €12.50; the evaluation would require substantial calculation time. The prototype was a single-touch-screen remote designed for one-handed use by either hand, with thumb-accessible primary buttons and a menu operated with the other hand. It included an LCD, customizable profiles, a curved overlay, rubber layers, and two raised contours intended to improve grip and stability, prevent rolling, create a youthful and dynamic look, and house electronics. Maximum holding thickness was discussed as 1.5 centimetres. The presenters described the concept as a more adult version of a children’s Weemote remote. Color discussion covered standard white or metallic grey, youthful fruity colors, and interchangeable optional covers. {{p:1}} cited a survey in Milan and Paris indicating older users were more willing to pay for extras; the group favored a restrained fruity standard color, with removable covers including white and wood-style finishes as possible add-ons. The standard button arrangement was considered suitable.

{{p:4}} led a consensus-based seven-point evaluation of the prototype against prior user requirements and trend analysis. The age-under-40 criterion was discussed as roughly 3 because the design could also appeal to older people. Beauty was rated around 1, and fancy appearance was discussed as 3. Channel-switching buttons were judged big and clear; teletext was in a menu rather than a dedicated button, while volume buttons were present and important. Teletext-button clarity was debated around 5–6. The group considered whether the remote would be easy to find, including its unusual shape and fruity colors; {{p:1}} suggested glow-in-the-dark material, and scores around 4–5 were discussed. The rubber was considered somewhat soft but not too soft, with a score of 3. Ease of use was rated 2, balancing visible primary buttons against the risk that more buttons would compromise functionality and appearance. Innovation was rated 1; removable features and games were discussed, while speech recognition was not included. The group also considered parental advisory functions and built-in games, then calculated an overall mean of 1.86, described as fairly good; {{p:1}} said the requirements averaged between 1 and 2, or very true.

For the production-cost calculation, {{p:1}} set a €12.50 ceiling. The estimate reached €11 before all costs were accounted for, and the team found it was €4 over budget. Components discussed included a battery and kinetic mechanism (one each), no hand dynamo or solar cells, and an advanced chip estimated at €3; sensor and speaker components were excluded. The team agreed to redesign the double-curved body as single-curved, with a flat back, bringing the estimate to €12.50 while retaining the main look and core features. A regular chip and changes to the casing were discussed. Kinetic energy would raise the cost to €13.50 and require a flat design; {{p:1}} favored the single-curve compromise, while participants treated kinetic power as a possible promotional feature or cost-reduction alternative rather than the selected design. They also discussed rechargeable batteries, separately sold covers and a docking station, and noted wood was cheaper than rubber. {{p:3}} noted titanium could not use double curves.

In the project retrospective, participants said the first meeting was poorly structured and constrained by fixed information, while later meetings were more constructive and produced better consensus. They described teamwork as going well, with members collaborating while each held a separate task; some participants had less creative roles, while the design work allowed more creative freedom. The SMARTboard’s digital pen was slow, imprecise, difficult to use, and required adaptation; its oversized eraser made erasing difficult. Participants suggested faster software, easier handwriting and text entry, shape tools, image insertion, and a simple voting or group-decision application supporting scores from 1 to 7. They noted voting might reduce discussion, and discussed having one person enter a score while the rest deliberated.

{{p:1}} said the project was within budget and evaluated, but an end report still needed completion. It would summarize the meetings and decisions; {{p:1}} was working on it and proposed reviewing it together. {{p:4}} said ten minutes remained at one point and later said five minutes remained for finishing. The report was about 75 pages and read-only at that stage; {{p:4}} suggested saving it under another name. It covered functional design and needed correct role labels, including Management Expert and Marketing Expert. The final design summary described the most-used functions as immediately visible, the remote as simple and clear to use, and its target as younger users. {{p:4}} said channel switching should be at the top, with teletext and volume changing also noted. The design summary included batteries, a single-curved form, rubber, fruity colors, removable covers, buttons, a touchscreen, and Tetris and Snake under parental control. Participants noted the added functions had some development cost; {{p:4}} said parental control could be developed internally, and {{p:1}} said this could be discussed with Real Reaction’s board of directors. The meeting was declared finished after the end-report review.","mom":"### Meeting agenda and prototype presentation
{{p:1}} took the minutes, said they would not present, and set a 40-minute agenda: a prototype presentation by {{p:2}} and {{p:3}}, an evaluation against criteria and completion of an Excel file received in connection with finance, a process evaluation of the SMARTboard, laptops, and other tools, and a close. The team needed to check whether costs stayed below €12.50; {{p:1}} said the evaluation would require substantial calculation time and then invited the presenters to begin.

### Prototype design and features
{{p:2}} and {{p:3}} presented their first concept for a single-touchscreen remote. They described its form, button placement, and menu structure, aiming for a shape that could be held in either the left or right hand and would be less thick while still having an artistic element. Buttons on top would be usable by the thumb, while the menu could be operated with the other hand; the design should remain accessible to either hand. The basic remote would have an LCD screen and main buttons, which users could later change through profiles; an advanced menu and submenus were also proposed. The back view included two raised contours intended to give the design a youthful, dynamic appearance and artistic character, help it sit stably on a table without rolling, and make it sit comfortably in the hand. The raised areas could house electronics and allow a thinner central grip. The team discussed rubber layers to create a fluid, rounded surface over the panel. {{p:2}} said the maximum thickness for holding the device was 1.5 centimetres, leaving room for a battery and possibly other electronic chips; wiring and the touchscreen layer could keep the middle as thin as possible for grip.

{{p:3}} called the concept a more adult version of a children’s remote control, which {{p:1}} identified as a Weemote. The proposed initial colors included white or metallic grey, described as technological colors. {{p:2}} recommended interchangeable covers to appeal to different buyers: younger users might choose orange, red, blue, or purple, while older buyers might prefer white. {{p:4}} suggested selling the remote without a cover so customers could choose one in the shop. {{p:2}} responded that a cheap standard cover, perhaps white, would be needed to avoid exposing the LCD screen, while additional covers could provide extra revenue. {{p:1}} emphasized that the target was younger people and cited a survey from Milan and Paris indicating older users were more willing to spend on extra features. {{p:1}} therefore favored flashy, fruity colors as standard and more traditional or luxurious finishes as paid extras; {{p:3}} agreed this sounded logical. {{p:4}} suggested a wood-style cover for older users. The group discussed wood-style and white covers plus a few restrained, hip fruit colors such as banana and mango; the standard color should be attractive and somewhat flashy but not overly bright. They also considered whether the buttons should be standard and agreed that something like the shown button arrangement would work.

### Evaluation method and design criteria
{{p:4}} began evaluating the prototype against requirements and trend analysis established during the design life cycle, using a seven-point scale. {{p:4}} said judgments should be made by consensus as group decisions. The first criterion was whether the remote was designed for people under 40. Participants noted it was also intended for people over 40, so the group settled around 3 rather than 1; {{p:2}} said it would primarily appeal to people under 40 but could appeal to older users too. The beauty criterion was discussed around 1, with participants noting the marketing angle. For whether it looked fancy, the group discussed a score of 3. The team agreed that channel-switching buttons were big and clear. They judged the claim that the remote had teletext buttons false because teletext was in the menu, while volume buttons were present and important. The group debated teletext-button clarity, with scores around 5–6 discussed.

For ease of finding the remote if lost under a bed or elsewhere in the house, participants said the fruity colors and unusual shape might make it stand out, but differed over how much difference this would make. {{p:1}} suggested it could glow in the dark; scores around 4 and 5 were discussed. For the soft-material criterion, they noted that the remote would use rubber but should not be too soft, and gave a score of 3. Participants said the design was not the easiest to use: primary buttons would remain visible, but adding many buttons could compromise functionality and the intended appearance. They settled on 2. The group considered innovation, including the removable feature and built-in games, while confirming speech recognition was not included; the innovation score was 1. They also discussed parental advisory functions and calculated the results. {{p:4}} reported a mean score of 1.86 and considered it fairly good; {{p:1}} said the requirements averaged between 1 and 2, or very true.

### Production-cost calculation and redesign
{{p:1}} said the team needed to calculate production costs and could proceed with project evaluation if costs were under €12.50; otherwise, a redesign would be required. The group listed components and amounts: no hand dynamo (zero), one battery, one kinetic mechanism, no solar cells, and an advanced chip discussed at €3, with disagreement over whether it was one component or several. The sample sensor and speaker were not included. The team also discussed whether the device was flat or curved, concluding that the current form was double-curved. When the running total reached €11, {{p:1}} noted there was still a budget problem and {{p:3}} said to continue to see how far over budget they were. They found they were €4 over budget.

{{p:3}} proposed making the casing single-curved or uncurved. {{p:1}} suggested removing the kinetic feature, noting that it required shaking and was not very innovative. The group discussed replacing it with a good battery, and {{p:4}} proposed selling rechargeable batteries, covers, and a docking station separately. {{p:2}} observed that rechargeable batteries could already be used but would need to be recharged manually; {{p:1}} said omitting kinetic power could reduce costs. The team considered moving from a double-curved design to a single curve, flattening the back, and retaining the main design look; they also discussed using a regular chip rather than an advanced chip. {{p:1}} said the revised option would bring the cost to €12.50, the budget limit. Participants noted that wood was cheaper than rubber, contrary to their earlier expectation that wood would cost more. They considered kinetic power as a possible marketing promotion, but it would bring the cost to €13.50 and require a flat design. {{p:1}} favored the single-curve compromise. {{p:3}} noted that titanium could not use double curves. The discussion concluded with a single-curved design rather than a double-curved one.

### Project process, teamwork, and SMARTboard feedback
{{p:1}} asked whether there had been room for creativity in group or individual meetings. {{p:4}} said there had not been much room, mainly because the team received fixed information and was expected to work from it without searching independently online. {{p:3}} said {{p:4}} and {{p:2}} had less creative roles, while {{p:3}} and Jeroen had more design freedom. {{p:2}} said their role did allow creativity, including selecting a remote design. On leadership, {{p:4}} called the first meeting somewhat unstructured and said it could have been organized better; {{p:4}} had spoken for much of that meeting. {{p:1}} agreed and said they too had been dissatisfied with the first meeting. {{p:3}} said later meetings improved and produced good decisions through more consensus; {{p:2}} described them as more constructive. The group said teamwork went well, while noting that members worked together on the project but each had their own task. {{p:3}} said their pair had trouble with the digital pen. Participants found the pen difficult to use: drawing and writing took time, it was imprecise, and users had to adapt to the technology. {{p:2}} said writing with a normal pen and scanning the page would be simpler; the SMARTboard concept was good, but the pen did not work properly and added little value. {{p:1}} likewise said the SMARTboard was useful but the pen was not user-friendly. They also mentioned that the eraser was large and made erasing lines difficult.

The group said the SMARTboard’s functionality existed but was not ideal and took too much time. {{p:1}} noted that in a larger group, participants might have only two minutes each to present their case, making advance preparation in PowerPoint and use of a flip-board for quick drawings more practical. {{p:4}} suggested a decision or voting application for group evaluations, allowing people to enter scores from 1 to 7; {{p:1}} supported a voting mechanism. {{p:3}} cautioned that individual voting could reduce discussion, while {{p:4}} said the group could still discuss scores and that processing results digitally would be easier. They also considered having one person enter a score while the rest discussed it.

### Evaluation results and final report
{{p:2}} said the software concept was acceptable but needed improvement: it was slow, opened a program that nearly locked up the computer, and took too long, so users would prefer to write quickly on a page rather than download and save their work. They wanted a more user-friendly process, such as writing on a screen and having the result placed elsewhere without needing to adapt to the technology. {{p:2}} said users had to keep in mind that they were drawing on the screen, calling this a poor concept, though {{p:4}} considered it better than regular flip-overs because it could be saved more easily. Participants suggested adding text entry, circles and squares, and the ability to insert pictures; {{p:4}} mentioned scanner images and clip art, and {{p:3}} said a text function would be excellent. {{p:1}} said some predefined shapes were already available.

{{p:1}} said the project costs were within budget and the project had been evaluated, but an end report still had to be completed. The report would summarize the meetings and decisions; {{p:1}} was working on it and suggested reviewing it together. {{p:4}} said ten minutes remained to finish the report and later said five minutes remained for finishing. The report was about 75 pages and read-only at that stage; {{p:4}} suggested saving it under another name. {{p:1}} said it covered functional design and needed the correct role labels, including Management Expert and Marketing Expert.

The final design summary covered the most-used functions that should be immediately visible, the requirement that the remote be simple and clear to use, and its younger target users. {{p:4}} said channel switching should be at the top because it was the most-used function, with teletext and volume changing also noted. The group discussed the order of functions and conceptual design. {{p:1}} summarized the decisions, including batteries as the energy source, a single-curved form, rubber, fruity colors, removable covers, and buttons; {{p:3}} clarified that the final form was no longer double-curved. Added functions included Tetris and Snake under parental control, along with the touchscreen. Participants asked whether these added functions were included in the cost. {{p:4}} said parental control could be developed internally, though it would still have some cost; {{p:1}} said this could be discussed with Real Reaction’s board of directors.
